title: Exploring Art, Understanding Culture
description: This course will help students develop conceptual frameworks for exploring the arts as cultural practice and aesthetic experience. Concepts and issues in the study of expressive cultures will be introduced by drawing on periods, movements, genres and traditions from different world art cultures. The course will interweave experiential and analytical learning with socio-historic and critical interpretations, drawing on a variety of examples. Thematic units in the course include a consideration of art as experience; sensing, perceiving and feeling as cultural praxis; meaning making; social organization of cultural practices; power, identity and the politics of representation. Examples could be drawn from ancient, medieval, pre-modern, postcolonial and contemporary periods. Throughout the course, students will be encouraged to apply conceptual learnings to a cultural practice of their choice, giving them an opportunity to deepen their learnings from the course through immersive experience.

title: Pathways in the Arts
description:
This course will introduce the students to the wide array of
 possibilities and opportunities offered by the arts as a discipline
 beyond practice. The field of art writing and criticism is
 undergoing interesting experimentation in recent times with
 several critics and writers taking recourse to new creative forms
 in writing on art. Similarly, the arts are sustained by an interlinked
 scaffolding of supporters and allies, as can be seen in arts
 management, grant making, conservation, curation, advocacy,
 activism, journalism and scholarship. Practitioners in each of
 these fields, often called mediators or translators of the arts, help
 in the dissemination, perception, transaction, and value-creation
 of arts. In other words, they form the ecosystem within which art
 can thrive. In this course, students will learn how such mediators
 have engaged with the arts through a series of seminars, talks,
 and discussions. Through separate writing workshop modules and
 working groups, students will acquire basic skills in some of these
 practices. The course aims to instill students with a curiosity to
 explore future pathways into the arts, encouraging the use of
 their interdisciplinary skills and knowledge and expanding the
 horizon of the arts beyond professional practice into everyday
 life. This course is best augmented with the Performance
 practicum course offered as well as electives focussed in some of
 these practices.
 Learning Outcomes
 1. Introduction to various practices of mediation and
 engagement with the arts.
 2. Acquiring some basic understanding and working
 knowledge of some of these practices,
 eg. writing, curation, activism etc.
 3. Enabling future interdisciplinary pathways into the arts.

title: Art Technologies and Design
description:
Art Technologies and Design is an art technologies course introducing technical skills and proficiencies that equip students to participate in the ever-growing digital and multidisciplinary arts practices. We will discuss current trends in the fields of digital media design, sound art and communication. The course will focus on the philosophy of sound and listening, introducing students to industry-valued production practices in sound design for film and experimental mediums. The course will encourage learners to collaborate and innovate, based on their interests 
and experiment with professional technologies, be it hardware equipment or software. Through small-scale projects students will learn methods of recording sounds, manipulating them and stitching audio-visual narratives. Students interested in music will also be able to understand how to strike the right balance between sound design and backgrounds score in narratives. The three focal elements of the course are:
1) Introduce students to multidisciplinary forms in art and technology, with a focus on philosophy of sound and listening
2) Enable students with preliminary skills needed to handle the technical side of audio production
3) Encourage collaboration between students having different interests (for example between animators and sound designers, or photographers and musicians) and move towardsfuturistic,immersive art design projects.
Classes will involve practical and immersive tech sessions, interactions with industry
professionals and exploration of global immersive art scene in the pre and post-internet era.
Topics like phenomenology of sound, interdisciplinary approaches to art-technology, multimodal
documentation techniques and communication will be explored.

title: Performance Practicum - “This is how we Perform Today”
description:
The journey of performing traditions (dance, music and theatrical performances) into the 20th century is pregnant with its immediate cultural memory. This course will focus on embodied learnings of some of the traditions that have been altered because of the post-colonial censuring that led to a normative establishment of artistic traditions as “classical” and “folk”. Through the course, students will encounter art practices such as Lavani, Gujjili poetry, Karakattam/Kattai Koothu, Raaja paat or  Stri Paat theatre performance and Reality show performances. Through media- embodiment, we will gain foundational knowledge of these forms even as we draw attention to notions of “purity” and “honour” attached to artistic traditions that affect the way we have inherited them. The course uses corporeality in practice as a tool to encounter the socio-political and economic lives of the artistes who practice these arts.
The course does not require the student to have prior knowledge in any art form, but must be willing to participate in class practicums. Grading will be commensurate with willingness and enthusiasm to experiment and learn, rather than expertise in practice. This course is meant to offer further insights towards the Pathways in the Arts course by way of lending an experiential understanding of artistic traditions. The classes will be a mix of embodied learnings (music, dance and theatre forms), video footage viewings and some discussions on performative traditions.
Learning Outcome
Students will learn a range of performative forms, in practice
Students will learn to pause and analyse the nuances of technique in footwork, movements, dialogue delivery and rhythms in each section
They will develop a language of movements  and also learn of the history and politics of embodied performance

title: The Creative Economy
description: Understanding the creative economy, new business models for the 21st century given the digital economy, practical business concepts applicable to a value creator, culminating in a business pitch exercise for creative economy ideas to real-time investors

title: Music from Mud: Pottery Practicum
description:
Clay working, instrument making, rhythm, and music have been part of human craft and culture since even before the formation of civil societies. From China to Peru, in every ancient culture around the world, clay flutes or ocarinas, clay horns or water whistles, or some other form of musical instrument, have all used the innate resonant quality of fired clay or the space that it contains, to produce musical notes and specific sounds.
This practical, hands-on course will start off by introducing students to the basic techniques of working with clay and making hollow forms by hand. Once students have a grasp of the fundamentals, they will explore and create musical instruments, as well as forms that amplify sound, both in the fired as well as the unfired stage of the clay. 
As a complement to hands-on work with clay, students will also study some of the forms and simple instruments in a range of ancient as well as modern cultures around the world through readings, research, videos, and guest lectures.
By the end of the course, students will be encouraged to experiment with creating and attempting to play their own wind, percussion, or string instruments with clay.

BASIC MATERIALS AND EQUIPMENT WILL BE PROVIDED IN THE CERAMICS STUDIO, ON CAMPUS.
Each student will need to take responsibility to not waste material, and ensure that the tools and work space is respected and maintained well, and also clean up after themselves, according to the instructions given.

title: Arts of the Deccan: The Early Modern Epoch from Vijayanagara to the Marathas
description:
In understanding the history of Indian arts, knowing the Deccan, its place and role, is crucial. In this course we will travel the triangular realm of “Dachinabades” as named in the first-century Periplus of Erythraean Sea, exploring its contours through the lens of its artistic traditions,literatures and cultures. Since this exploration will become very ambitious if we were to cover all aspects of Dakhina (Prakrit) arts, we narrow it down to the Early Modern Period (fifteenth-century onwards), a momentous time of which we have an immediate cultural memory, making the study of artistic heritages a traceable historicity. We will study the Deccan’s unique art forms and cultural practices through music, dance, literature, architecture, paintings, food and fabric that reflect the multicultural and cosmopolitan socio-political ambience in which rulers such as
Krishnadevaraya, Adil Shah, Raghunatha Nayaka, and  Serfoji each played significant roles.
Through readings, viewings and other detailed digital archival material we will learn to close- watch performative arts of the early modern era as milestones in the cultural history of India. The aim of the course is to enable students identify the distinct features of each of historical period such as the Vijayanagara, Sultanate, Nayaka and Maratha as well as to have a panoptic view of early modern era’s artistic legacies whose essence manifests in diverse cultural encounters. The course will prod us to think of deliberate omissions and censoring when the nation-state regrouped its artistic heritages. Coursework will include readings, class discussions-seminars and presentation style disseminations requiring high level of class participation, interactive assignments and some writing work. While the course does not demand any art practice background, those who are practitioners of any genre will be encouraged.
Course Objectives / Learning Outcomes:
To introduce some artistic traditions across genres from the early modern era and help
students learn/read the movement of art through its socio-political legacy
To work on some aspects of embodiment, wherever possible to add value and inspiration
to the course work
To interweave with the domain of history bringing a multi-perspective approach to
learning the arts, history, and society.

title: Philosophical, Aesthetic, and Social Dimensions in Bhakti: An Introduction
description:
This course offers an interdisciplinary exploration of the tradition of Bhakti as an embodied practice of attention, to understand one’s relation with self, the divine, and the world. Through close readings of poetry, song, and performance across diverse Bhakti traditions (translated and in original wherever available), students will learn how to listen to various shades of expression of bhakti and what it implies; ultimately reaching an understanding that devotion, indeed, is an inadequate translation of it.
The course explores regional and vernacular Bhakti traditions through the voices of female saints like Meera, Andal, Akka Mahadevi, and Janabai. Listening to their poetry and songs in class will help students reflect on love, desire, and the subversion of social and gender norms. We then turn to Nirgun (Formless) Bhakti and the radical critiques of Kabir and Ravidas, examining their challenges to caste, ritualism, and hypocrisy, and their vision of an anti-caste world. Listening becomes a critical mode of engaging with Bhakti across its diverse textual and performance contexts. The course concludes with the introspective poetry of Lalla Ded (Lalla) of Kashmir and the living musical tradition of the Bauls of Bengal.
Drawing from religious studies, literary studies, ethnomusicology, gender studies, the course uses poetry, song, performance recordings, live performances, and films to facilitate a participatory understanding of Bhakti. Students will listen, participate in singing, read, and reflect not only on texts and performance, but also on the sensory and affective worlds they create.

title: Moving Pictures, Moving Words
description:
Written texts have long informed audio-visual media, whether as the basis of story, research or in more subtle ways. Cinema and photography also have a notable history of inspiring writers, and writers sometimes experiment with weaving visual elements into their writing in a manner where the photographs are not merely illustrations of the text, and the text does not simply caption the pictures. Instead, the reader experiences the integrated, mutually enhancing relationship created between text and image.

We will examine the history of this complicated and fruitful relationship between words and pictures, whether in books, in direct film adaptations or in inventive recreations. We will view different kinds of non-fiction films, from classic documentaries to more poetic and elliptical uses of the cinematic medium. Discussing and analysing these will widen the understanding of how words, both spoken and written, work when forming partnerships with moving images and sound.

Course Objectives / Learning Outcomes: Discussing and analysing these will widen the understanding of how words, both spoken and written, work when forming partnerships with moving images and sound.

title: The Tactile and the Material
description:
In an increasingly digital and online world we are losing touch with the physical, tactile world around us and the act of creating with our own two hands. Existing creative pursuits are turning digital and the opportunity to engage in tactile craft practices, creating using physical tools and materials, is increasingly rare. 

 This course introduces students to techniques of crafting and expressing creatively using a variety of tactile materials, and gives them the opportunity to learn a hands-on skill.
 All students will have introductory sessions of basic drawing, colour theory, colour mixing, printing, paper manipulation, clay work, yarn, fibre, simple looms, fabric, sewing, dyeing, and using found materials.

 They will then each pick one of these mediums to explore in depth and undertake disciplined practice of, while situating it in a historical and traditional context.
 
 There may be a field trip too.

title: Modern day Storytelling: An introduction to documentary filmmaking and its use in peoples and environmental movements
description:
Documentary films are modern, technology driven storytelling. A medium that can turn anyone’s life and its stories into interesting visual narrations. This course follows the journey of the camera from being a tool that exudes aesthetics, creativity, and capturing of memories, to becoming the strongest instrument of resistance in the struggles of ordinary people. Through a series of interactive lectures the students will explore how the medium of documentary filmmaking can bring stories that are invisibilised, to light. 
At the core of documentary filmmaking lies the critical concept of integrity, the ability to visually capture stories of people and the world just as we see it. Hence, this course will allow students to not only immerse themselves in historicity, but also develop ethics in practice.

title: Creative Makers Studio
description:
A practicum course that offers students with creative ideas and projects to be matched to industry mentors and work on their projects through to execution. Creative ideas that can be tested out in the real world, venture ideas that can be incubated and see initial proof-of-concept, research ideas that go from page to stage, productions that can be staged - all of these constitute the world of creative ideas within the ambit of the course. Specific weeks focus on different phases of creative ideation, and examples from different creative domains are used to illustrate and mentor students on project progress.
Students will work on a creative product from idea to execution. Design thinking practices, project management tools and ideation workshops will enable students to work on producing a market-ready product. Emphasis is placed on showcasing the product at relevant public forums and thus act as a bringing together of learnings from several disciplines.

title: The World(s) of Music (Practicum)
description:
The different worlds of music - genres, traditions and movements are surveyed with both conceptual overviews and practical guided listening sessions. The course culminates in students working on a music production project - which can be a recital, a composition or even a music podcast - depending on the nature of self-paced exploration that they choose to undertake. 
Through guided listening, small compositional projects, analysis and discovery – we discover the diverse world of music in this practicum. We explore traditions, contexts and usage, while studying similarities and dissimilarities across different musical genres and forms. The course will culminate in a music production project - where the class participates in an audience-facing composition.

title: Shooting The Godfather
description:
The course will begin with a reading of Mario Puzo's 1969 betseller The Godfather, followed by close viewings of the two films by Francis Ford Coppola based directly on the novel – The Godfather (1972) and The Godfather Part 2 (1974). This will become the platform from which we will explore the relationship between written fictions and cinematic adaptations. Viewing the films, we will analyse the choices made by Coppola and Puzo as scriptwriters. What parts of the story were included and excluded in the first film and why? Which bits were then used as a basis for the second film? Which were the completely new story elements? How did that work? As we do this we will also discuss basic western narrative
structures leading up to Hollywood's all-pervading 'three-act' structure. In the latter part of the trimester we will look at the many different 'avatars' and spinoffs the basic Godfather narrative has taken on since the early 70s, both in the west and here in India.
We will view and discuss segments from commercial Bombay cinema's idea of 'The Don' to the plethora of gangster films from the late 1980s onwards, such as Nayakan, Satya, The Gangs of Wasseypur etc. Towards the end of the course we will become familiar with some
of the critiques of and alternatives to the three-act structure in cinema and in written fiction. The course will be based on intensive participative discussions that will center around how written narrative feeds into cinema and also how cinema and cinematic elements now feed
into creative writing of all kinds.
Course Objectives/Learning Outcomes: To understand better the interaction between written fiction and its screen adaptations. How to start thinking cinematically. Students will also gain a basic understanding of scripting, shot-breakdown, dialogue, art direction, acting, camerawork, sound, music, editing and how these contribute to the finished film. Through a process of comparison and analysis the student will better understand how a particular "base-narrative"; can become the fertile ground from which vastly different versions of itself are
generated.

title: Jaalis: Cutting through from the Past to the Present
description:
The cut work windows, or “jaalis”, as an aesthetic as well as a practical architectural feature, has been used in multiple cultures through history, typically in hot and arid places. This was most famously used, and most well-crafted (in stone), during the Mughal era. Jaalis have been made in wood, stone, ceramics, and even, (rarely), in metal. As this is a ceramics course, we will touch upon all of them and their histories, but concentrate mostly on the designing and making of terracotta clay jaalis.

In this course you will study the history of jaalis and then go through the process of sketching patterns, drawing inspiration from what we see around the campus, to develop and execute your own modular jaali design. You will learn to convert your designs from 2D to 3D and make a sample jaali window section, and fire it. You will learn the processes that the material requires and learn about utility specific design and execution, giving you an appreciation for craft and craftsmanship.

title: Documentary Film Documentary Film-Making in the Times of Crisis
description: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of the critical role that independent documentary filmmakers play in portraying and questioning India's complex socio-political landscape and offers practitioner’s insights and insider information on the realities on the ground about independent documentary film making. From decoding ideologies, knowing the nuances of identifying, approaching and filming sensitive subjects and navigating dangerous terrains while on the field to shoot, such as riots and andolans, the lens of the filmmaker becomes the unsettling truth teller of immutable visuals, facts and footage. How to negotiate between critical aesthetics and practical questions of safety, security, permissions and ethical concerns, will be taught in this course. Students will explore the breadth of documentary film maker’s daring journeys and documentary films/ raw footages and archives as the crucible of the times we live in, be it the Emergency, Delhi Riots or CAA protests. The crux of the course is how much truth can one tell in a climate of censorship and how?

title: Bio-X: The Interconnectedness of Life
description:
Welcome to an exhilarating journey through modern biology—a discipline that sits at the intersection of every major field of human inquiry. This course will take you on a dynamic exploration of life's interconnectedness and the innovative ways we study it. Beginning with life's origins and evolutionary foundations, we'll traverse scales from molecules to ecosystems, discovering how biology interfaces with various fields ranging from physics and chemistry to psychology and data science. Each module showcases cutting-edge research and real-world applications, such as CRISPR gene editing, AI-powered drug design and pandemic preparedness. Focusing on interdisciplinary thinking, through this course you will see how physics has helped decode photosynthesis at quantum scales, how machine learning revolutionizes protein structure prediction, and how systems biology integrates vast datasets to understand complex diseases. A hands-on laboratory tour midway through the course brings these concepts to life, while modules on global change biology and epidemiology demonstrate biology's critical role in addressing humanity's most pressing challenges. The course culminates in collaborative presentations where you'll envision "Biology X"—the next frontier of biological discovery that excites you most.
Whether you're considering biology as a major, exploring it as a complement to another discipline, or simply curious about how life works, this course reveals the extraordinary career possibilities at biology's rapidly expanding frontiers. From biotechnology startups to conservation initiatives, from computational biology to public health—the skills and perspectives you'll gain in biology are increasingly valuable across sectors.

title: Life at Different Scales
description: Based upon selected case studies, this course covers notions of scale from building blocks of life to biomes, organisational levels and integration of biological units, and the primacy of description. We start with Aristotelian classification and proceed through Early Modern natural philosophy and natural history to the discipline of biology itself in the present day. We consider the development of particular philosophies and forms of technology from the 17th to 19th centuries and corresponding development of elements of biology at different points in time, including such concepts as biogeography, ecology, evolution, cell biology, genetics, anatomy, and physiology, even as theological holds over the subject begin to waver.

title: Molecular and Cellular Biology
description: This course is an introduction to the principles that guide the multifarious processes in the cell at the molecular and cellular levels and is intended for a college level audience. The content is an answer to the question: What is the molecular basis of cellular structure and function? Concepts covered include the storage, transfer, and regulation of genetic information, the interactions between molecules, and their assembly and disassembly in cellular functions, the cytoskeleton and its role in cell and tissue shape, molecular traffic between the various cellular locations and across the membrane boundary, signaling within the cell and between cells, cellular metabolism, the cell-cycle, division, growth, development, differentiation and death, and the energy conversions that power all these processes. The course will focus more on principles than on encyclopedic detail, and will be linked to modules taught in earlier trimesters to enable comprehension.

title: LAB I
description:
The course aims to bring together and synthesize the various concepts taught in the Biochemistry and Microbiology courses, to enable a better understanding of these subjects through practical application. The practicals will include instruction in basic laboratory procedures, such as the maintenance and use of a laboratory journal, acquaintance with basic laboratory rules and safety regulations, the preparation of solutions and buffers, the measurement of mass and pH, calculation of solution concentrations as normality, molarity, molality, or as mass/volume, volume/volume etc, the preparation of solutions and buffers, the estimation of error in measurements of mass, volume, pH and other variables*, the use of basic laboratory glassware/plasticware and instruments, the extraction and estimation of protein or DNA in solution, the use of the compound- and stereo-microscopes, the gram staining of bacteria, the preparation of bacterial media (Luria Bertani or another), the sterilization of labware and media, the preparation of culture plates, the inoculation and culture of media by various means, and the extraction and analysis of bacterial deoxyribonucleic acid by chromatography. The course may also include exercises in the laboratory using data drawn from the literature.
*Instruction in the estimation of error will be provided in PHYS lab classes intended for PHYS, CHEM, and BIOS students.

title: Microbiology
description: The course is designed for a college level audience, and is intended as a comprehensive foundation for advanced courses that students may opt for in the future. Course topics will be contemporary, and will focus on conceptual understanding and not encyclopedic detail. The course will involve the study of microbes of the various taxa, viz viruses, protozoans, bacteria, algae, and fungi, their place in the evolutionary order of things, their diversity and distribution, and their relevance in the Anthropocene. The course will use a bacterial-centric approach in its treatment of microbial taxonomy, metabolism, genetics, multiplication, and growth. Industrial, agricultural, environmental, and clinical applications and value will be highlighted wherever relevant using microbial archetypes; this will include certain clinically important pathogens and their control, fermentation as an industrial process, the use of engineered microbes in waste processing and pollution control, and agricultural pests and pest controls. The contribution of microbes to human health (as the microbiome, and as probiotics), and societal and environmental health (as degraders of waste) will be discussed. Students will be taught to isolate bacteria from their surroundings, and to examine, identify, propagate, and preserve them. Emphasis will be placed on bacterial genetics, especially the bacterial extra-chromosomal DNA (the plasmid) and its centricity in recombinant DNA techniques or genetic engineering. The course will enable the student to understand the multitudes of microbes cohabiting with humans, and the nature and degree of interaction between the two. Care will be taken to cross-reference concepts taught in this course with relevant concepts taught in earlier courses.

title: Biochemistry
description: The course is intended for second year undergraduate students and is meant to be an introduction to the physical and chemical principles that underlie and underpin the biology of organisms. The course will help students understand the molecular logic of life; it will enable them to find answers to questions pertaining to the various aspects of a biological system; these are some samples. How, in biological systems, is energy created or captured, stored, and transmuted, and how is the need for energy sensed? What are the energetic and kinetic bases of a biochemical reaction, which is in turn a unit of a physiological process? How are the various biomolecules synthesized and degraded, and how is the balance between anabolism and catabolism maintained? What are the guiding principles of this homeostasis? How are the various physiological processes orchestrated and synchronized at the level of the system? How does a bodily fluid such as blood act as a buffer, and how is this physiologically important? What are the various classes of biomolecules that make up molecular superstructures, and how do their structures help them perform their function? Instruction in the above will help the student to begin to learn to interpret experimental data, and to better understand biochemical research.

title: Comparative Genomics of Bacteria
description:
Bacteria are the most dominant forms of cellular life on earth. Their ability to adapt to the entire gamut of environments
on our planet is coded somehow in their DNA. We will discuss how this fascinating kingdom of life adapts to its
circumstances by studying the structure, organisation and evolution of their genomes. We will take a conceptual and
computational approach towards these aims. A particular goal of this course will be to help students conceptualise,
design and implement (at least in part) a mini-project analysing bacterial genomes.

title: Genetics
description: From classical to molecular genetics, this course seeks to provide a close understanding of the processes involved in heredity. Beginning with the famous experiments undertaken by Gregor Mendel in the early 1860s, we move to the rediscovery of his work in 1900 and its employment in the elucidation of such aspects as linkage and crossing over, as well as chromosomal aberrations and mutations. The molecular basis for genetics finds root in the Evolutionary Synthesis and foundational work involving the implication of nucleic acid as genetic material. In this context, we study the chemical nature, physico-chemical structure and replication of DNA. Both DNA and RNAs are considered in their combined role for protein synthesis. The elucidation of the genetic code and the mechanism and regulation of gene action, such as with the operon model are investigated and their implications considered. Extrachromosomal inheritance will be treated as well. The course concludes with the promise and perils of genetic engineering (Recombinant DNA) and its applications, including, controversially, gene editing and cloning.

title: Plant Diversity and Reproduction
description: This course is a primer to plant life, covering what comprises the plant Kingdom, how to identify different plants, and how plants reproduce. The first part of the course will explore the diversity of plants from algae to angiosperms. This will include discussions of plant evolution and phylogeny, how and when the first land plants arrived, how plants are classified, and how to identify broad groups of plants including some common Families of angiosperms. We will also explore morphological, anatomical, physiological and other adaptations of plants that allow them to grow in diverse environmental conditions. The second part of the course will focus on the different reproductive strategies of various groups of plants. Some aspects unique to plant reproduction will be discussed, such as alternation of generations in lower plants, and monoecy, dioecy, pollination strategies, double fertilization and embryogenesis in higher plants.

title: Advanced Cell Biology
description:
The Advanced Cell Biology course builds upon the foundational Cell and Molecular Biology course and is a deeper dive into the working of the cell in the context of a system. The course is a problem and exercise based approach to understanding specific aspects of the cell in the context of its physiological milieu and system (Human/Animal). The course will begin where the Basic cell and molecular biology (BIOS 205) course ended. This is an ideal and probably very important subject for students who want to pursue MSc/PhD and want to build a career in research in an academic or industrial setting. This course will connect with other areas of bioscience (microbiology, physiology, Immunology) to understand the connections between these related areas. It will delve into the cross talk among different cell types across tissue/organs and their role in health and diseases.
The syllabus include,
Visualizing and analyzing molecules, cells, and systems (contd from BIOS 205)
The Cell Cycle: its control and regulation; aberrations in its control and the consequent effect on the cell and system; growth, development, differentiation.
Cell death; apoptosis and programmed cell death, autophagy, senescence; stem cells and cell lineages
The evolution of the rogue cell and its contextual behavior
Cell signaling archetypes in eukaryotic cells and systems; their control and regulation; redundancy; defects in signaling systems and their ramifications, as in NCDs
Drug discovery and delivery : Current trends

title: Evolution
description: How did life first arise on Planet Earth 4 billion years ago? In this course, which comprises both organismal and molecular evolution, we will begin with early theories of evolution that lead up to Darwin and Wallace's theory of natural selection. We thus gain insight into the process of scientific inquiry that resulted in one of the most important theories in the biological sciences, before concluding by integrating it with Mendel's theory of genetics referred to as the Evolutionary Synthesis. The course will look at the evidence of macro and micro evolutionary processes, and the evolution of plants and animals to understand the basis of the diversity of living organisms on Earth. Through numerous examples, students will learn about adaptive strategies at the level of individual organisms that may underlie evolutionary changes at the level of a population. At a molecular level, we trace the evolution of life, starting from self-replicating molecules, to the RNA world, to the evolution of cellular components. Along the way we will discuss the role played by the constituent molecules of life. We will discuss the origin of the field of molecular genetics from the Evolutionary Synthesis, bringing the disparate fields of evolutionary biology and genetics together. We will discuss the development and employment of the molecular clock and the salience of neutral mutations in establishing relatedness among organisms, using such markers as mitochondrial, chloroplast, ribosomal and nuclear genetic material, aided considerably by such technological advancements as protein electrophoresis, leading to the amplification of DNA using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for whole genome sequencing. This course will briefly discuss how the sequence information comes together with the current computational power to draw the phylogenetic tree of life.

title: Form and Function
description: In this course, we examine biological systems through the lenses of anatomy (structure) and physiology (function), that make life possible across scales of complexity - from the simplest forms to the most intricate. Through this approach, all courses that we have encountered so far will be considered in establishing how we can begin to comprehend what life, in a biological sense, means. Apart from such familiar systems as encountered in school (the digestive, respiratory, circulatory, excretory, nervous and reproductive, for instance), we explore concepts like homoeostasis and thermoregulation.

title: Biostatistics
description: This course will equip students broadly interested in the biological sciences and allied disciplines to develop fundamental skills for managing, exploring and analyzing data, and interpreting and communicating findings. The course provides a hands-on learning experience using data from multiple fields of study to master basic statistical tools widely used in the discipline and become familiar with the range of advanced quantitative tools to inform avenues for further specialization. The course will introduce students to basic and advanced programming techniques in R, which is rapidly becoming the programming language of choice for biostatistical applications, and will train them in using R to carry out common statistical analyses. In addition to imparting skills to quantify single variables and relationships between multiple variables, the course will use real-world datasets to help students learn how to deal with noisy data, uncertainty of findings and ethical concerns that are common to the discipline.

title: Genetics and Cell Biology Lab
description: The course will bring together various topics in Genetics and Advanced Cell Biology. The portion on genetics will include procedures and experiments using the fruit-fly Drosophila melanogaster as the model organism, for instance the observation of wild type and mutant characteristics using the compound and stereo microscopes, the culture of Drosophila, the longitudinal observation of their life-cycles, the proper and meticulous use of a lab notebook/ journal, computational exercises in phylogeny, and, time permitting, recombinant DNA techniques. The Advanced Cell Biology course will include procedures for nucleic acid analysis including nucleic acid extraction, chromatography, and quantitative PCR, and for protein analysis by chromatography.

title: Chemistry for Biologists
description: Chemistry for biologists: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles of chemistry with an explicit focus on their relevance to biological systems. Topics are motivated by examples drawn from cell biology, physiology, biochemistry, and microbiology. Experimental demonstrations and in-class problem-solving exercises connect chemical principles to the phenomena students encounter in their biology courses. The course has been designed to give biology majors the quantitative and conceptual chemical foundation necessary for advanced study in biochemistry, molecular biology, microbiology, pharmacology, and biomedical research

title: Physics for Biologists
description: Physics for biologists: The course uses basic biophysical concepts and experimental illustrations to explaining the physical principles that govern biological systems at the molecular level. The course combines classroom teaching with discussion of scientific observations that concur with theories. The course also aims to illustrate how various biomolecules behave as outliers, allowing for modification of these theories while providing a biophysical explanation for their behavior.

title: Ways of Knowing: Instrumentation in Biology
Ways of Knowing: Methods and Communication
description: This offering, the other of a two-part course, will use a seminar-style format to expose students to literature in the biological sciences to serve three important and interconnected purposes. The selected pieces of work will expose students to forms of inquiry used in the biological sciences to produce new knowledge and to advance the discipline. Students will also learn multiple types of communication in the discipline. Finally, students will learn to assess critically the work and findings reported in the primary literature. The course will bridge the gap between simplified concepts in standard biology textbooks and the rigour, complexity and uncertainty of findings in the primary literature, including, among others, journals and theses.

title: Animal Behaviour
description: This course will begin with an overview of animal behaviour and how it has integrated concepts from many disciplines to advance the field. Next, animal behaviour will be studied from an evolutionary perspective before understanding the bases for the variation in behaviours within and among individuals, populations, and species. With these concepts in mind, a range of behaviours will be examined using case studies. Finally, more complex behaviours related to social interactions among animals will be considered.

title: Immunology
description: The course comprises a study of the human defense system against pathogens and disease causing agents. It will start with the genesis of the immune system from the lymphoid cells of bone-marrow tissue, and its maturation. It will go on to the molecular basis for determination of self- and non-self, and how an aberration in this process causes the immune system to go rogue and cause auto-immune disease. The course will center around the humoral and cell-mediated immune responses, of their attendant molecular and cellular events, and how the immune system evolves throughout the lifetime of an individual. It will address different aspects of the immune system such as the genetic control of immunoglobulin gene expression, and antibody production, maturation and diversity, and the roles of the thymus, spleen, and lymph nodes. The modulation or suppression of the immune system for tissue and organ graft will be discussed, as will be the reciprocal effects of disease and the immune system, allergies and the inflammatory response, and the use of the immune-system as therapy against cancer and other diseases as drugs or vaccines. The course will also include the mechanisms pathogens have evolved to evade the immune system, and the state of our knowledge of these systems. The reconstitution of the human immune system in mice will be discussed at length to further enable the student’s understanding of the same.

title: Ecology and Conservation Biology
description: This course covers the fundamental principles of ecology and ecosystem dynamics, relating these with evolutionary processes and introducing concepts of disturbance and resilience. The focus is on the principles of life, how it functions at the population, community and ecosystem levels, relating these with adaptations to unique environmental conditions. This course will be split into four interrelated modules. The first module, population ecology, will deal with the fundamental concepts of habitat and niche, population dynamics (e.g., population growth and regulation) and population structure (e.g., metapopulations). The second module, community ecology, will focus on species interactions (e.g., interspecific competition, predation and mutualism), the nature of communities (e.g., community structure and function). The third module, ecosystem ecology, will take a in depth look at ecosystem structure and function (e.g., energy flow and nutrient cycling), ecosystem dynamics (e.g., ecological succession) and major concepts related to biogeography (e.g., the theory of island biogeography and the major biogeographical zones of India). The final module, conservation biology, will bring together the previous modules and show how the field of conservation biology has harnessed the principles of ecology to manage biodiversity. The course will focus on the principles of conservation (e.g., the design and management of protected areas), ecological restoration and will conclude with some important case studies, frorm India and across the globe, that showcase various conservation/management strategies.

title: Molecular Biophysics
description:
This course introduces the physical chemistry of biological systems. The topics include an introduction to the basics of statistical mechanics to understand the connections between macroscopic thermodynamic properties and microscopic molecular properties, chemical potentials, equilibrium states, binding cooperativity, behaviour of macromolecules in solution and at the interfaces, and solvation. We will
discuss protein structure, genomic analysis, single-molecule biomechanics, and biomaterials. To foster a deeper appreciation of the empirical aspects of the discipline, we will discuss Nuclear Magnetic Resonance measurements and provide practical demonstrations using the NMR spectrometer at Krea University. We will also discuss the recent developments in the use of Artificial Intelligence in
solving really hard Biophysics problems of understanding protein structure and dynamics. We will implement the computation of protein structure for practical sessions.

title: Introduction to Bioinformatics
description: This course introduces algorithmic concepts and hands-on experience in the use of relevant tools/techniques for many key biological sequence analysis problems in Bioinformatics/Computational Biology. We will introduce various algorithms and heuristics for pairwise sequence alignment, multiple sequence alignment, molecular evolution and phylogenetic analysis, genome sequencing and annotation. The students will be introduced to the key algorithms and their applications of key Bioinformatics tools like BLAST and its variants, CLUSTALX, tools like PHYLIP for phylogenetic and evolutionary analysis. This course will be cross listed with Computer Science and assumes a prior background in either “Introductory Biology” or “Discrete Mathematics” and will be open to third and final year students majoring in Biology/Computer Science/Mathematics.

title: Microbial Genomics
description: Bacteria are the most dominant forms of cellular life on earth. Their ability to adapt to the entire gamut of environments on our planet is coded somehow in their DNA. We will discuss how this fascinating kingdom of life adapts to its circumstances by studying the structure, organisation and evolution of their genomes. We will take a conceptual and computational approach towards these aims. A particular goal of this course will be to help students conceptualise, design and implement (at least in part) a mini-project analysing bacterial genomes.

title: Misconduct in Science Research
description: This course explores the darker side of scientific research — the deliberate falsification, fabrication, and plagiarism that have led to the retraction of biomedical research papers. Through a series of case studies, students will investigate how misconduct was detected, how it propagated through the literature, the consequences for the individuals and institutions involved, and the broader implications for scientific credibility. The course also examines systemic pressures that foster misconduct and the evolving safeguards implemented by journals, funding agencies, and institutions.

title: Quantified self
description: This course examines the psychological, biological, biomedical, and sociotechnical dimensions of self-tracking practices in contemporary digital life. With a central focus on the biological and cognitive mechanisms underlying self-regulation, feedback, and sense-making, the course explores how digital technologies enable a prospective approach to health management, and how they mediate and reshape attention, decision-making, memory, emotion, and embodied experience; the course also  Drawing on perspectives from biology, cognitive neuroscience, behavioral psychology, and cultural theory, students will critically engage with topics such as neurofeedback, affective computing, persuasive design, and the cognitive labor of managing personal data. The course also addresses broader social and ethical implications, including surveillance, inequality, and the politics of measurement. Through interdisciplinary readings and experiential assignments, students will investigate how cognitive processes are both reflected in and transformed by the quantified self.

title: Plant Anatomy and Physiology
description: The course begins with introducing the plant’s meristem and its histological organization to the students, followed by the anatomy of the leaf and other simple & complex tissue structures and their organization. Water is important to plant life, and other mechanical phenomena happening inside plants, such as diffusion, osmosis, plasmolysis, imbibition, guttation, transpiration, etc., are considered. It introduces the stomata & the mechanism of opening & closing that enable gas exchange between plants and the atmosphere. Identifying the essentiality of nutrients is foregrounded, along with their roles, the mechanism of uptake of nutrients, and the mechanism of food transport within plants. What role does gravity play, and how will plants grow in space? We learn about concepts of photosynthesis and pigment systems/photosystems. Other important phenomena are discussed, such as photophosphorylation, the Calvin cycle and photorespiration in plants. Carbon fixation, indoor and otherwise. How pollution affects them etc. We consider how and why plants go under nitrogen metabolism, how molecular nitrogen fixation happens, and its significance to the world. Plants also need/use hormones for their growth and development. We discuss how growth hormones such as auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid, and ethylene work. We complete the circle by looking at the seed. We introduce students to seed dormancy, its germination, and the concept of photoperiodism and vernalization. We talk about genetically modified plants and seeds (GMOs) and the hazards and ethical issues around them. The genetic basis of the adaptations in plants and how they vary with the types of climates, for example, how do they become resilient to drought? A brief introduction to modern plant biotechnology and gardening is also discussed. Concept integration and awareness about ecosystems, global warming, forests and the plantation of trees

title: Global Change Biology
description: We are living in what many consider to be a unique period of time in the history of planet Earth, the Anthropocene era, wherein humans are modifying Earth’s environment through myriad pathways, including the burning of fossil fuels, overexploitation of natural resources and large-scale changes in patterns of land-use. These changes have major consequences for ecological systems at multiple levels of biological organization from the individual and population to the community and ecosystem. This course will not only focus on the mechanisms through which humans are altering the air, water and land of planet Earth, but also to apply concepts from ecological and evolutionary biology theory to understand how these changes are likely to impact life on Earth. Students will learn to critically evaluate the primary scientific literature related to the field of global change biology, and also to address specific questions through the graphical and/or statistical analyses of real-world data. The course will pay particular attention to the most critical crises associated with anthropogenic global change, and also on how these changes can impact health and well-being of humans through various mechanisms ranging from reduced access to ecosystem services (e.g., clean air and water) to the increased risk of emergence of novel diseases (e.g., COVID-19).

title: Protein Folding and Dynamics
description:
This is a seminar course where we will discuss and analyze research papers, and solve problems as assignments, and there will be presentations of the papers.  
Proteins are fascinating molecular machines that carry out every function inside the cells whose properties are so useful that we employ them as therapeutic agents, catalysts, and materials. Many diseases stem from protein mutations impairing their folding, structure, or activity. This course will discuss the physical chemistry of protein molecules. This course is for students of Biological Sciences who are comfortable with mathematics. This is also a course for chemistry and physics students who want to think about proteins.

title: Bacterial Gene Regulatory Networks
description: This course will discuss molecular aspects of gene regulation in bacteria. Gene regulation is fundamental to bacterial adaptation to their environments and is achieved by a complex network of regulatory proteins and their interactions with DNA. How this network functions and how it sustains bacterial life as we know it are the key themes this course will cover.

title: Introduction to Accounting and Finance
description: This course aids students in donning multiple hats so as to understand the respective decision-making process of different fiduciary stakeholders that are based on financial statements of a reporting entity. For example, shareholders use accounting information to determine the intrinsic value of the stock, which helps them to decide whether to buy, hold, or sell the companyâ€™s share. Bankers and lenders rely on firmâ€™s financial statements in order to decide whether to lend money or not to firms. The course also discusses the significance of relevant accounting standards and the evolving regulatory landscape in the preparation and interpretation of financial statements. This course is also designed to provide students with a deeper understanding of nature and workings of corporate financial management. The course aims to provide the framework, concepts, and tools for analysing financial decisions based on fundamental principles of modern financial theory. It introduces the students to the many ways in which corporate management both evaluates investment opportunities and finances investments. It also teaches basic financial concepts and provides students with the tools necessary for evaluating the intrinsic value of a corporation, as well as assessing a corporation's effectiveness in maximizing its value. Further, the course highlights the important real-world applications of the various theories.

title: Foundations of Marketing
description: The word ‘Marketing’ is embedded in conversations of everyday life, and general perception that marketing is all about selling and advertising. However, marketing is a much larger concept that drives an organization with great societal impact. 4P of product, place and distribution, promotion, and price - comprise the original "Marketing Mix." Together with rigorous and complete analysis of the environment, customers, and competitors, they are the key activities of marketing management, and the crucial ones: failure to find the right combination of the "mix" often result in irretrievable product (or service) failure and severe damage to organizational finances and credibility. This course shall follow a blended pedagogy of interactive lectures, case and caselet discussions, and class activities to introduce the fundamental concepts of marketing to the participants.

title: Supply Chain Management
description:
1.	Course Description: 
Supply Chain Management (SCM) is a cross-functional discipline concerned with the movement of products, the use of business resources, the flow of information, and the deployment of services in the value chain. In this introductory course, students are provided with a comprehensive overview of the business processes, value-creating activities, and best practices for managing a supply chain.

2.	Learning Objectives 
(1)	Provide a comprehensive overview of SCM-related business processes and problems and pinpoint the strategic role of SCM and relationship to other business disciplines. 
(2)	Equip students with SCM best practices and related basic analytical models/tools. 
(3)	Provide a roadmap to more specialized courses on SCM-related topics.
3.	Learning outcomes

1)	Students will understand the main processes and common challenges in supply chain management and how SCM integrates with other business functions.
2)	Students will be able to identify and apply best practices and basic analytical tools to solve supply chain management problems effectively.
3)	Students will have a foundational understanding that prepares them for more specialized courses and career development in supply chain management.

title: Information Systems and Data Analytics
description: Information systems (IS) refer to the embedding of work processes, within and across organizations, in information and communication technologies (ICT) such as computers, communications devices and networks that interconnect them. The mediation of work through information systems can save cost and improve quality, potentially granting competitive advantage to organizations that invest in such systems. Data accumulated through the operation of information systems are also further analyzed using statistical algorithms (data analytics) to reveal novel yet reliable patterns that can be exploited to improve the efficiency and quality of work processes.

title: Strategy and Innovation
description:
Strategy is the process of deciding how to best position the organisation in its competitive environment in order to achieve and sustain competitive advantage. The pace of change in the business environment has increased significantly in recent years leading to disruptions in business models, supply chains and organisation structures. Performance, within the conversation of strategic management, deals with superior value creation for stakeholders. The issue is studied by raising two critical managerial questions:
●        How and why do some firms create superior value for stakeholders?
●        How do they sustain such performance?
The above questions are reviewed in the course by invoking various concepts from microeconomic theories and the functional disciplines of management and integrating them into a coherent whole. A systemic approach, involving internal and external environmental analysis, identifying opportunities, formulating strategies at the business unit level and at corporate level are covered in the course.

title: Introduction to People Management
description: The course deals with Principles and Practices of People Management in organizations as relevant to the roles and responsibilities of managers across functions. It develops a detailed understanding of the people management process- Workforce planning, Recruitment and Selection, Training and Development, Performance Management System, Labor Laws and Employee relations etc.

title: Building a Rocketship - Entrepreneurship
description:
Entrepreneurship: 
What do we need to launch a successful entrepreneurial venture? How can we make it happen? How do
we transform an idea and a blank piece of paper into an operating business with customers, cash flow,
and profits?
This course is an introduction to, and an overview of, these fundamentals of entrepreneurship. You might
already have an idea and are probably eager to start your own business, or you merely want to learn
more about what an entrepreneurial career would be like – either way, this course exposes you to the
challenges of entrepreneurship – starting from conceptualizing new ventures to building them and
ending with, managing those ventures.
We'll begin with brainstorming and idea generation, finding opportunities, and building on those. We’ll
then move on to subjects such as testing business ideas, finding traction, evaluating go-to-market
strategies, developing a business model, and understanding the fundamentals of business plans. We’ll
also learn how to pitch yourself and your venture.

title: Blockchain Technology: A Managerial Perspective
description:
Ever since the introduction of Bitcoin in 2008, Cryptocurrencies and the Blockchain technology
have become very popular contributing to a lot of excitement and hype in business circles. While
crypto-currencies have not been welcomed warmly, especially by the regulators, the usefulness
of Blockchain, the technology underpinning Bitcoin has been universally recognized 1 (even by
detractors of cryptocurrencies). Increasingly, Blockchain technology is finding applications
outside the Fintech industry including areas such as Supply chain management, fraud detection,
health, agriculture, education, government and the like. With this kind of proliferation, it is not
inconceivable that present and future managers will encounter Blockchain in some form sooner
rather than later.
This course intends to equip student, the present and future managers, with relevant and working
knowledge of Cryptocurrencies and the Blockchain technology. Blockchain, a potentially
disruptive technology has various known and potentially useful applications across various
industry verticals.
Course Objectives:

The main objective of this course is to equip students with an understanding of the emerging
technology of blockchain that will enable them to:
- Assess the applicability of Blockchain technology and its business benefits in business
contexts that are characterized by “trust” mechanisms.
- Understand the interaction between different Blockchain components.
- Where and how to implement Blockchain
- Design innovative Blockchain Applications

title: Consumer Behavior
description: If consumers in developed markets had been consuming corn flakes with cold milk for decades, why should a brand like Kellog’s advertise that cornflakes should be taken with hot milk, almost two decades after its entry into India? Why should a brand like Surf (or for that matter most detergent brands) weave a “story” around its brand with a drama-like ad? Why should Indian brands spend so much on cricket or film celebrities”[1]. Consumer behaviour is a fascinating subject. The course is not meant for addressing the above illustrative questions but for making you learn concepts that can come of help in thinking about how to approach such questions. Aren’t we all consumers, whether we snack on a samosa or go to a gym? Consumer behaviour is “the study of consumer’s actions during searching for, purchasing, using, evaluating, and disposing of products and services that they expect will satisfy their needs”[2]. At the end of the course, you should know the consumer decision-making model, with its stages and their respective elements: input (e.g., marketing mix, sociocultural influences), process (e.g., need recognition, information search, evaluation), output (e.g., purchase, use, post-purchase evaluation). Mastery of the subject will give you an edge for pursuing dream jobs in brand management, advertising, and consumer research. Not only that, but you can also pursue higher studies and path-breaking research.

title: Advanced Topics in Accounting
description:
Introduction: 
Accounting is the language of Business: Manufacturing and trading entities are important organs of the world’s economic dimension. The economic dimension of the world is often described as economy.
 In an economy, financial transactions are inherent.  Companies and other entities need to communicate to the employees and the public and statutory administrative bodies about the transactions they perform which have financial implications.  This need is precisely addressed by a language called accounting. Accounting framework is an important edifice like technical, legal and other entities.
Accounting is perhaps the single largest edifice of a business edifice with, and around, which the whole gamut of other edifices are built and intertwined. 
Accounting is very often the basis for decision making – both internal and external. Whether to increase prices or cut costs or “Buy, Sell or Hold” decisions, companies need to have their accounting systems in place. 
Course Design:
The Course on Advanced Topics in Accounting is designed with the following focus: 
1.        To enable students to understand certain advanced Accounting standards 
2.        To enable students to better appreciate the contents of financial statements – to be read along with other aspects of annual reports (like Chairman’s report / Board of Directors report) 
3.        To enable students to apply various management accounting tools used for decision making and control especially in the context of Strategic Cost Management

title: Basics of Digital Marketing
description: Hardly 25 years back, most of the technology that is in use today, did not exist. Personal computers in its rudimentary avatar entered our work spaces only with the economic liberalization of the early 1990s. Both mobile telephony and the Internet were born a few more years later in 1995. The turn of the millennium saw the market getting flooded with laptops with the early versions testing our weight lifting skills. Forget 25 years, just about 10 years back there were no smartphones, no Cloud Computing as we know it today, no connected intelligent devices and most importantly no Facebook! To be more generic, there was no social media space at all a decade ago. Linked In was launched in 2003; Facebook in 2004 and Tweets were born, thanks to Twitter in 2006. The first version of iPhone was launched in 2007. The iPad hit the market in 2010. Thus, what we consider as a technologyâ€“deluged world is a fairly nascent world. The overwhelming envelope of technology is affecting every sphere of our life. In the personal space, the way we communicate, interact and socialize has significantly altered with technology being the key harbinger of this change. In the business space, the way we produce, transport, sell and service in any business is all governed by some interesting facet of technology. This 10 Session module focuses on the all-pervading influence of technology in the realm of Marketing. The main objective of this course is to take the â€œBrickâ€ activities to the next level of â€œClickâ€ activities and leverage the power of the Web to the students of Marketing. This Course will give an overview of various digital marketing platforms that can be used for formatting Digital Strategies. It will give insights into the art and science of search engine marketing and social media marketing. It will cover facets of search advertising and search engine optimization. It will enable broad understanding of key social media such as Facebook, LinkedIn and Twitter. The Course will arm marketers with an understanding of web analytics and metrics with which they can measure the performance of their digital marketing campaigns. The Course will help students to understand web engagement, Lead Generation and Conversions. The Course will equip Students with the tools and techniques of digital marketing so that they can integrate digital into their marketing plan. Insights into digital marketing will enable marketing students to get enhanced performance. The course will give a holistic approach for students on the overall digital marketing platforms and strategi

title: Security Analysis & Portfolio Management
description:
The course aims to give students a comprehensive understanding of portfolio
management principles, including constructing and evaluating portfolios.
Topics we cover include the market indices, efficiency frontier, the Markowitz portfolio,
capital asset pricing, model, arbitrage pricing theory, factor models, active and passive
investing, smart beta, beta core, bucket investment, simulation, optimization, Sharpe
ratio, Traynor ratio, Mutual funds etc.
Learning Objectives:
1. Understand risk and return
2. History of stock returns
3. Market efficiency
4. Risk return relationship
5. Construct and evaluate portfolios

title: Financial Management
description:
Course Coverage:
Financial Management
Time value of money – advanced concepts
Investment Appraisal Techniques
Technical and Fundamental Analysis
Risk Management – Options, Futures, Forwards and Risk Management
Learning Outcomes:
At the end of the course, the students would be able to:
1. Understand general and specific cash flows, based on which financial analysis is carried out
2. Apply investment appraisal techniques to determine the financial feasibility of the projects
3. Valuation of shares and bonds; determination of WACC
4. Use of fundamental & technical analysis to determine the value of a share / company / business.
5. Determine working capital requirements of a business and how to optimize the same
6. Advanced topics in Financial Management – including options & futures (to manage risk better)

title: Basics of Finance & Banking
description:
This course is primarily designed to help students understand the basics of finance and
banking, operational dynamics and day-to-day transactions at bank branches. It will cover the
finance essentials related to banking, the latest global developments in banking in the areas of lending, risk management, asset liability management and the impact of technology in modern
day banking. It will also give them a practical perspective of the day to day challenges faced
by banks.

Learning Outcome:
1. How banks are functioning today
2. Main banking products
3. What new products and services have come into the market
3. Challenges faced by banks and opportunities available to them
4. The technological changes shaping banking
5. The future of banking

title: Personal Finance & Wealth Management
description:
Course Description:
Managing personal finances and wealth is the key for the successful and stress life of an
individual. This course helps the students to make informed financial decisions in their
life by reducing the risk of ending in financial turmoil. This course aims to provide a
strong foundation for managing personal finance and wealth of students through real-
world applications, case studies, and interactive activities. Students will develop the
knowledge and confidence to achieve financial stability and growth.
Learning Objectives:
Students will develop practical skills in budgeting, saving, and investing, while also
gaining an understanding of credit management, tax planning, and retirement
strategies. By exploring various financial instruments available and equip them to
optimize their wealth-building efforts and achieve financial security. The course also
emphasizes the importance of risk management, financial psychology, and consumer
protection, ensuring that students can navigate financial challenges with confidence.
Ultimately, the course aims to cultivate responsible financial habits and long-term
wealth management strategies for a secure and prosperous future.

Learning Outcomes:

After completing this course, the participants should be able to:
1) Students will be able to learn how to prepare and manage the personal budget viz.,
expenses, savings effectively.
2) Students will get an overview of investment options available to build their wealth.
3) Students will learn how to plan financially for their higher education, home loan,
retirement, health and Insurance.
4) Students learn on assessing financial risks, recognize fraudulent schemes, and build
strategies for secures future.

title: Measuring Impact
description:
This course introduces students to A/B testing in modern businesses. This topic has increased considerably in importance over the last decade, as entrepreneurs have learned to think creatively about how to generate data in more rigorous ways and as developments in information technology have facilitated the development of better data gathering. Key to this area is the insight that correlations do not imply causality and, in almost all cases, cannot measure impact. This course helps design and use experiments and natural experiments to measure impact. The class will assume no prior knowledge. However, some knowledge of statistics will be advantageous, and an interest in writing codes in R will be a bonus.
LEARNING OUTCOMES 
At the end of the course, the students would be able to learn: 
1. The difference between correlation and causation. 
2. Link theory with actionable business decision. 
3. Understand how AB tests work. 
4. Understand how analytics can shape business decisions.

title: Entrepreneurship
description:
This hands-on entrepreneurship course transforms students from idea generators to pitch-
 ready entrepreneurs. Students will experience the complete entrepreneurial journey by developing a real business concept, conducting market research, building prototypes, and culminating in a Dragons' Den-style pitch competition. The course emphasizes learning-by-
 doing through simulations, case studies, and real-world applications rather than theoretical frameworks alone.

title: Business Readiness Bootcamp
description:
This is a practical, skill-based professional readiness program designed for final-year liberal arts
undergraduates. This course bridges the gap between academia and the corporate world by
equipping students with the mental models, skills, behaviours, and business awareness needed
to transition confidently into the workplace.
Students learn how organizations function, how companies create value, how to navigate
workplace culture and expectations, and how to build a strong professional identity.
The course is structured to level the playing field for new entrants to the corporate world -
focused on empowerment, awareness, and competitive advantage.

title: Introduction to Financial Time Series Forecasting
description:
Forecasting is an emerging domain in the field of business during this time. In Finance
and Economics, we need to know about the value of risk, volatility, asset pricing,
portfolio allocations, interest rate modelling, and inflation rate. The forecasting
technique helps them to get an idea about the risk factors. This course aims to provide a
strong foundation of forecasting and time series econometrics and financial risk
management. Application of all the models will be discussed using real life data.

title: Capital Markets - Trading, Analysis and Investment Strategy
description:
This dynamic capital markets course transforms students from market observers to informed investors through hands-on trading simulations, real-time market analysis, and portfolio management. Students will navigate the complexities of stock markets, bond markets,
derivatives, and alternative investments while building practical skills in financial analysis, risk assessment, and investment strategy. The course culminates in a Portfolio Management Competition where students present their investment strategies to a panel.
Learning Objectives:
1. Understand the structure and functioning of global capital markets
2. Master fundamental and technical analysis techniques for investment decisions
3. Develop practical skills in portfolio construction and risk management
4. Gain hands-on experience with trading platforms and financial data analysis
5. Learn to evaluate and present investment strategies effectively

title: Carbon based molecules
description: This course will provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental principles and concepts of chemical bonding (Hybridization, MO theory) structure-property relationship (dipole moment, acidity, basicity) in organic molecules. This course aims to equip students with the problem-solving skills in Organic Chemistry. By successfully completing the course, students will have a fundamental background in Organic Chemistry and reaction mechanism.

title: General Chemistry Lab
description:
Titration is a laboratory technique used to determine the concentration of an unknown solution by reacting it with a solution of known concentration. This course will introduce students to the various titrimetric 
experiments based on acidimetry, redox titrations, pH metric
titrations

title: Atoms, molecules & elements
description: This course aims to introduce the students to quantum mechanics and demonstrate how the ideas of quantum mechanics help in understanding chemical phenomena and the layout of the periodic table. The role of quantum mechanics in explaining atomic structure and bonding will be established. This is a novel approach and is different from the historical development of the field.

title: Physics for Chemists and Biologists
description: This introduces physics concepts that will be required for a deeper understanding of chemical and biological systems from a microscopic perspective.

title: Inorganic Chemistry Lab
description: Demonstrate an understanding of safety protocols and best practices in a laboratory setting, including proper handling, and disposal of chemicals, as well as emergency procedures. Develop proficiency in fundamentals of qualitative analysis. Students will learn about various methods of detecting acid and basic radicals, techniques of group separation

title: General Chemistry
description:
This course will enable prospective chemistry majors to be in
touch with their basics, and also help those who are
undecided on their majors. The topics covered here are those
that will help the chemistry majors to prepare for the later
courses in the chemistry curriculum.  This course will introduce basic concepts of
electronic structure and periodic properties, Chemical bonding, the behavior of gases, and basic thermodynamics.
We will also talk about acid-base chemistry and chemical
equilibrium. Then we will discuss about structure of basic
organic molecules and some organic reactions. Finally, we will
introduce the concept of light-matter interaction.

title: Statistical Thermodynamics
description: This course builds on CHEM215 and offers a molecular approach to the concnept of entropy

title: Energetics and Kinetics I
description: Provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental principles and concepts governing the behavior of chemical systems concerning energy transformation.

title: Analytical Chemistry & Spectroscopy
description: Spectroscopic techniques play a very important role in science and technology. It is important to understand these methods to know their advantages, applicability and limitations.  Spectroscopy plays a pivotal role in our understanding of matter, energy and their interaction; in addition, it also plays a very important role in materials characterization. A few non-spectroscopic methods will also be discussed in this course. This course will cover the principles and application of the various experimental methods and basic instrumentation.

title: Chemistry Across Periodic Table
description: This course will introduce the concept of inorganic chemistry. Students will learn the evolution of the periodic table into a systematic arrangement of elements. The focus will be on the understanding of chemical properties of various inorganic molecules. Following the discussion on periodic table students will learn the chemistry of s-block, p-block, d-block elements

title: Advanced Energetics, Kinetics and Materials
description: This course builds on CHEM215 and offers more advanced topics in thermodynamics and kinetics. Topics include  chemical kinetics, enzyme catalysis, ionic and phase equilibria, solid state and surface chemistry

title: Coordination and Bio-inorganic Chemistry
