description: Metal complexes, in which a single central metal atom or ion is surrounded by several atoms or ions, play an important role in inorganic chemistry, especially for the elements of the d- block. Here students will learn about the nature of the ligand-metal bonding in terms of valence bond theory, crystal field theory, molecular orbital theory. Students will also learn about bio-inorganic chemistry

title: Symmetry and Group Theory
description: This course will introduce students to the symmetry elements in molecules, concept of point group, character table, use of group theory in conceptualizing symmetry properties, application of group theory in understanding spectroscopy, chemical reactions and bonding phenomenon

title: Molecules of Life
description: Molecules of Life introduces the fundamental biomolecules that form the basis of living systems. The course explores the structure and function of proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids. Students learn how these molecules interact to support cellular processes and metabolism. Emphasis is placed on the relationship between molecular structure and biological function. This course provides a foundation for understanding biochemistry and molecular biology in advanced studies.

title: Physical Chemistry Lab
description: This course will introduce students to the various advanced physicochemical experiments such as conductometry, pH metry, surface tension, viscosity, potentiometry and spectroscopy.

title: Systems Biology
description: The cell is an integrated device made of several thousand types of proteins molecules, each of which is a molecular machine to carry out very precise tasks. The cell lives in a complex environment and must make decisions about input signals including temperature and osmostic pressure, biological signalling molecules from other cells, beneficial nutrients and harmful chemicals. Information about the internal state of the cell, such as the level of metabolites and cell damage is also important. The information processing functions, that is, responding to these signals, is largely carried out by the transcription factors and networks. In this course we will discuss the engineering principles of biological networks and their implications in cellular functioning and diseases.

title: Physical Organic Chemistry
description: A detailed study of how organic reactions occur, emphasizing structure–reactivity relationships, energy profiles, acidity/basicity, isotope effects, catalysis, and the role of electronic, steric, and solvent effects in determining reaction pathways.

title: Making Carbon based Molecules
description: This course will introduce students to the methods of organic synthesis, common name reactions, and the mechanisms in organic chemistry. The focus of the course will be the organic mechanisms that will guide the students to perform stereo-specific organic synthesis. The major ingredients of the most common organic syntheses will be discussed.

title: Spectroscopic characterization of molecules
description: Spectroscopic characterization of molecules and materials. This course builds upon the fundamentals the student learned in CHEM216 and provides practical usage of key spectroscopic tools to identify various materials. Following a brief recap of the key principles covered in CHEM216, the course will extensively cover the use of infrared spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, nuclear magnetic spectroscopy, and ultraviolet spectroscopy for the structural elucidation of various materials.

title: Organic Chemistry Lab
description:
This course acquaints students with all basic organic laboratory procedures, presented in three major parts: (1) Techniques in organic chemistry laboratory, (2) Single-step organic synthesis, and (3) Organic qualitative analysis. 
The techniques section acquaints the students with standard techniques such as recrystallization, extraction, distillation, thin-layer chromatography, and column chromatography. Also, the techniques section has a relatively simple illustrative experiment with each. The synthesis section involves experiments related to simple reactions such as nitration, halogenation, esterification, etc. The Organic Qualitative Analysis section involves the characterization and/or identification of various organic compounds. In this section, students study and perform the characteristic chemical reactions of organic functional groups

title: Electrochemistry
description: This course aims at introducing concepts of electrochemistry and its application in various basic and industrial processes.

title: Cheminformatics
description: This course introduces students to the principles and applications of cheminformatics, an interdisciplinary field at the intersection of chemistry, computer science, and data analysis. The course covers molecular representation techniques, structure-property relationships, database management, virtual screening, molecular docking, and the use of machine learning and artificial intelligence in drug discovery and materials science. Students will gain hands-on experience with cheminformatics tools and software, enabling them to analyze chemical data, predict molecular properties, and design novel compounds. By the end of the course, students will be equipped with the computational skills and theoretical knowledge necessary for advanced research and applications in chemistry and related fields

title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging
description:
Brief General Overview of Imaging Science - Optical image capture
(camera and microscopy), electron microscopy, X-Ray Diffractometry
and Radiology, CT Scans, Ultrasonics, PET scans, Magnetic Resonance
Imaging (MRI)
· Introduction to Magnetic Resonance - Spins in a ‘Zeeman’ magnetic
field - establishment of ensemble nuclear magnetization at thermal
equilibrium - transitions between spin states - excitation and detection of
Nuclear Magnetic Resonance signals - time domain and frequency
domain description - echo formation. Spin relaxation.
Principles of Spatial encoding in Magnetic Resonance - application
of magnetic field gradients - Larmor frequency as a function of position -
frequency encoding - the generation of profiles in NMR and ESR
experiments run in the presence of gradients
· Combination of frequency encoding with phase encoding for 2D
imaging; ‘field of view’ in phase and frequency directions; the basic
Fourier imaging experiment (‘spin warp imaging’) - gradient echo
imaging; spin echo imaging; chemical shift selective imaging
· The MRI signal - Reciprocal space (k space) description of MR
imaging experiments - parallel scans, radial scans and single pass raster
techniques

title: Food Chemistry
description:
This course delves into the role of major food components such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, water, vitamins, and minerals. Students will gain an understanding of the chemical reactions that influence food quality, safety, flavor, texture, and nutritional value.
⮚ The course also covers the chemistry behind food additives, colorants, preservatives, and the interactions between food components and environmental factors. Through lectures, few laboratory exercises, and discussions, students will explore the chemical reactions behind common food phenomena like fermentation, browning, emulsification, and preservation. Practical examples such as the fermentation of dosa batter, the Maillard reaction in browning bread, role of preservatives in extending shelf life will be used to illustrate key concepts.

⮚ Food science is the study of the physical, biological, and chemical makeup of food and the principles underlying food processing, preservation, safety, and distribution. Food chemistry is a branch of science that focuses on the chemical composition, structure, and properties of food, as well as the changes it undergoes during preparation, storage, and consumption. This field combines principles of chemistry, biology, and nutrition to understand how various components in food interact, how they contribute to the sensory attributes like taste, color, and texture, and how they affect human health.

title: Basics of Food Chemistry
description:
⮚ This course delves into the role of major food components such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, water, vitamins, and minerals. Students will gain an understanding of the chemical reactions that influence food quality, safety, flavor, texture, and nutritional value.
⮚ The course also covers the chemistry behind food additives, colorants, preservatives, and the interactions between food components and environmental factors. Through lectures, few laboratory exercises, and discussions, students will explore the chemical reactions behind common food phenomena like fermentation, browning, emulsification, and preservation. Practical examples such as the fermentation of dosa batter, the Maillard reaction in browning bread, role of preservatives in extending shelf life will be used to illustrate key concepts.

title: Molecular modelling and Simulations: Biomolecules and rational drug design
description: This course aims to expose students to various computational methods to study many problems of interest in chemical and biological sciences. Students taking this course will learn the principles of computer simulations,  and applications  proteins . This course will be helpful to students who wish to pursue advanced research in computational chemistry and materials science and those who wish to pursue research careers in the industry.

title: Application of Group Theory
description: This course will introduce students to the symmetry elements in molecules, concept of point group, character table, use of group theory in conceptualizing symmetry properties, application of group theory in understanding spectroscopy, chemical reactions and bonding phenomenon

title: Organic Synthesis and Estimation
description: Demonstrate an understanding of safety protocols and best practices in a laboratory setting, including proper handling, and disposal of chemicals, as well as emergency procedures. Develop proficiency in fundamentals of organic synthesis, various chromatographic techniques

title: Molecular Modelling and Simulations - A Quantum Chemistry Approach
description: This advanced course provides an in-depth exploration of molecular modelling and simulations with a strong emphasis on quantum chemistry techniques. Students will gain theoretical knowledge and practical skills in using computational methods to investigate the properties and behavior of molecules. The course covers the principles of quantum mechanics as they apply to molecular systems and introduces various computational tools used in modern quantum chemistry.

title: Advanced Spectroscopy
description: This course provides a foundational understanding of stereochemistry, the study of the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in molecules and its impact on chemical behavior. Topics include chirality, enantiomers, diastereomers, conformational analysis, stereoisomerism in organic and inorganic systems, and the influence of symmetry elements. The course emphasizes the role of stereochemistry in physical and chemical properties, reactivity, and biological activity, with examples from natural products, pharmaceuticals, and materials. Students will develop skills in visualizing and representing stereochemical relationships, and in applying stereochemical principles to predict molecular interactions and reaction outcomes.

title: Stereochemistry
description: Spectroscopic techniques play a very important role in science and technology. It is important to understand these methods to know their advantages, applicability and limitations. Spectroscopy plays a pivotal role in our understanding of matter, energy and their interaction; in addition, it also plays a very important role in materials characterization. A few non spectroscopic methods will also be discussed in this course. This course will cover the principles and application of the various experimental methods and basic instrumentation. Basic high school mathematics and an introductory course on quantum chemistry are prerequisites.

title: Instrumental Methods of Analysis
description: This course will introduce students to the various spectroscopic experiments based on absorption, emission and FTIR spectrosocpy

title: Introduction to two dimensional NMR spectrscopy
description: This course provides an introduction to the principles and applications of two-dimensional (2D) nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Students will learn the theoretical foundations of 2D NMR, including the concepts of spin interactions, coherence transfer, and pulse sequences. The course will cover key techniques such as COSY, HSQC, HMBC, and NOESY, with a focus on their utility in structural elucidation of organic and biomolecular compounds. Through a combination of lectures and problem-solving sessions, students will develop the ability to interpret 2D NMR spectra and apply these methods to solve complex structural problems in chemistry and biology.

title: Advanced Inorganic Chemistry
description: This course provides an in-depth exploration of advanced topics in inorganic chemistry, emphasizing the theoretical and practical aspects that define the field. Key areas of focus include advanced coordination chemistry, organometallic compounds, reaction mechanisms, and the role of inorganic compounds in catalysis. The course also covers bonding theories, electronic structure, and spectroscopic methods used in the characterization of inorganic systems. Contemporary applications such as materials science, energy storage, and environmental chemistry are integrated to highlight the relevance of inorganic chemistry in modern research and industry. Through lectures, problem-solving sessions, and research-based discussions, students will deepen their understanding of the fundamental principles and current trends in advanced inorganic chemistry. he bioinorganic chemistry section focuses on the function of metal ions in biological systems, such as metalloenzymes, electron transport, and metal homeostasis. The course also examines recent advances in medicinal inorganic chemistry and the design of metal-based drugs.

title: Advanced Analytical Chemistry
description: This course delves into advanced concepts and techniques in analytical chemistry, focusing on both theoretical principles and practical applications. Topics include modern instrumental methods such as advanced spectroscopy (e.g., NMR, mass spectrometry, and X-ray techniques), chromatography, electrochemical analysis, and hyphenated techniques (e.g., GC-MS, LC-MS). Emphasis will be placed on data analysis, signal processing, and error minimization to ensure accurate and reproducible results. Students will explore applications of analytical chemistry in fields such as environmental monitoring, pharmaceutical analysis, forensic science, and material characterization. Hands-on laboratory sessions, case studies, and discussions on cutting-edge research will equip students with the skills needed to tackle complex analytical problems in both academic and industrial settings.

title: Programming and Computational Chemistry Lab
description: This lab course introduces students to the fundamentals of programming and computational techniques used in chemistry. The course focuses on leveraging computational tools to solve chemical problems and analyze data effectively. Students will gain hands-on experience with molecular modeling, quantum chemistry calculations, and statistical analysis of chemical data. Topics include molecular dynamics simulations, electronic structure calculations, reaction mechanism modeling, and visualization of chemical systems. Emphasis will be placed on developing programming skills, algorithmic thinking, and the application of computational methods to real-world chemical challenges. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to independently approach and solve problems in computational chemistry and contribute to research projects in the field.

title: Molecular Modelling and Simulations - A Quantum Chemistry Approach
description: This advanced course provides an in-depth exploration of molecular modelling and simulations with a strong emphasis on quantum chemistry techniques. Students will gain theoretical knowledge and practical skills in using computational methods to investigate the properties and behavior of molecules. The course covers the principles of quantum mechanics as they apply to molecular systems and introduces various computational tools used in modern quantum chemistry.

title: Programming literacy
description:
This is a 2-credit; bridge elective course in programming; for students looking to pursue programming intensive disciplines. It helps students construct, think about, and work with computer programs as objects by

teaching compositional modeling and incremental program decomposition, drawing from How To Design Programs using Racket.

title: Discrete Mathematics
description: Discrete Mathematics course will provide students with their first glimpse of how to think rigorously about discrete and finite phenomena. The course will begin by introducing students to the language and grammar of mathematics. It will then proceed to an axiomatic construction of the natural numbers, and introduce the fundamental mathematical notions of sets, relations, and functions. The remainder of the course will be organized around three distinct modules: number theory, permutations and counting, and graph theory.

title: Introduction to Computation Through Programming
description: This course offers a foundational understanding of essential programming methods, with a focus on their practical applications. The objective is to facilitate fluency in programming and the ability to switch between various programming languages. The course introduces fundamental algorithms and data structures, and how they can be used to solve computational problems or extract information about given data.

title: Programming, Algorithms and Data Structures
description:
The course builds on the first course in programming to serve as a gentle introduction to more
 advanced ideas in programming with more advanced data structures. Further, it ties up the
 practice of programming with reasoning about program performance and correctness. The
 questions that motivate the course include:
 (1) What does it mean for a program or an algorithm to run at a particular time or
 consume a certain amount of space?
 (2) What do data structures have to do with run-time and space? How do we build more
 efficient data structures, which can computationally capture a range of objects?
 (3) How do we make them more efficient? Or handle complex trade-offs that are involved
 in this regard.
 (4) How do we use all that we know about programming to build implementable interactive
 programs of intermediate scale?

title: Introduction to Linear Algebra
description:
Linear Algebra (Vectors, Vector Spaces, Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors, Linear Transformations,
 SVD). This course offers an introduction to a range of essential mathematical topics centred around linear
 algebra of finite dimensional real vector spaces, multivariable calculus, and probability. This course is aimed
 at both computer science and data science major/minor students, who have to/wish to pursue advanced
 courses without the necessary background in mathematics. The focus will be to inculcate familiarity with the
 language of continuous mathematics and develop an understanding of the intuition behind the concepts, and
 an ability to apply these concepts. It will further develop an ability to write basic proofs in these topics.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
description:
Algorithms are unambiguous instructions for solving problems. From a utilitarian perspective, efficient use of computer machinery is both desirable and necessary. One of the key concerns regarding efficiency in computing is the time taken by a computing machine to run an algorithm. This course introduces some general principles and guidelines which enable designing faster algorithms for a wide range of computational problems.
 
 Learning Outcomes include:
 Learn to distinguish slow algorithms from faster ones by quantifying the amount of time taken by an algorithm to solve a problem through asymptotic analysis.
 A view of the general
 paradigms used for solving a problem, and an 
 overview of basic complexity classes.
 Prove the correctness of an algorithm, and do a runtime analysis.
 Ability to abstract computational tasks, and applying algorithmic techniques towards problem solving.

title: Systems Programming
description: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of systems through systems programming in C, delving into the intricate workings of processors, memory subsystems, and program execution. We will examine the process of compiling C programs into machine-level instructions, gaining insights into compiler mechanics and code optimization techniques. Throughout the journey, students will acquire invaluable skills for developing secure, reliable programs that leverage computing resources effectively.

title: Introduction to Deep Learning
description:
This beginner-level deep learning course is
 designed for 3rd- and 4th-year students and can also serve as a fresh
 introduction to modern machine learning. It provides a thorough
 foundation in core concepts by beginning with classical methods such as
 regression and classification, and then building naturally towards shallow
 and deep neural networks.
 The course begins with regression through a simple curve-fitting
 example, introducing key ideas such as error functions, regularization,
 and the bias–variance trade-off. Regression and classification are then
 presented as single-layer networks, highlighting linear models,
 discriminant functions, and generative vs. discriminative classifiers.
 
 These methods motivate the shift from fixed basis functions to learning
 representations directly from data, naturally leading to neural networks.
 Students are then introduced to deep neural networks, with a focus on
 gradient descent, backpropagation, and regularization. The course
 concludes with an introduction to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
 and their practical applications

title: Applied Probability and Statistics
description: This course offers a foundational understanding of probability and statistics essential for study of randomized algorithms, modeling and data science.

title: Principles of Artificial Intelligence
description: This course provides an introduction to the principles and practices of artificial intelligence (AI) Safety, Ethics and Society, focusing on the design of intelligent agents. Students will explore how agents represent knowledge, reason, plan, learn, and interact with complex environments.

title: Principles of Programming Languages
description: Principles of Programming Languages is a deep dive into analytical foundations of programming languages, their design, and implementation. These foundations have proved to be of enduring importance, and hold the key to understanding future developments in programming languages. These foundations are centered around the semantics of program elements, which reflect how program elements are interpreted as a program is executed. This course will use interpretation of programs as the approach to learn these principles - a “mental model” - of programming languages. It will draw on the PLAI (“Programming Languages: Application and Interpretation”) body of  material and will be  taught using Racket, a dialect of Scheme. In this course, “language” does not refer to “surface structure”, also known as “syntax”, but will focus on the “semantics” or meaning of programs

title: Principles of Computer Systems
description:
This course delves into the intricate workings of computer systems, focusing on the 
  interaction between application programs and the underlying system software. Through theoretical 
  exploration and practical exercises, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of how 
  programs are executed on a system, the role of operating systems in managing resources, and 
  techniques for efficient program communication and concurrency. Topics include the role of the 
  linker in combining program components, the cooperation between modern operating systems and 
  hardware, and the management of program execution and memory. Students will build a strong 
  foundation in the interaction between programs and hardware, setting the stage for advanced 
  exploration. Students will also learn about the basic I/O services provided by Unix operating 
  systems and how to leverage them to build applications for various purposes, such as web clients 
  and servers. Special attention will be given to techniques for writing concurrent programs, enabling 
  efficient utilisation of multi-core processors and enhancing program performance. By the end of 
  this section, students will possess the skills to develop robust, high-performance applications 
  capable of handling diverse communication scenarios.

title: Machine Learning
description: This course is a hands-on introduction to tools and techniques in machine learning to model complex phenomena and solve problems in a variety of domains including bioinformatics, computer vision, computer science, computational finance, econometrics, operations management, and sports data analytics. This course covers the following topics: (i) Simple Linear Regression, Multiple Linear Regression, Training and Validation, standard error measures and analysis of model predictions, model selection, and regularization; (ii) Classification: Logistic Regression, Linear Discriminant Analysis, and support vector machines; and (iv) Overview of Unsupervised Learning: Principal Component Analysis and Clustering techniques. This course will also introduce Python tools and libraries.

title: Models of Computation
description: It is imperative for any graduate of computer science to understand the formal definition of computation, and the possibilities and limits of computing. Moreover, any distinction between decidability and undecidability needs a good mathematical model of computers and computation. This course introduces the powerful idea of mathematical models to analyse computation, and the nature of the relationship between formal languages, logic and machines. This course introduces the classical mathematical models used to analyse computation, including finite state automata, grammars, and Turing Machines.

title: Network Security
description:
This course will provide an overview of
a. Computer networks, architecture of the Internet, and a detailed discussion on some of the important protocols and algorithms associated with the transport and network layers
b. Fundamental principles of network communication security and some important cryptographic techniques

title: Logic
description: Formal logic has played a key role in development of modern computer science, with applications ranging from architecture, databases, verification to AI and theory of computation. This course will introduce students to proofs and techniques of soundness, completeness and provability in the formal systems. Formal systems introduced in the course include (but are not restricted to) propositional and predicate calculus. It will additionally include some of the resolution theorems from proof theory, which are essential to understand automated theorem proving.

title: Understanding Language: An Exploration of Chomskian Linguistics
Computer Vision
description: This course aims to offer a comprehensive introduction to computer vision, focusing on how computers can make decisions by extracting information from digital images and videos. Key applications include robotics, manufacturing, and healthcare, where visual feature extraction, detection, and classification are essential functions. Students will learn fundamental concepts such as camera imaging geometry, feature detection and matching, multiview geometry (including stereo and reconstruction), and machine learning techniques like linear regression, logistic regression, and image classification along with brief overview of convolutional neural networks (CNNs).

title: Introduction to Applied Computing
description:
Computational engineering is an emerging field that focuses on using computer simulations and
modeling to solve complex engineering problems. It bridges the gap between theoretical science
& engineering principles and practical applications by leveraging computational tools and
techniques of computer science.
The “Introduction to Computational Engineering” course is a semi-advanced view of how
computer systems execute programs, store information, and communicate. The intent is two fold
-
a) to give the CS students the exposure to apply their knowledge in few applied areas and
b) the students from other fields of basic sciences (physics, chemistry, biology, economics)
the exposure to understand computing a bit deeper.

title: Type Systems and Alternative Semantics
description: This course complements COMP308 with some extended topics – type systems and alternative application semantics. Understanding type systems is crucial for many modern programming languages and the course will develop that understanding (similar to COMP308) through implementation of a range of type systems and proving their soundness. Students will also be introduced to goal search as a programming paradigm with the associated concepts of unification and backtracking, with an introduction to Prolog. Lazy evaluation and implementation strategies for it will also be dealt with. The course will continue to use (Typed) Racket as in COMP308.

title: Algorithms for Social Choice
description:
Social choice theory is the study of aggregating individual preferences. One of the
 immediate applications is voting: how to aggregate each individual’s choice into a
 collective choice. In the recently concluded New York City mayoral elections, voters ranked the
 candidates. On the other hand, in the upcoming Bihar elections, voters will choose
 their favourite candidate. Which system is fairer? Social choice, however, is not just restricted to voting but to welfare economics in general where the state has to distribute welfare in a way that maximises public satisfaction. In this course, we will look at social choice from a computation lens. We will contemplate on the consequences of theoretical results and provide
 computational safeguards to manipulation tactics like bribery.

title: Quantum Programming
description:
This course provides comprehensive knowledge of implementing quantum
 algorithms using Qiskit. Qiskit has been an integral part of practical quantum
 computing. A key component of the course is implementing known quantum
 algorithms in using IBM Qiskit, understanding various challenges due to the effect of
 noise and methods to mitigate them.

title: Security: Technology, Privacy and Ethics
description:
Much of the contemporary life in the post internet era relies on information security. This course teaches the basic concepts and principles of information security, and the fundamental
 approaches to secure computers and networks. It mainly focuses on security fundamentals, standard cryptographic functions and protocols, threats and defenses for real-world
 systems, privacy, legal & ethical issues of security, computer forensics, malicious software, denial of service, and firewalls.

title: Algorithmic game theory
description:
What connects routing in computer networks to IPL player auctions? What connects dynamic pricing of flights to arms control negotiations? It turns out all of these scenarios are where there are sequences of decisions to be made. Decisions that are driven by some rationale: enhance efficiency of networks, get the best players at lowest price, sell all flights tickets at high prices, etc.
Game Theory is the mathematics of decision making that demystifies the complex logic of such interactions. It remains one of the most fundamental concepts in economics; in fact, multiple game theorists have won the Economics Nobel Prize, the most famous being perhaps John Nash.
With high-stakes trading and the rise of multi-agent AI, modern game theory has a particularly computational flavour, that requires not only a mathematical understanding of decision making, but also to compute those decisions quickly.
This course is designed for computer science students with an interest in real-world algorithms and economics students with an interest in the computational aspects of the subject. It will cover classical topics and then give an overview of modern trends.

title: Autonomous Agents and Sequential Decision Making in AI
description:
This course examines how autonomous computational systems observe, reason, learn, and act across increasingly complex environments. Structured around a unified “agentic systems” framework, the course introduces students to sequential decision-making through deterministic search, strategic planning, probabilistic reasoning, reinforcement learning, and modern tool-using AI agents. Rather than treating classical AI, reinforcement learning, and contemporary LLM-based systems as disconnected paradigms, the course presents them as successive architectural layers of intelligent agency. Students progressively construct computational agents that evolve from search-based solvers into adaptive systems capable of planning under uncertainty, learning from interaction, invoking external tools, maintaining memory, and operating within safety constraints.
Through an integrated practical lab structure, students maintain a cumulative software repository that is incrementally extended throughout the semester. By the end of the course, students will have designed and deployed a robust autonomous system that combines formal algorithmic rigor with contemporary AI engineering practices.
The course emphasizes durable conceptual architectures over transient frameworks, ensuring students understand the computational foundations underlying modern AI systems while remaining adaptable to future technological developments.

title: Topics in algorithms
description:
This 2-credit elective course bridges the gap between classic polynomial-time algorithms (COMP210) and advanced problem-solving paradigms required for computationally intensive optimization challenges of importance in the real-world.
The course introduces the notion of NP-completeness and then introduces paradigms for tackling NP-hard problems. The course focuses on foundational algorithmic problems such as Network Flows and Vertex Cover across multiple frameworks to give a cohesive understanding of how an algorithmic strategy shifts
depending on the computational constraints and desired solution accuracy.

title: Introduction to Natural Language Processing
description:
This course provides a hands-on introduction to Natural Language Processing (NLP), blending practical applications with core theoretical concepts. It covers essential lexical and semantic operations such as text normalization and word embeddings, along with standard metrics for measuring content similarity, text classification techniques, and methods for modeling context and meaning in language data. The course concludes with an accessible introduction to the practice and theory of Transformers and Large Language Models (LLMs).
 Throughout, the focus will be on implementing the concepts discussed in class. Students will work with leading NLP libraries including SpaCy, NLTK, and Scikit-learn. By the end of the course, they will have gained both practical skills and a solid theoretical foundation, preparing them for advanced study or professional roles in NLP.

title: Software Design Practical
description: This is a project based course that works towards students having built a complete application of their choosing from ground up, with guidance from instructors. Students will be introduced to programming methodologies and tools and processes (iterative approaches) that will help them with the task. They will also be introduced to the required architectural components and how they interface with each other. The human side of building such applications includes requirements gathering, basic user study, ethics issues and broadly “responsible engineering”.

title: Mathematical Foundations of Computer Science 3, MFCS-3
Fundamentals of Digital Image Processing
description:
The purpose of this course is to introduce the fundamentals of 2-D digital image processing with emphasis in image enhancement techniques, image filtering design and applications such as
 fingerprint recognition, industrial machine vision for manufacturing sectors, medical diagnosis, assessment of crops or weather prediction, object detection or recognition etc. This course introduces
 students to the steps of a typical digital image processing pipeline , geometric image transformations, interpolation and enhancement techniques.

title: Introduction to Computer Music
description: This course presents this fascinating field spanning music composition, sound synthesis, new ways of thinking about music, computer programming, languages invented for music composition, audio signal processing and mathematics of music.

title: High Performance Computing
description:
This course introduces students to the concept of high performance computing (HPC). Students will be taught the fundamentals of HPC and the techniques to solve numerical/programming problems where performance is critical.

Topics covered include refresher course on C++ programming, algorithmic and procedural problem solving in shared and distributed memory systems using multi threading (OpenMP) and message passing (MPI) respectively.

title: Python for Data Science
description:
This course will introduce the students to (i) Elements of Programming (variables,
 assignments, built-in data types, conditionals, loops, arrays, input-output processing; (ii) Functions and
 Modules; (iii) Object-Oriented programming; and (iv) basic algorithms and data structures (data frames,
 dictionary, list, tuples, etc) for sorting and searching. This course will also introduce the students to a
 collection of open-source tools that are required to analyse data and solve data science problems including
 pandas, NumPy, and matplotlib, and seaborn.

title: Introduction to Data Science
description: This course introduces the students to the field of data science and the kind of problems that can be solved by data science. Students will learn key data science skills, techniques, and concepts, including data analysis, statistical modelling, and some insight into some standard AI/ML algorithms. The course would also bring the perspectives of data from multiple branches of social sciences and provide a fundamental understanding of how data is conceptualized through the prism of humanities and social sciences. Further, the course will cover how data science skills can be used to address some of the vital problems in the field of social sciences. This would be done by a series of guest lectures by faculty members from social sciences. This is a hands-on course where after a quick primer on Python, the student will start with sourcing, processing, and cleaning a dataset. Then, use Python to mine data from its source and analyse available data by using NumPy and Pandas. Subsequently, the student will be introduced to modelling data to perform predictions using the SciPy, scikit-learn, and stats models libraries. In addition, the student will be introduced to visualization methods using the matplotlib and seaborn library to visually understand the patterns in the data. By the end of this course, students will be able to work on data science tasks practically with different Python libraries and achieve their goals.

title: Mathematical Foundations of Data Science
description: This course will cover the following topics that are fundamental to the field of data science: Discrete Mathematics: logic, sets, functions, relations, mathematical induction, counting, recursion, trees, and graphs.Probability: axioms of probability; conditional probability and independence; random variables; continuous random variables and limit theorems.

title: Applied Statistics
description:
This course will begin by providing an overview of statistical thinking: descriptive statistics,
 simulating various standard discrete and continuous distributions in R, sampling distribution and its
 connection with the law of large numbers and central limit theorem. Secondly, this course will introduce
 statistical inference: sampling and its distribution characteristics, point estimation, and hypothesis testing.
 We illustrate this module by solving some inference problems using time series data obtained from different
 contexts.

title: Data Structures and Algorithms
description:
This course will provide a rigorous introduction to elementary data structures and their
 analysis and applications to various computational problems in computer science. In addition, this course
 will introduce students to key algorithmic techniques for design and analysis of data structures for various
 problems that arise in the field of computer science. The course provides a broad overview of fundamental
 concepts involved in the design of algorithms and their complexity analysis.

title: Data Management
description: This course focuses on database system concepts and architectures, various data models, Database Design using ER models, UML, Relational Algebra etc. Database as well as web-based programming using SQL, PHP etc., will be covered. It also introduces theoretical concepts on database design and normalization, data storage with the corresponding file structures based on indexing using B-Trees, B+-Trees etc. Further, transaction processing and concurrency control principles will be introduced. Some applications on Information Retrieval and Data Warehousing will be covered.

title: Business Applications of Artificial Intelligence
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is all around us. It‘s how Google answers our searches, Amazon recommends products, ChatGPT helps answer questions, and Spotify plays another song. Artificial Intelligence is changing the way decisions are being made in the world today. This course is intended to enable students to understand a critical aspect of AI, i.e., industry applications, scenarios, and use cases. The course covers this very critical aspect of AI, i.e., use cases of AI in a variety of industries such as Sales and Marketing, Retail Manufacturing, Healthcare, Education, to name a few.

title: Introduction to C Programming
description: This course offers a comprehensive introduction to C programming, focusing on developing problem-solving skills and a strong understanding of foundational programming concepts. Students will learn to learn to work on different data structures and write structured, efficient, and modular programs using control structures, functions.

title: Introduction to Calculus
description:
This course provides an overview of the following topics: Calculus (Limits, Continuity, Basic
 Overview of Differential and Integral Calculus with Applications that involve modelling, and Differential
 Equations). Multivariable Calculus: Derivatives, partial derivatives, differentiation with respect to a vector;
 gradient, Hessian, Jacobian. Taylor's theorem in 1 and n dimensions, with Lagrange remainder.
 Optimization in 1 and n dimensions, classification of stationary points. Constrained optimization and the
 method of Lagrange multipliers.

title: Financial Analytics
description: The Financial Analytics course is designed to provide students with the analytical skills and techniques necessary to navigate the complex world of financial markets, investment strategies, and corporate finance. The course focuses on integrating quantitative methods and data-driven insights into financial decision-making processes. Through a combination of financial theory, modelling techniques, and hands-on analytical applications, students will develop a strong foundation in financial modelling, portfolio optimization, risk analysis, derivatives trading, and technical analysis. The course will enable students to use descriptive analytics to summarize financial data, prescriptive analytics to optimize investment strategies, and predictive analytics to forecast market trends and price movements.

title: Digitalization and Society: Understanding Risks, Promoting Justice
description:
In an era dominated by digital technologies, which have seemingly integrated themselves in every  realm of life, and have been taken up by industry, business, policymakers, civil society alike,  understanding the impacts of digitalization on society is paramount. This course delves into the  complexities of digitalization, exploring both its risks and opportunities while emphasizing the  pursuit of societal justice through informed design and ethical considerations. It encourages  students to go beyond the usual narratives of the benefits of digitalization and ask critical  questions which can help shape it in ways that recenter the emancipation of diverse types of end users. The course draws primarily from academic work in the fields of Science and Technology  Studies (STS), Critical Social Science, Feminist Posthumanities and Media Studies. 
This course offers a unique opportunity to explore cutting-edge issues at the intersection of  technology, society, and ethics using ‘real world’ case studies from India, Europe, the US and  beyond. By gaining insights into the complex societal impacts of digitalization, students will be  equipped to navigate challenges on the topic in both academic and industry settings. Whether  pursuing further research or embarking on a career in technology, this course aims to provide a  solid foundation for understanding and promoting justice in the digital age.

title: Generative AI, Agentic AI, and the Importance of Responsible AI
description:
This course introduces students to the transformative world of Artificial Intelligence, with a focus on
 Generative AI, Agentic AI, and the critical need for Responsible AI. Through real-world case studies,
 accessible tools, and thoughtful discussions, learners will explore how AI is reshaping creativity,
 decision-making, and ethics in modern society.

title: Applied dynamical systems
description:
This is an introductory course on applied dynamical systems for the data science major. The
 main aim of the discipline of dynamical systems is to model the phenomenon of dynamics or
 change that is ubiquitous in the real world. The earliest examples of dynamical systems
 addressed by humankind were the motion of planets and other celestial bodies, changes in
 seasons, and observations of the life cycles of plants and animals.
 Though it is impossible to track the change in each and every aspect of a given system with
 many dynamic parts, overall patterns persist that capture gross features of the system.
 Examples include periodic recurrences of phenomena, irreversibility of certain processes,
 and so on. The theoretical model of a dynamical system aims to capture such overall global
 features of the system in mathematically precise terms.
 An important idea that pervades the study of dynamical systems is chaos: the sensitivity of a
 dynamical system to initial conditions. The phenomenon of chaos is indeed the norm rather
 than the exception in the real world, and it appears in a variety of forms with different
 mechanisms as well. In this course, we will give an introduction to chaos and its importance
 in understanding the time dependence of real-world phenomena.
 A good understanding of the basic concepts in Calculus and Linear algebra is encouraged,
 but the course is designed to be self-contained and will include a review of the important and
 
 relevant concepts. The emphasis will be on visualizing the important ideas rather than on
 rigorous proofs. The course also aims to give a flavour of the interdisciplinary nature of the
 discipline via many case studies in biology, electric circuits, mechanics, finance, and so on.

title: Numerical Methods for Data Science
description:
Numerical methods are practical methods to find appropriate solutions to
 mathematical problems that cannot be solved analytically. This includes both problems
 described by algebraic and differential equations. In addition to solving the equations,
 inevitable data analysis techniques like interpolation and extrapolation are also carried out
 numerically. Understanding these methods are essential for a Data Science student. In this
 course the students will be taught about numerical methods involving non-linear and linear
 equations for finding roots, interpolation, extrapolation, numerical differentiation, integration
 and solution of ordinary differential equation and partial differential equation.

title: Geometry for Computer Vision
description:
How do computers "see" the world? The mathematical foundation of computer vision lies in
 understanding how shapes and images transform—and this course will teach you that
 language from the ground up.
 Starting with the familiar geometry of high school (Euclidean), we'll discover how different
 types of transformations create entirely new geometries. You'll learn how allowing shapes to
 be scaled gives us Similarity Geometry, how parallel lines behave in Affine Geometry, and
 ultimately how Projective Geometry explains why railroad tracks appear to meet at the
 horizon—the same mathematics that lets computers reconstruct 3D scenes from 2D
 photographs.
 This isn't your typical geometry course. Following Felix Klein's revolutionary approach, we'll
 see geometry not as a collection of theorems about triangles and circles, but as the study of
 what stays the same when shapes transform. This unified view connects ancient Greek
 mathematics to cutting-edge computer vision applications like facial recognition, autonomous
 vehicles, and augmented reality.
 No advanced mathematics required—just high school algebra, basic calculus, and curiosity
 about how mathematical ideas connect. Through concrete examples and visual reasoning,
 you'll build intuition for concepts that usually appear only in graduate courses.
 
 This course sets the foundation for Computer Vision II, where you'll apply these geometric
 tools to real-world vision problems. Whether you're interested in AI, robotics, computer
 graphics, or just want to see mathematics from a fresh perspective,

title: Introduction to Computer Vision (DATA)
description:
How does your phone straighten a photograph of a document? How do panorama apps stitch
 multiple images seamlessly? How do self-driving cars understand depth from stereo cameras? This
 course bridges the mathematical foundations from Geometry for Computer Vision I to real-world
 computer vision applications.
 Building on your solid understanding of projective geometry from Course I, you'll learn how cameras
 capture 3D scenes as 2D images and how to reverse this process computationally. Through hands-on
 programming projects, you'll implement the algorithms behind everyday vision applications—from
 document scanning to 3D reconstruction from photos.
 The course balances mathematical understanding with practical implementation. You'll derive key
 algorithms to understand the mathematics, then implement them in Python to see how they work
 on real data. A substantial optimization primer ensures you understand the mathematical
 foundations underlying computer vision algorithms—what is a cost function, how gradient descent
 works, why RANSAC handles outliers.
 
 No advanced mathematics required—just the geometry from DATA239/COMP239, linear algebra,
 basic calculus, and willingness to learn Python. Through weekly programming assignments, you'll
 build proficiency so that by course end, you'll have implemented core algorithms from scratch and
 built a substantial team project suitable for your portfolio.
 This course sets the foundation for understanding both classical geometric computer vision and
 modern learning-based approaches. Whether you're interested in AI, robotics, AR/VR, or just want
 to understand the technology you use daily, this course offers a unique blend of rigorous
 mathematics and hands-on application.

title: Natural Language Processing (DATA)
description:
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to Natural Language Processing
 (NLP), covering foundational concepts, classical machine learning techniques, and
 modern deep learning architectures. Students will learn practical methods for text
 preprocessing, feature extraction, and building NLP models for applications like text
 classification, translation, and summarization. The course also explores real-world
 applications of NLP in domains such as finance, cybersecurity, and healthcare,
 equipping learners with skills to implement and evaluate advanced NLP systems

title: Multivariate Analysis
description: The course will present the concepts and methods of muItivariate analysis to the readers who have read at least one statistics course. The applications of multivariate methods is emphasized. The concepts of matrix algebra are very important. Matrices simplify the presentation of muItivariate techniques. Normal distribution and Regression models are discussed in the multivariate setup. Further, we introduce key concepts like principal component analysis, factor analysis, discriminant analysis and cluster analysis etc., which are quite relevant for data science.

title: Fundamentals of Applied Cryptography
description:
Cryptography is the science of designing encryption and decryption algorithms for
 providing secure communication between parties over an insecure channel. In the
 present age, cryptography has gained importance and is widely used in many
 disciplines.
 This is a first course in cryptography, with a focus on the algorithmic foundations of
 real-world cryptosystems, aiming to strike a balance between theory and application.
 In this class, we will cover the basic mathematics necessary to better understand
 various cryptographic protocols, algorithms, and attacks. This will provide a solid
 understanding of the practical issues involved in applying cryptographic techniques
 to design secure systems.

title: Application of Matrices to Arts and Sciences
description:
Matrix analysis has become a very important subject in data science which connects
data to various fields. In today’s world, computers are inexpensive and fast, and it is
easy to procure large amounts of data, and many outcomes are dependent on the
interplay between several disciplines and data. This course, therefore, takes an
interdisciplinary approach and attempts to connect a wide range of subjects, from
economics and finance to biology, using the language of matrices. It will provide
students a sound understanding of many practical issues faced in data science.

title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence (Data)
description: Recent advances in computing and information technologies, including hardware, software, databases, networks and communications have enabled the commercialization of many applications of Artificial Intelligence. Specifically, in the case of Supervised Learning, Deep Neural Networks and related algorithms have been able to achieve or even surpass human-like accuracy in applications like face recognition, voice recognition, automated driving, language translation, etc. This has given rise to multiple deployments of AI-based applications not only in the private sector but also in the Government. These deployments in areas such as recidivism prediction, algorithmic online ad targeting, drug addiction risk prediction, criminal intentionality detection in early stage shoplifting, etc. promise the effectiveness and efficiency of evidence-based decision-making. This early success has spurred rapid and frantic development of solutions using AI/ML and associated technologies without adequate safeguards and regulations. However, of late, multiple cases of bias and unfairness have been reported in the decisions made by AI/ML based algorithms, thus, raising ethical questions. In addition, AI/ML-based decisions cannot be explained easily due to their “black-box” nature. Impenetrability of AI/ML algorithmic decisions has reduced “trust” in the very algorithms that promised so much. This has spurred a call for Explainable AI (XAI) – AI-based decision-making that incorporates the notions of fairness, accountability and transparency.

title: Introduction to Statistical Learning
description: This course is a hands-on introduction to tools and techniques in machine learning to model complex phenomena and solve problems in a variety of domains including health care, medical diagnostics, image recognition, stock prediction, and sports data analytics. This course covers the following topics: (i) Simple Linear Regression, Multiple Linear Regression, Training and Validation, standard error measures and analysis of model predictions, model selection, and regularization; (ii) Classification: Logistic Regression, Linear Discriminant Analysis, and support vector machines; and (iv) Overview of Unsupervised Learning: Principal Component Analysis and Clustering techniques. This course will also introduce Python tools and libraries including scikit-learn, imblearn etc.

title: Deep Learning (DATA)
description: The course essentially is a hands-on introduction to various types of neural networks used in  machine learning and decision trees. Topics include Decision Trees, Bagging Random Forests and Boosting,  Introduction to Basic Neural Networks, Activation Functions, Deep Neural Networks (Convolutional Neural  Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (LSTM), Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks  (GAN), and transformer architectures with applications to problems in Image Processing and Computer  Vision. This course will also introduce Python tools and libraries including scikit-learn, Keras, TensorFlow,  and PyTorch.

title: Applied Network Science
description:
Network science plays a crucial role in modern data science for modeling and analyzing
 relationships among complex systems. Graphs provide a powerful framework for
 representing and studying interactions across domains such as social networks, biological
 systems, brain connectivity, and technological networks. This course offers an applied
 introduction to graph-theoretic concepts and network science using Python.
 Students will learn how to represent data as networks and analyze their structural properties,
 including connectivity, paths, centrality measures, and clustering. The course further
 introduces network models such as random, small-world, and scale-free networks to
 understand real-world structures, along with community detection techniques to uncover
 hidden patterns within networks.
 Through hands-on exercises and case studies, students will construct and analyze networks,
 implement key algorithms, and interpret results in real-world contexts. The knowledge gained
 will support applications in areas such as social network analysis, biological and brain
 networks, graph-based machine learning, and data-driven decision-making systems.

title: Principles of Economics
description: The Principles of Economics course introduces students to foundational economic principles, introducing tools and models that enable a rigorous examination of everyday economic phenomena. It presents fundamental theories in micro- as well as macroeconomics, covering markets and prices, trade-offs, efficiencies, externalities, as well as the behavior of individuals and firms. The course initiates an examination of broader systemic phenomena such as trade, growth, poverty, employment, and inequality. At the end of the course, students should be familiar with foundational economic terminology, develop a basic understanding of markets and their potential failures, begin to appreciate the linkages between economic phenomena, and most importantly, recognize the importance of a rigorous approach in exploring economic questions.

title: Microeconomics I
description:
This course is the first of a two-part sequence aimed at providing a thorough understanding of the concepts and methods of microeconomics. 
  
  In this course, we will study consumer behavior in detail – looking at consumer preferences, budget constraints, and the utility maximization problem in the framework of Marshallian analysis. We will then learn how consumers allocate consumption, get an insight into income and substitution effects, and derive consumer demand functions. We will take a quick look at game theory, which investigates strategic decision-making among a small group of players. We will also briefly touch upon the theory of producer behavior, beginning with a stylized model of the firm, and understanding how economists model production, and how firms minimize their costs. 
  
  Part two of the Microeconomics sequence will cover producer behavior in greater detail, and examine how producers, consumers and the government interact in different settings.

title: Macroeconomics I
description:
This course will aim to introduce the students to the basic concepts of Macroeconomics. Transitioning from the individual and firm behaviour of microeconomics, it will focus on the aggregate economy incomes and economic growth.  It will build on the introductory concepts like consumption, savings, investment, government spending, GDP, money, inflation, wages, unemployment, current and capital accounts, fiscal deficits, role of expectations etc. Students will learn about the engine room of the macroeconomic world- the aggregate demand function and the IS and LM.
Topics: Economic methods, Defining and measuring macroeconomic aggregates-national output and income-CPI, WPI, Deflator, Introduction to Aggregate Incomes-Growth, Productivity, & Technology, Unemployment, Inflation, Core of Macroeconomics-Aggregate Expenditure and Equilibrium Output, Government- Fiscal Policy, Credit Markets and the Monetary System. Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply. Introduction to ISLM Framework.

title: Econometrics I
description:
This course introduces students to mathematical and statistical techniques for conducting empirical analysis in economics. It lays the foundations for the study of techniques to estimate and test hypotheses connected to quantifiable economic relationships. Students will learn to estimate and test basic regression models. The course will also prepare students to interpret estimated regression models and enable them to explore model biases that arise because of data limitations, misspecification, heteroscedasticity, and other factors. This course is a mix of conceptual understanding and practical application. Concepts will be explored through recourse to the textbook, and class notes and discussion. These concepts will then be applied to data sets while using R, the statistical programming language. 
  
  While a deep treatment of the issues surrounding causal analysis is beyond the scope of this course, we will take a close look at the conditions necessary for causal inference while we cover the course material. Through such scrutiny, we will gain insight into when statistical relationships may be considered ‘causal’ and when merely ‘correlational’.
  
  Topics: Data types, simple regression, multiple regression, estimation, inference, asymptotics, qualitative variables, heteroscedasticity, collinearity, diagnostics, hypothesis tests, miscellaneous specification and data issues.

title: History of Economic Thought
description:
The economy, which we have come to think of as a distinct sphere of human activity, is a peculiar conceptual construct with an even more peculiar history. This course introduces economics majors to influential intellectual traditions that continue to shape how we think about the economy and the laws that govern it. Along the way, the class will revisit and historicize commonplace categories in the field of economics: commodity, money, capital, prices, wages and rents, supply and demand, business cycles, and so on. 
 
 The course begins with the 18th century, when the field of political economy was still in its nascent stage. The first three weeks of the course focus on the classical tradition of political economy, centred around the work of Adam Smith and David Ricardo. This is followed by two weeks of Marxian political economy, and two weeks on neo-classical economic thought. After an excursus into institutional, socialist, utopian, and historical traditions in economics, the course concludes with a deep engagement with the Keynesian revolution and its lasting influence on the field. Students will also read and engage with work that looks at how intellectual currents in political economy and economics shaped modern institutions, in European nations, in India, and in global governance.

title: The Indian Economy
description: This is a course on the economic history of Modern India, conventionally dated as the period from 1757 to the present. It aims to introduce to the students economic development and policies pursued in India. It attempts to engage students in locating the Indian economy within the world economy and understanding how the relationship has evolved over time. As contesting perspectives exist they will be exposed to them. The course commences with a study of colonial economic policies and the impact they had on India’s economy. In this section students read the work of some major historians. The course then moves on a study of the evolution of India’s economy since 1947, taking the student through the Nehru era, the Indira Gandhi years, the reforms of 1991 and economic performance under the Modi government. In this section the students will read the work of leading Indian economists. The topics covered will include the Colonialisation of India’s economy, the De-industrialisation debate, Land tenure legislation and its enduring consequences, Famines and the Raj, Colonial institutions, the Origins of modern industry, the Nehru era: Planning and its critics, the Green Revolution, initial Liberalisation moves, ‘1991’, the Modi years: initiatives (‘Make in India’, demonetisation) and shocks (Covid 19).

title: Macroeconomics - II
description: This course is a sequel to Macroeconomics I. It shifts focus to the long run and introduces students to the economics of growth, the role of capital accumulation and technological progress as well as the policy related aspects of economic growth. This course also introduces students to open economy macroeconomics including topics such as the IS-LM model in an open economy, balance of payments, exchange rates, typologies of exchange rate regimes and the effectiveness of the monetary and fiscal policies under different exchange rate regimes.

title: Microeconomics - II
description: This course is a sequel to Microeconomics I, and will focus on the study of producer behavior. We begin with a stylized model of the firm, and then understand how economists model production, and how firms minimize their costs and maximize their profits. With a basic understanding of consumer and producer behavior, we will then look at how the two interact in a market. The concept of the market equilibrium will be introduced, and we will learn how the characteristics of this equilibrium vary across different market structures such as perfectly competitive markets, monopoly and oligopoly. We will then learn about conditions where the market fails to achieve an equilibrium, focusing on externalities, public goods, and markets with asymmetric information.

title: Mathematical Methods for Economics - I
description:
Economists primarily use mathematical methods to make and study economic arguments. Mathematics brings in the rigour and precision that are required to ensure that the economists’ statements are true and logically sound. This course is intended to familiarize students with mathematical concepts and methods typically used by economists, and introduce ideas from topics in differential and integral calculus, optimization, linear algebra, and financial economics. A course in these topics will lay the foundation for more rigorous courses in (various branches of) economic theory, statistics and econometrics.
 
 The goal of the course is not to delve into the theorem-proof route, but rather to help the students develop their mathematical reasoning and intuition, and become comfortable talking about economics using mathematical shorthand.

title: Statistics for Economics
description:
This course has a dual focus: First, to introduce you to probability theory and the basic statistical concepts that are used to explore and understand economic phenomena. Second, to show you how this statistical knowledge can be applied to real world data using widely available spreadsheet tools like Microsoft Excel. Therefore, this course has been designed very much from a practitioner’s point of view. You will find that the material that you learn in this course will have direct application in your jobs and further studies. Sound grasp of material from this course will also be essential for your further coursework in econometrics and advanced microeconomics.
 
 The topics covered in this course fall into three broad categories: descriptive statistics, probability & distributions, and hypothesis testing. Descriptive statistics deals with the visualization and summarization of statistical data. You will learn simple tools for visualizing data on one and two variables, as well as statistical concepts for summarizing the central location and dispersion of your data. In the probability & distributions section, you will learn about probability and surrounding concepts like sample spaces, random variables, and combinatorics. You will also learn about some common discrete and continuous probability distributions. Hypothesis testing deals with questions of statistical inference: when are our conditions supported by the data and when are they not? You will learn about samples, and populations, point and interval estimates, and the apparatus of hypothesis testing about one or two variables.

title: Introduction to Statistical Programming
description:
This course is aimed at introducing economics students to statistical programming, using R and Stata. In this course, students will learn the basics of programming – such as downloading and installing the programme(s), managing libraries and packages, and good coding practices. Students will learn to perform simple computations, including basic mathematical operations, creating vectors and variables, and working with frequently used tools such as conditionals and loops. 
 
 Through a combination of lectures, hands-on exercises, and projects, students will be exposed to different data structures, and learn the tools to manipulate and analyse data – importing data from different sources/in various formats, and transforming them into a format suitable for analysis, cleaning data and dealing with missing information, and data visualization/description – creating and formatting charts and tables. Based on students’ comfort level with these foundational skills, the course may also touch upon additional topics related to simple statistical tests and analyses.

title: Introduction to Finance: Concepts and Methods
description:
The Great Recession of 2008 dealt an important lesson to economists – that the real economy and the financial world are closely interconnected and lacking an understanding the world of finance is no longer tenable for economists. An understanding of finance and how the world of finance operates is an essential ingredient in the toolkit for a practicing economist. With this motivation, this First Course in Finance is designed to provide an introduction to the world of finance. As a first course, it gives an introductory glimpse into the various parts of the field of finance. For anyone planning to gain deeper understanding in the field of finance by taking additional more intense courses in finance, this course serves as a preparatory, foundational step. By providing a comprehensive overview of the subject it would also serve students who are seeking only a basic but broad understanding of finance.
This course is focused on business finance, to the exclusion of personal finance and public finance. Starting with a definition of finance as the organizing principle, the course content is structured around agents that demand finance for business, namely, business organisations. The first part of the course develops an understanding of the business organization – its goals, its forms, and the accounting of its financial transactions. The financial accounts are key to keep track of the financial health of the business. A healthy business generates finance internally and is also able to access external sources relatively easily for its daily business needs and also for investments. The second part of the course covers concepts and methods relating to business investments, like valuing cash flows from investments, and profitability and risk in investments. Business finance is accessed in financial markets through financial institutions that intermediate between savers and the borrowing business organisations. The third part of the course covers these aspects – sources of finance, financial markets and financial institutions. Finally, we look at how prices are determined in the financial markets – bond prices, stock prices, exchange rates – and how this links to the macroeconomy. We also take a brief overview of quantitative finance, which provides a toolkit for financial analysts and managers.

title: Macroeconomics III
description: This is a one-term course in certain core areas of macroeconomics that could not be covered in some detail in Macroeconomics I and Macroeconomics II. In seeking to first establish a strong foundation in economic analysis, and in macroeconomic analysis in particular, the preceding two courses in macroeconomics stayed away from controversies in macroeconomic theory between different schools of thought. Further, some important parts of applied macroeconomic theory, like financial markets and financial crises, could not be dealt in detail in the earlier courses. This course will seek to give a more detailed treatment to these foregoing topics. A serious student of economics should not shy away from controversies and unsettled issues in macroeconomics, and should have the confidence to apply his knowledge to popular and important topics like financial markets and financial crises. The focus in this course will be on certain specific topics that any serious student of economics must have knowledge of. Six topics have been chosen for inclusion in this course at an intermediate level: different approaches to macroeconomic theory, theories of business cycles, macroeconomic policy, financial markets, macroeconomic crises and economic growth theory. This course will be pitched at a level that acts as a bridge, for the undergraduate student to continue onto graduate level studies, and also for those who wish to pursue other avenues like business management and employment as economic analysts. Students in this course will be required to do group projects that shall be designed to give a hands-on experience in using software tools for macroeconomic analysis with these objectives in view.

title: Microeconomics - III
description: This course is a sequel to Microeconomics II specially designed for the students enrolled in the FYUP. It will focus on the study of market failure under second best settings. It will also dwell deeper into game theory, public goods, factor markets, and time costs. The concept of the market equilibrium will be re-introduced, and we will learn how the characteristics of the market vary in the real word leading to conditions such that market fails to achieve an equilibrium, focusing on externalities, public goods, markets with asymmetric information and imperfect competition. The course would develop a rigorous set of tools to analyze such conditions while unraveling how choices can interact and persist leading to strategic outcomes and payoffs.

title: Development Economics
description:
This course introduces students to key topics in the field of Development economics and policy, particularly those centered around the colossal challenges facing the global poor.
The first part of the course will introduce students to the fundamental question of why we still see extreme levels of poverty around the world, why some countries are rich while the others are poor. We will review selected classical and contemporary models of development to explore structural and institutional factors that impact the process of development. The second part of the course will dive deep into the concept of poverty at a micro level, i.e., at the level of individuals and households. The course will introduce and encourage students to think about how the poor make decisions, what constraints they face and what difficult trade-offs they make. We will learn about the actions and policies taken by various entities (Governments, international organizations, and NGOs) to improve the lives of the poor. Using modern empirical techniques, we will understand which of these policies have been successful, and which have not. 
At the end of the course, the students will develop a deeper appreciation for the dynamics of the development process and the challenges involved in ending poverty across the world, and have a better understanding of how poverty affects various aspects of human development.

title: Econometrics - II
description: This course introduces students to advanced econometric techniques for conducting empirical analysis in economics. It introduces students to several families of distributions and explores commonly used empirical approaches to identify causality. The course also features advanced topics such as instrumental variable estimation, panel data models, and limited dependent variables. At the end of this course, students should be able to have a deeper appreciation for the link between theory and empirical work, and also be able to engage meaningfully with current empirical literature in economics.

title: Labor Economics
description: Labor economics, in a comprehensive sense, involves examining how individuals, firms, institutions, and the public sector interact to influence employment and wage outcomes. Throughout this course, we will delve into both theoretical and empirical aspects of labor economics, placing a significant emphasis on practical applications. We will focus on discussing research designs aimed at empirically measuring theoretical predictions and assessing the impact of policy interventions.

title: Economics and Public Policy: An Introduction
description:
Given the increasing wealth inequalities, should governments look at Universal Basic Incomes for certain sections of the society? Should AI replace low-cost jobs? Should borders be open or secured? Given rising fuel costs, should governments invest more in alternative fuels or increase subsidies for public transportation? Should government departments and enterprises (railways, airlines, telecom, petroleum) be privatized?
