These are examples of public policy questions that are inextricably linked to questions in economics. The goal of this introductory course is to prepare students to look at larger public policy questions of this kind and others through the lens of economics, stakeholders, resources use and resource constraints.
  This course hopes to cultivate in students an understanding of the underlying issues that influence policy. With political economy becoming the crucial issue of this century, there is a persistent need to develop a deep and specific understanding of the behavior of the markets and the actions of government and the purposes that fashion such arrangements. As the discourse between the economy, society and government becomes clear, so does the use of public policy. It then becomes a visible hand of the government to supplant the invisible hand of the market to achieve desirable societal goals. Working through monetary directions, governmental regulations, legislations, taxation and redistributed transfers, public policy aims to create a level playing field in societies to create growth and development of priority and emerging sectors. In this class, we will develop an in-depth understanding of what public policy is and why we sometimes justify government involvement in solving economic and social problems.
  This course aims to provide students with the basic tools to develop an understanding of practical and theoretical issues of the public policy process. Students will get familiar with the nature of public policy and its process, read and discuss theoretical materials explaining the public policy process and describe and analyze practical policy issues policy making - from agenda setting, policy design, policy formulation and adoption, implementation and evaluation. They will also discuss scenarios to simulate efficient and equitable outcomes and also understand the reasons behind policies failing. It will rope in economics concepts of moral hazard, free rider problems, virtue signaling among others.

title: Game Theory
description: Game theory studies interactive decision-making and our objective is to understand the impact of interactions of multiple players and the resulting dynamics in a market environment. The introductory course in game theory will familiarize students with strategic behaviour and its applications in business decision making and several fields such as industrial organization, corporate finance, environmental economics, trade and political science. The course will cover several solution concepts starting with Nash Equilibrium, which will be modified under imperfect and incomplete/complete information scenarios. The concepts will be applied to case studies in bargaining, negotiation, pricing and market entry decisions.

title: Health Economics
description:
This course addresses issues related to health care, health policy, using tools from empirical and theoretical economics. We will use the tools of microeconomic theory to study topics such as micro foundations of health (demand for health care), socioeconomic and gender disparities in population health outcomes, health insurance design (moral hazard and adverse selection), determinants of health care spending, technological change in the health care sector, public health insurance policy, and the interaction between economic variables such as consumption and labor supply and health. The primary focus of this course centers on health-related outcomes and healthcare systems in developing countries, with a specific emphasis on India.
  Through a combination of lectures, problem sets, response notes to articles and podcasts, exploratory data analysis, and the presentation of research papers, students will learn about research methodology in health economics and applied microeconomics.

title: Institutions & Economic Outcomes
description:
This course introduces the field of political economy to institutions and economic outcomes. It will begin by addressing the definitions of institutions and frameworks of economic outcomes. It will study the interrelations between the long-term effects of institutions on economic growth and other societal outcomes. The course will delve into the significant variations in economic and political development among nations with similar appearances.
  Drawing upon historical evidence, it will examine if institutional development, even unplanned, has delivered profound and far-reaching economic consequences.
  
  This course is designed to provide students with a deeper understanding of both the institutions and organizations of the world economies and their roles in shaping divergence in the distribution of earnings, wealth, and opportunities. The course will explore the merit behind the concept that the world can pursue economic development by establishing suitable economic institutions, emphasizing the significance of private property and competition. Additionally, it will examine whether better economic outcomes happen in open and pluralistic political systems.
  
  This course will also familiarize the students with the frontiers and tools of policy research topics and complement public policy and economic development courses. It will allow the students to understand and participate in academic discussions on emerging economic issues. It will provide insights into the political and public-policy debates that address the widening inequality and possible means of addressing it.

title: International Trade
description:
Since Adam Smith and David Ricardo, economists have sought to understand the causes, patterns, and consequences of trade among nations. This course introduces students to the key concepts, theories, institutions, and macroeconomic dynamics of international economics. It traces the historical evolution of the global trading system - from Mercantilism and the Gold Standard through Bretton Woods, GATT, and the WTO - and examines why countries trade, what they trade, who gains, and how governments shape trade through policy. Students will engage with the principal theories of trade (Absolute and Comparative Advantage, Heckscher-Ohlin, economies of scale and imperfect competition) and evaluate trade policy instruments including tariffs, quotas, subsidies, anti-dumping measures, and non-tariff barriers.
The course also covers the monetary dimensions of international economics: exchange rate regimes (fixed, floating, managed, pegged, spot, forward, and trade-weighted), balance of payments accounting, capital account convertibility, and global capital flows, analyzed through open-economy frameworks including the IS-LM-BOP model. Historical episodes - the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, the oil shocks of the 1970s, the rise of the US dollar as reserve currency - provide context for contemporary debates around the US-China trade conflict, Trump-era tariffs, supply chain disruptions, economic nationalism, industrial policy, digital and services trade, climate-related trade measures, and the geopolitics of regional agreements and groupings such as the QUAD. The course equips students with the analytical tools to navigate the rapidly changing landscape of global economic relations.

title: Ecological Economics
description: This course will examine the links between economic and ecological systems. We will use concepts from welfare economics, common pool resources, ecosystem valuation and environmental ethics and apply them to the problems of fisheries and forest management, biodiversity conservation and global environmental change. The course will also focus on the relationship between economic growth, ecosystem services and human flourishing in pursuit of sustainable development.

title: Economics of Education
description:
This course delves into the economic aspects of education, with a specific focus on developing nations. It begins by tracing the historical trajectory of the economics of education, positioning it as a pivotal discipline amidst a broad spectrum dedicated to educational studies. Through an economic lens, it thoroughly examines diverse research avenues within education, such as human capital theory, educational production, cost analysis, funding mechanisms, educational planning, teacher dynamics, and the dynamics of educational markets and choice. The exploration involves not only the scrutiny of economic theories but also practical implications encompassing educational policies. 
 Additionally, this course provides an encompassing view of fundamental concepts and the challenges embedded in various research paradigms and methodologies utilized within the realm of education economics, including detailed insights into econometric approaches. Students are guided to hone their research skills and discern between robust and contentious research papers. 
 Of paramount importance within this course is the spotlight on education within developing countries. Education is recognized as a crucial element intertwined with social, political, and economic frameworks essential for nurturing sustainable growth in impoverished nations. The course underscores how education acts as a catalyst, elevating productivity levels, fostering innovation, and paving the way for enhanced democratic values – all pivotal factors propelling progress and development within these regions.

title: Mathematical Methods for Economics II
description: This course is a continuation of the course Mathematical Methods for Economics I, pitched at a more advanced level, particularly for students in year 4 (under FYUP). The students will be introduced to the mathematical tools and concepts that are most frequently used in economic models of the firm and consumer behavior. To this end, the course will cover the topics of optimization (both constrained and unconstrained) with one and more than one choice variable, linear programming models, differential equation, difference equations and integration. The course will also cover in more detail some of the topics learned in Mathematical Methods for Economics I, like matrix algebra, rules of differentiation and limit theorems with specific focus on economic applications. Throughout the course, we will take an intensive approach to mathematics, but most of the emphasis will be on the applications or economic models rather than abstract mathematical theorems or concepts.

title: Heterodox Contributions to Macroeconomics
description: There is today a definite mainstream in macroeconomics. While ideas that do not fit into this received framework tend to be ignored they can be crucial to understanding the working of the world economy, including India’s. Some of these are part of an entire approach to macroeconomics while others are standalone ideas/constructs addressing issues as broad as economic growth and as specific as financial crises. This course aims to introduce students with these heterodox approaches and ideas, with a view to enhancing their understanding of both how economic issues have been framed and how the economy actually works. The course is meant for students with an interest in economic ideas and evidence-based analysis of the economy.

title: Mixed Methods in Impact Evaluation
description: The course will review a variety of evaluation designs for assessing the impact of interventions, may it be policies, programs or products, in the context of implementation research. The concept of counterfactual and causality will be discussed. The importance of considering mixed methods approach to impact evaluation will be highlighted. Mixed methods approach combines quantitative methods, qualitative methods as well as process evaluation for monitoring of the intervention. Practical examples from LEAD’s own work as well as from other published studies in the social sector will be used throughout the duration of the course.

title: Economics Through Games
description: Game theory studies interactive decision-making and our objective is to understand the impact of interactions of multiple players and the resulting dynamics in a market environment. The introductory course in game theory will familiarize students with strategic behaviour and its applications in business decision making and several fields such as industrial organization, corporate finance, environmental economics, trade and political science. The course will cover several solution concepts starting with Nash Equilibrium, which will be modified under imperfect and incomplete/complete information scenarios. The concepts will be applied to case studies in bargaining, negotiation, pricing and market entry decisions.

title: Anthropocene: Past, Present and Predicted Environments
Climate Change: Science, Economics, and Policy
description:
This course offers an in-depth exploration of global climate change, examining its scientific, economic, and policy dimensions. We will begin by discussing real-world manifestations of climate change and the fundamental science behind Earth's climate system. This includes understanding weather patterns, energy balance, the role of greenhouse gases, and the carbon cycle, along with future scenarios and tipping points.

Students will engage with the latest scientific reports, such as those from the IPCC, to grasp observed and projected changes in climate. We will critically analyse issues of equity and responsibility in climate change. We will deconstruct the concept of “net-zero” emissions, discussing carbon budgets, sequestration techniques, the outcomes of international climate negotiations, and the geopolitics of climate change.

In addition, the course covers practical aspects like carbon footprinting and the evaluation of real-world commitments to achieving carbon neutrality. We will study the impacts of climate change, including compound events, and explore both mitigation and adaptation strategies. Economic aspects such as carbon markets and various economic models will also be discussed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the approaches to addressing climate change.

An overarching theme running through the course will be the issue of climate (in-)justice, which we will examine from multiple perspectives. The course will culminate in end-term projects, in which groups will synthesize and apply the knowledge gained throughout the course.

This course embodies interwovenness, drawing from different disciplines – physics, chemistry, ecology, economics, behavioural science, and geopolitics. Some modules are scientifically and mathematically heavy, and others are reading heavy. Students taking this course are required to keep an open mind.

title: Tools and Methods in Environmental Studies
description: This course will provide the basic vocabulary that students require to navigate the environmental sciences, humanities, and social sciences. Through systematic close readings of influential texts, we hope to enable students to use the tools and methods employed by these disciplines in the context of the environmental studies. We begin the course by charting out primary motivators and drivers of work in each discipline. We will then home in on cutting-edge research within each discipline. For example, in the environmental sciences, we will focus on the concept of thresholds and safe operating spaces for humanity. During our engagement with the environmental humanities, we will focus on how progress in the digital humanities has enabled visualisation and textual analysis of environmental history, philosophy, ethics, literary theory, art, and education. Lastly, in the environmental social sciences, we will pinpoint how ethnography and narratives are now becoming invaluable tools for understanding how society interacts with the environment.

title: Environmental History
description: This course introduces various themes in environmental history, taking as its point of departure the beginnings of the formalised movement of the field in Great Britain and the United States of America, and then forging its way across various parts of our globe in what will be in equal parts survey and case study, though with an eye on the Indian subcontinent. Particular attention will be paid to the effects of environmental thinking in the colonial world as well as to contemporary issues, in particular, climate change and conservation. The themes of the course will be suitable to an introductory level approach to the subject such that students will be in a position to make intelligent and thoughtful contributions to a greater environmental consciousness through the work they may undertake in time to come. To this end, projects will be designed using course and supplemental material and with an emphasis on work conducted outside the classroom to be discussed and portrayed within it as final output.

title: Environmental Communication
description:
Environmental studies encompass not only the science of climate change or environmental harm but also communicating these for various kinds of publics. 
 This course moves away from objective and expert accounts of environmental risk and policy to focus on popular and public-facing forms of environmental communication. 
 Students will read and analyse genres of Environmental Communication like science and nature writing and the photo essay. This course is writing-intensive and the focus will be producing various kinds of short written and visual pieces and forms of public outreach around case studies drawn from neighbouring ecosystems. As far as possible we will arrange student interaction with some practitioners of these forms.
 
 
 The theme for this year will be Water.

title: Environmental Materialisms
description:
Materials have shaped history and our everyday lives. The social, political, and economic structures determining access to materials create varying environmental outcomes. Environment outcomes in turn shape societies and its practices over time via the provisioning of materials. Our current thinking about sustainability, conservation, and environmental crises are all largely shaped by the ramifications of our material relationships. While philosophers have expounded on the dialectic tensions between the material and the ideal as an intrinsic feature of the human condition for a long time now, only relatively recently have the implications of this dialectic tension been explored by scholars of the environmental studies to better understand environmental and social concerns, both of the present-day (overproduction, consumer culture, social-ecological fallout), and leading into the future (New Materialism).
 This course is designed to be a whirlwind tour of the various ways to think about environmental and social contexts underpinning various kinds of materialisms. Past and present cautionary tales of humanity’s precarious relationship with the material world ⎯the bedrock upon which the dialectic of the material and the ideal hinges on⎯ have culminated in ecological collapse and social strife. However, political, historical, and economic contexts complicate these simplistic cautionary tales to a large extent with regards to causality. Lastly, materials are what nourishes our body and our mind, and brings joy to our lives; we delight in the textures, noises, colours, and tastes of things. Discussions on future materialisms could be much less likely about how we value material things too much, but rather about how we don’t value them enough (Thorpe 2014).

title: Introduction to Environmental Science
description: Environmental science is the study of patterns and processes in the natural world and their modification by human activity. To understand current environmental problems, we need to consider physical, chemical and biological processes that are often the basis of those problems. This course will give you the skills necessary to address the environmental issues we are facing today by examining scientific principles and the application of those principles to natural systems. This course will survey some of the many environmental science topics at an introductory level, ultimately considering the sustainability of human activities on the planet.

title: Introduction to Environmental Law and Policy
description:
This course provides an introduction to environmental law and policy
 with a focus on India. International, regional and global examples are
 included, with a prioritisation of bioregional, South Asian, and global
 South examples. The course emphasis is distributed between
 foundational perspective-building and practical problem-solving and
 skill application. The course curriculum covers conceptual and historical
 terrain, main sources and functional forms, constitutional context, and
 structural dimensions (including main institutions and networks) of
 environmental law and policy, with a deep dive into specific sub-fields
 including biodiversity and wildlife, climate change, energy, forests,
 pollution, urban environments, and water. Special attention is devoted
 
 Page 2 of 2
 
 to environmental and social justice concerns across the different sub-
 fields, laws, and policies. The course will be of interest to anyone
 seeking to develop a rigorous approach towards understanding the law
 and policy context, implications, and possibilities of most current
 environmental issues and problems.

title: Political Ecology of Biodiversity Conservation
description: The conservation of biodiversity and the protection of habitat that are repositories of biodiversity are now considered to be critical for ecological and social wellbeing. The narrative from which this tapestry is woven is remarkably similar across geographies and cultures; that biodiversity is threatened due to human action such as deforestation and degradation, unsustainable harvest, and due to the fault-lines created by competing objectives of environmental protection and human development. Articulated this way, biodiversity, and lands that contain it, become scarce resources within a political economy. Responses to the biodiversity crisis within a political economy engenders the separation of humans from nature, the commodification of nature by projecting its economic value, and the relentless strengthening of centralization. In recent years however alternate narratives to the dominant political economy have emerged. One of these is the political ecology counter-narrative. Political ecology subsumes learning from multiple disciplines to analyze the appropriation of nature (including its distribution and consumption) as an inherently political process linked to social relations and control, and the analysis of embedded power relations, domination, and inequality that result from this process. Examined in this fashion, biodiversity conservation is not a value-neutral term, but one that needs to be critically unpacked from multiple perspectives including ecological justice and social equity.

title: Environmental Chemistry
description:
Introduction to the Environmental Chemistry 
 The environmental chemistry is an interdisciplinary science that includes chemistry of atmosphere, hydrosphere and soil and the effect of anthropogenic activities on the environment.
 The well-known events in climate change, triggered by greenhouse gases and the stratospheric chemistry of ozone depletion by chlorofluorocarbon molecules will be discussed.
 The wastewater treatment and purification along with the various water quality parameters (including conductivity, pH, alkalinity, hardness) and their measurement will be examined.
 The treatment of solid waste and soil pollution will also be covered.

title: Environment and Ethics
description: The question of ethics is at the core of our relationship with the environment. Do humans as moral agents have a moral obligation towards other living beings and environmental components? Do our moral obligations change knowing that the environment is the only moral subject? How do we define value? Are all values defined solely by reference to ourselves or our kind, or is there a realm of value that extends beyond the human domain? This course illustrates the history of nature-human relationship and the moral and ethical debates that emerge owing to the present dismal state of this relationship. Students learn about various ethical schools that are in place and further gain an in-depth understanding of the necessary ethical debates by comparing and contrasting these ethical viewpoints. After giving exposure to the theoretical underpinnings of environmental ethics, the second half of the course delves into the practice of ethics by charting out the trajectory of the growth of major environmental movements and the major treaties at the global scale. It will delve into present debates concerning resource conflicts, developmental goals, and societal values to locate the role of ethics in the human-environment relationship. With the advent of the discourses on climate change, the ethical response to the environment became an even more conflicted issue. This course ends with addressing the dilemma of the individuals’ vs. institutions' responsibility and the larger effectiveness of ethical actions.

title: Alternative Energy on a Finite Planet
description:
Transition to carbon-free electricity is central to addressing climate change. These are generally solar, wind, hydro and nuclear – often termed ‘renewables’, ‘green’ or ‘sustainable’. The use of such terms conceals the substantial limitations and impacts of these alternative sources of energy. Energy extraction by solar panels and wind turbines (i.e. their efficiency) are inexorably limited by fundamental physics. Their power densities are substantially lower than those of fossil fuel power plants, and therefore require correspondingly larger land areas for installation relative to a fossil fuel plant of equivalent output. Unless the installation is on degraded land, they can cause serious disruption to wildlife habitats and agricultural lands. We have already witnessed the deleterious impacts of large hydro projects in parts of the country, and those of nuclear energy in other parts of the world. The raw materials that alternative energy installations are composed of and constructed from – metal ores, plastics, minerals – are in finite supply. Many are concentrated in certain parts of the world (e.g. Lithium in Chile, Nickel in Indonesia), therefore subject to the vicissitudes of geopolitics (and pandemics). Large solar and wind power farms also substantially affect the microclimate of their installation sites causing local warming. It is also unclear how the vast – and exponentially rising – quantities of spent solar panels and wind turbines that will emerge within the decade can be effectively recycled. The intermittency problems of solar and wind power are well known, and therefore the need for battery technology – with its own land, water, material and chemical footprints. What does all this mean for India’s ambitious alternative energy programme of 500 GW of non-fossil energy by 2030? What will it affect carbon emissions, air pollution, wildlife, agriculture, and human settlements? This course will be a joint exploration of many such questions. 

This is a **quantitative course** but pitched at high school level of mathematics. The goal of the course, subject to interest and coding skills, is to divide into teams and create maps of India identifying the regions with greatest potential for alternative energy with least impacts – from interwoven science, socio-economic, and ecological perspectives.

title: Introduction to Sustainability
description: This multidisciplinary course provides a comprehensive and critical exploration of sustainability, focusing on the interconnectedness of its environmental, social, and economic dimensions. It examines the historical and scientific origins of the sustainability movement and its evolving principles, while critically assessing contemporary global challenges such as water scarcity, food insecurity, energy demands, rapid urbanization, pollution, waste management, and the impacts of war and violent conflict. It introduces sustainability frameworks and models and, through global examples and case studies, explores both actionable strategies and limitations for addressing sustainability challenges. The course engages critically with sustainability concepts and trade-offs, drawing from disciplines such as ecology, economics, ethics, and development studies. The course fosters reflection on the complex stakeholder interplay, values and behaviours of individuals and groups, examining concepts of power dynamics, inequality and social justice, and emphasizing their impact on individuals and communities.

title: Creative non-fiction: the art and craft of long form journalism
Introduction to GIS
description:
Geographic Information System (GIS) is widely used across sectors for data analysis and
visualization. The GIS software equips the user to understand and analyse complex issues at spatial and temporal scales. This course intends to expose students to the basics of GIS with hands-on training so that students can use these acquired skills in their respective areas of interest.

title: Environmental Impact Assessment Laboratory
description:
Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is an essential tool used to assess the potential impacts of human activities on the environment, including natural habitats and human health. As human populations continue to grow and expand, and natural resources become increasingly scarce, it is critical that we evaluate the environmental impact of our actions to ensure the sustainability of the planet for future generations.

EIAs provide a comprehensive framework for identifying and analyzing potential environmental impacts of proposed activities, such as land use changes, industrial processes, and infrastructure development. By conducting an EIA, we can identify potential impacts and take necessary measures to minimize or mitigate negative impacts, such as air and water pollution, soil erosion, habitat destruction, and loss of biodiversity. In addition, EIAs can also help identify potential risks to human health, such as exposure to hazardous chemicals, pollution, and infectious diseases.

The Environmental Impact Assessment Laboratory Course is designed to provide students with hands-on experience in conducting environmental impact assessments. The course will cover a broad range of topics, including the principles of chemistry, and biology that are relevant to environmental impact assessments. The course will be entirely composed of laboratory experiments that will teach the principles and techniques involved in environmental impact assessments.

title: Remote Sensing
description: Remote sensing forms an essential component of earth system science research. Most of our knowledge on climate change impacts and environmental degradation relies on datasets obtained by remote sensing. Remote sensing methods are applied in a variety of fields and many of them are touched upon in this course. Often, remote sensing and GIS are combined as a course, however, such courses focus primarily on a subset of remote sensing wherein 2 dimensional images over a region of interest are processed as geographic information. This course differs from such an approach in that the focus is on the concepts and techniques adopted in remote sensing measurements. The course has three demonstration classes where students will be exposed to the remote sensing datasets with the guidance of the instructor. In addition, the students need to carry out group projects on their own.

title: Environment versus Development: the policy dilemma
description:
The growth versus environment debate has been one of India’s nay the global community’s major policy dilemmas for over a century now, exacerbated in the era of global warming and climate change. Further deepening the dilemma are the processes set off by globalization, privatization and liberalization combined with the role of technology in people’s lives.
 Yet, this debate has also spurred a new line of thinking and public policies in recent times.
 Growth is an imperative for material needs or poverty alleviation. But ecology, too, needs to be healthy, in the absence of which there’s a heavy price to be paid by the humanity, as witnessed in the unprecedented disasters: landslides, recurring floods and droughts, water scarcity or the devastation caused by extreme weather events and the society’s unpreparedness in such cases.
 It’s a quintessential “wicked problem” – to borrow from the term coined first in a 1973 paper by Horst W J Rittel and Melvin M Webber, professors of design and urban planning at the University of California at Berkeley (Dilemmas in a general theory of planning) – that does not allow for the best solution but rather only the acceptable compromises.
 Questions abound: Is there such thing called sustainable economic growth, as advocated by the different stakeholders? What’s the history and philosophy of environmentalism and the many different tensions centred around these two ideas? How does public policy factor in both?
 This course, drawing from field work and theoretical foundations, would offer students of social and environmental sciences with a keen interest in public policy a thorough review of this classical dilemma and the choices a society has and makes. 
 From the earliest debates over the construction of large dams, to industrial development, to the ideas of green economy or degrowth, and the history of India’s environmental legislation, the week-by-week sessions would build on the different thematic aspects of this debate and pose before students the confounding questions integral to understanding a public policy dilemma.
 For instance, the social and economic fallout of the land acquisition for development projects by the State using the whip of Eminent Domain: What happens to the people who are displaced by development projects? This itself posits several questions for consideration: Is development possible without any environmental, ecological or social harm? Or is there a need for a paradigm shift to strike a balance between the two processes, as the world runs out of time to deal with and eventually fix the global poly-crisis, a term coined by historian Adam Toonze.
 With class-rooms discussions intermittent with lectures, presentations and anecdotal stories from the field, this course will dwell upon the theoretical foundations as well as the real-life situations to explore tensions between the cause of environmental conservation and preservation and an inevitability of development for economic growth.

title: Natural Hazards and Mitigation
description:
Natural disasters are among the greatest threats for human lives and quality of life. This course introduces students to almost all the natural hazards that can cause disasters, from well-known frequently occurring ones to extremely rare ones. The course discusses the causes and consequences of natural hazards, efforts undertaken to predict them in advance and the complications of such efforts, in a fundamental level. The causes of natural disasters are understood based on the underlying scientific investigations. To predict them, routine measurement networks and scientific modelling are required. Finally, mitigating their effect depends on the support and efforts provided by the policy makers.
Contents:
Lithosphere based: Earthquake, Tsunami, Volcano, Landslide, Sinkhole
Weather based: water and wind both contribute to natural disasters: Cloud burst, Flood, Hailstorm, Snow avalanche, Draught, Cyclone, Tornado, Dust storm, Pollen transport, Lightning, Forest fire
Biological hazard: Pandemics and epidemics 
Space based: Space weather effects, meteor or asteroid impact, proximal supernova or black hole 
Role of climate change and other anthropogenic activities in aggravating the hazards

title: Introduction to Cryosphere-Climate Interactions
description:
Cryosphere is that part of earth that consists of snow (seasonal/permanent),
 glaciers, ice sheets, sea ice and permafrost. The cryosphere (especially ice sheets
 and glaciers) are responsible for lowering the heat budget of the earth by reflecting
 large portions of the incoming solar radiation as ice is a good reflector of radiation.
 Increasing global temperatures has led of reduction of the extent of the cryosphere in
 recent times. In this course, the students will be exposed to basic concepts and
 terminologies related to the field of climate-cryosphere interactions. In addition to
 that, the students will be asked to read and present simple research papers in this
 field with the guidance of the instructor.

title: Theatre Of The Climate: Performing A Just Future
description:
Theatre of the Climate: Performing a Just Future is an interdisciplinary course that
 bridges environmental sciences and the arts to explore climate change as both a systemic
 crisis and a human story. As climate realities become increasingly urgent, understanding
 them requires not only scientific insight but also emotional resonance, cultural memory, and
 ethical imagination. This course invites students to examine climate change through the
 lenses of social and ecological justice, considering how inequalities of caste, gender and
 geography shape vulnerability and responsibility.
 Blending systems thinking, ecological theory, and participatory art practices in theatre,
 dance, storytelling, and visual arts, students will explore the role of traditional knowledge
 systems, in making the climate crisis personal and public. Drawing on readings from
 science, performance studies, and decolonial thought, alongside engagements with artistic
 practitioners and community archives, students will develop original art-based interventions.
 The course culminates in collaborative performance prototypes that embody just and
 sustainable futures. It is ideal for students pursuing environmental sciences, global arts, or
 any other discipline with an interest in climate action and creative expression.
 Theatre, dance, and visual arts can bring to life the narratives of those affected by
 environmental injustices, offering audiences a visceral understanding of these complex
 issues.
 This course is proposed to be capped at 15 students.
 Learning Outcomes:
 1. Students will be able to analyse climate change as a “super wicked problem”
 using systems thinking and social-ecological frameworks.
 2. Students will critically engage with the intersections of climate injustice and
 social inequality through caste, gender and class lenses.
 3. Students will develop and apply performative, visual, and narrative art
 practices to sense, express, and communicate climate experiences and
 knowledge.
 4. Students will collaboratively design and present creative interventions - such
 as performances or installations - that address climate justice and imagine
 alternative futures.

title: Introduction to Environmental Toxicology
description:
This course provides a necessary foundation in environmental toxicology, emphasizing
how chemical, physical, and biological agents adversely affect living organisms and
ecosystems. It explores the sources, occurrence, fate, transport, bioaccumulation,
toxicokinetics, and toxic effects of pollutants in air, water, soil, and food systems.
 Students will analyze how environmental changes and pollution contribute to human and
ecological health risks, while developing an understanding of toxicokinetic processes
(absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) and factors influencing toxicity.
 Through case studies such as the Bhopal gas tragedy, oil spills, and e-waste
contamination, the course connects theory to global environmental health issues. It
concludes with the principles and applications of Environmental Health Risk Assessment,
enabling students to evaluate exposure, hazard, and risk characterization within
environmental contexts.

title: Global sustainability transitions: Context and Scalability
description: There is growing awareness that large scale social-ecological changes are necessary towards affecting a meaningful transition towards sustainability. Alternative economic models such as degrowth, steady-state, and doughnut economics have been proposed to this end. Philosophies such as Buen Vivir and Ubuntu have likewise attracted increasing attention. However, the complexities of the real world mean that there are few, if any, examples of large scale uptake of these philosophies or models. However, interesting case studies of large-scale transitions are underway in different parts of the world. For example, political churning of the past 2-3 years in Chile have led to a new draft constitution with progressive – even radical – ideas on social and environmental protections. ‘Rights of Nature’ are being contemplated and instituted in an increasing list of countries, perhaps most famously in Ecuador. Radical ideas on gender equality have emerged and been instituted in parts of Kurdistan. Yet, many of these initiatives are nascent and fragile. The new draft constitution of Chile may be defeated in a referendum, and the gender rights movement in Kurdistan may be motivated by strategic political concerns relating to identity. In this course, the purpose is to identify and study key examples of large-scale social, environmental and economic transitions of the past decade, and to interrogate the historical context in which these came about. We will ask whether these changes are robust, and whether progressive policies developed there could be carried over to similar contexts elsewhere in the Global South. The purpose is to come to an understanding of whether such changes were incidental and fleeting ,or whether genuine social tipping points were triggered.

title: Environmental Justice
description:
This interdisciplinary course prepares prospective academics, activists, ethicists, leaders, researchers and policy-makers for environmental justice challenges and opportunities in India and across the world. The initial course module focuses on the theoretical foundations and conceptual contexts of environmental justice. Next, an experiential education module guides learners in developing familiarity with the practice of environmental justice. The concluding module on institutional and societal changes for environmental justice further develops and synthesises the theoretical and practical insights generated earlier in the course.

Environmental justice - a discourse that straddles research, policy, and activism – focuses on the dynamics of justice/injustice in environment-related thinking and action. Concepts closely linked to justice, for example - equity, equality, fairness, responsibility, difference, recognition, liberty, dignity, violence, goodness, rightness, etc. - necessarily get included in any analysis of environmental justice. A crude definitional attempt would be to say that environmental justice is concerned with who wins and who loses in any given environmental context, why and how this happens, why this matters to those involved and to all of us, and what can be done to change things around. Further, good environmental justice theory is attentive to questions of difference and colonialism and the multiple crises of contemporary global capitalism; some political thinkers, for example, explicitly identify the goals of green politics as striking at the very heart of the polluted, materialist, consumerist, unequal, and industrial capitalist society.

Mainstream discourses of climate change, sustainability and sustainable development often obscure the injustice and inequity of specific kinds of human activity relating to the environment. Framing issues in the language of environmental justice therefore allows us to excavate these silences in the mainstream discourses of climate action and sustainability, which in turn makes possible a more informed critique of how power operates in the political and governance systems (in India) that govern the environment. Such an understanding allows for an ethical and truly meaningful environmental practice in fields such as academia, business, journalism, law, media, policy, etc.  
Making the quest for environmental and social justice a central concern requires confronting the fundamental underlying processes (and their associated power structures, social relations, institutional configurations, discourses, and belief systems) that generate environmental and social injustices. A coherent political account of how we could respond to these challenges requires the conceptual arsenal provided by environmental justice theory and practice. Ideas of environmental justice therefore enable “new critical engagements with the relations between economy, environment and society, and illuminate the radical potential of sustainability” (Harvey 1996). Such an approach gives environmental practitioners a suitably nuanced, historical, comparative, and ethical orientation for their specific practice. 
Another question of relevance for this course is: what would distinctly non-Eurocentric environmental justice agendas for India and the global South look like? The analysis here could focus on questions such as: do vulnerable people in India suffer the most from current models of development? If so, why is this and what can be done to correct the situation? How can we balance the tension between economic development and environmental protection in specific Indian geographies? What might be the tensions and polarities between conservationists and resource-dependent communities? What kinds of movements, campaigns, programs and projects are successful in achieving environmental justice in the distinctively Indian contexts of unstable federalism, rampant poverty, violent state action, low literacy, identity and coalition politics, endemic official corruption, poor enforcement machinery, etc.? What can environmental justice practitioners in India learn from the global environmental justice movement and from movements in other places in the global South?  

Summarizing the above discussion, an environmental justice approach as understood in this course, therefore: 
a)        critically, contextually and holistically re-examines the foundations of environmental/sustainability thinking and action from the standpoint of justice, and;
b)        applies the insights gained from such a critical re-examination to ethically devise, implement and evaluate new approaches and solutions to pressing socio-environmental problems.   

The course enables learners to develop an 'environmental justice mindset' and to develop familiarity with some commonly-used approaches, methods, tools and resources to augment the practice of environmental justice in varied sectoral/disciplinary/professional contexts. The course will be built around specific exercises and experiential components focused on professional practice that responds to some key problems of environmental injustice. Workshop-style segments will focus on brainstorming, envisioning, strategising, project design, research methodology, team-work, prototyping, documentation, fund-raising, and communication for professional practice relating to climate change.

title: Pan Asian Environmentalisms: a short history
description: This course explores how the various Asian communities that lived along land and maritime trade routes, which linked different parts of Asia, understood the environment and nonhumans. How did the movement of people, as well as the spread of ideas, literature, religions, art, commodities, from pre-modern times to the present, in Asia, shape notions about the nonhuman? How did understandings of the environment rest on religious, medical, cultural and social beliefs?

title: Introduction to Atmospheric Science
description:
This course will act as a comprehensive introduction to atmospheric science with a
 focus on the whole atmosphere of the Earth. Students will develop a quantitative
 understanding of atmospheric thermodynamics, radiative balance, atmospheric
 dynamics, mesoscale and synoptic-scale weather systems, and a prelude to
 principles of climate.

title: Sources of the Self: India in the Second Millennium A.D.
description:
This course explores the most significant developments of medieval and early modern India. Second Millennium is also the time period when regional cultures, linguistic and literary traditions as well as popular religions were produced. It is important to note that these constructs inform our social, cultural and religious lives today and in that sense constitute our sources of the self. In that sense, our goal is to examine the medieval in our contemporary world. 
 We will study the following six themes in this course. 
 First, the emergence of regions and regional cultures, which are often based on bhashas or regional languages. While some of these languages had already been in existence for several centuries, it is mostly towards the end of the first millennium AD that Indian bhashas emerge from the shadows of Sanskrit or Prakrit and begin to be used for political, literary, religious and discursive purposes. This moment also marks the emergence of regional political formations and regional cultures, primarily based on bhashas, across India. Our first objective is to explore the emergence of bhashas, their connection to political power and the new expressive possibilities available for their speakers. Note that such linguistic and regional cultures have been the basis for linguistic states in independent India. 
 Second, we will consider the nature of state formation and imperialism across India by considering examples such as the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara and Bahamani kingdoms as well as the Mughal empire. We will also study political and administrative innovations as well as the political culture produced in this period. Note that the political elites produced in this era continue to exercise their influence over South Asia until the present. 
 Third, we will study the increasing complexity and diversity of Indian religious imaginations of this era, in which Islam and Christianity become an important part of Indian religiosity. Our specific focus will be on developments in popular Hinduism, specifically bhakti religiosity in different regional languages and cultures. Additionally, we will examine the presence and spread of Islam, particularly through Sufi traditions and the question of conversion to Islam.
 Fourth, we will examine how the Indian landscape was transformed with new forms of monumental architecture, urbanism and water reservoirs, all of which were intimately connected to medieval political projects. Medieval monuments, be they temples, palaces, mosques, forts, mausoleums or water bodies, were built using enduring material and continue to be a part of the built environment. Medieval cities such as Delhi, Surat and Bangalore, though transformed during colonial and modern era, continue to inform Indian urban culture. 
 Fifth, Our final major theme will be to look at the economic developments of the Second Millennium, specifically the expansion of agriculture, manufacturing, trade and commerce and urbanization. This is the period when Indian economy is integrated into the global economy and trading networks. 
 Finally, we conclude the course by considering India’s engagement with the early modern world. Since modernity is seen as a European achievement, we want to end this course by asking whether other cultures, specifically India in our case, contributed to the making of European modernity or fashioned their own modernity. 
 Note that in our exploration of the above mentioned six themes, we will foreground the movement of people, ideas, cultural practices within India and from places such as Central Asia, Arabia, Turkey, Persia, Africa and Afghanistan, all of which leads to the remaking of Indian landscape, demography and civilization.

title: From Mughaliyah Saltanat to Sovereign Republic: India in Transition
description: This course studies the history of India from the death of Emperor Aurangzeb in 1707 to the founding of the Republic of India in 1950. The collapse of the Mughal Empire was followed by a period of competition between various rising powers including the Sikhs, the Marathas, Hyderabad and the Europeans, which eventually resulted in the emergence of the British Raj in India. British colonial rule transformed India. It changed what it meant to be Indian and led to new ways of thinking about nation, religion, and what it meant to be modern. The collapse of British rule in India in 1947 was accompanied by immense violence and lead to the creation of two new countries; India and Pakistan. This course will focus on six key themes; the contest for power among the successors to the Mughal Empire, the rebellion of 1857, the history of the Indian princes, the emergence of Indian nationalism, the two world wars and finally the making of an independent India. The course will prove useful to students interested in Indian history and politics.

title: How We Became Modern: World History from 1750 to the Present
description: In this course we will study the history of the last two hundred and fifty years through a focus on key events that have shaped the modern world. This includes the end of European empires in the Americas and their growth in Asia and Africa, the emergence of nationalism, industrialisation and its environmental consequences, the world wars, the Cold War and globalisation. We will look at a wide variety of interesting historical actors from the gaucho cowboys of South America to the final remnants of the samurai in Japan. We will also encounter various important historical figures including Napoleon Bonaparte, Isambard Brunel, Joseph Stalin, Margaret Thatcher and Barack Obama. In studying this course we will gain a foundational understanding of the politics and history of the world in which we live.

title: Tools, Time and Terrain: Exploring the Prehistoric Archaeology of South Asia
Historical Reasoning
description:
History is not simply the study of what happened in the past. It also involves reflections on the nature of the past itself and how we come to know it. Such reflections on the ontology of the past, our ability to access it and the narrative forms in which the past is presented – have all been extensively discussed in the philosophy of history and historiography. Combining theories and insights from metaphysics, epistemology, hermeneutics and ethics, this course intends to explore the nature of historical thinking and reasoning. As such, this course has two objectives. First, to seek conceptual understanding of categories such as past, time, history, myth, chronology, causation, historical necessity and contingency. Second, this course also explores some key
 questions often raised in the philosophy of history: How do we know, represent and explain the past? Is historical truth objective and absolute or relative and contingent? Does history have meaning or direction? What do historical accounts focus on – individual actions, social structures, cultures, nations and civilizations, different time periods? Finally, do historical accounts carry moral imperatives? To respond to these questions, we will study a number of thinkers such as Vico, Herder, Hegel, Marx, Nietzsche, Collingwood, Michel Foucault, Paul Ricoeur, Hayden White and Ankersmit. Course readings will include a combination of selections from the writings of above-mentioned thinkers and accessible scholarly writings.

title: The Art and Architecture of Medieval South Asia
description:
Is it possible to read physical objects such as paintings and works of architecture as manifestations of economic, political, social and environmental transformation in Medieval South Asia? Given the extent to which scholars have come to rely on texts to narrate the history of medieval South Asia, when and for what reasons might one turn towards physical artifacts and objects as sources of historical information? This course answers the aforementioned questions by bringing attention to artifactual cultures spanning 550 years in South Asia, beginning towards the end of the 12th century and concluding in the mid- eighteenth century. 
 
 The course commences with framing questions around “the medieval” in South Asian History and the ways in which that concept comes to inform debates around community and stateformation, the exercise of sovereignty and power, religiosity, patronage, travel, colonialism, and more recently, populism and nationalism. Subsequently, the course explores the ways in which the periodization of the medieval comes to encompass visual artifacts spanning the Ghurid, Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Vijayanagara, Sharqi, Lodhi and Mughal periods. The course ends with the debates surrounding the emergence of an “early modern period” in South Asian history and the peculiar manner in which the artefactual culture of medieval south Asia comes into conversation with that of the early modern. At the broadest level the course will not only introduce students to a wide array of works of art and architecture in the region, it will also encourage them to develop interpretative descriptions of these works by drawing on a variety of primary and secondary sources.

title: Contemporary India
description: How do we make sense of India? Is India a rich country with poor people? Is it a scientific superpower or a land of superstition? Answering these questions requires an understanding of the contemporary history of India. We will first look through the first fifty-three years of Indian independence to see how different political parties rose and fell, how society and the environment have shaped politics, how India’s foreign policy is made and how the leadership styles of different Indian Prime Ministers varied. We will study a wide variety of important personalities including Jawaharlal Nehru, the Dalai Lama, Lalu Prasad Yadav, Salman Khan and Amartya Sen. We will also look at interesting changes in Indian history from the writing of the constitution to the 1962 Sino-Indian war to the rise of McDonalds. The course will be of interest to students of Indian history, politics and society. More broadly it will be of interest to anyone who is interested in the historical events that defined the lives of their parents and grandparents.

title: Ancient World
description: This course introduces ancient civilizations, specifically focusing on the Indus Valley with discussions on Mesopotamia, Egypt, and China, and an overview of developments in other regions of Asia, Africa, and the Americas. We discuss alternate theories regarding urbanisation and definitions of civilizations. We also highlight discoveries and theoretical and methodological approaches in archaeology that have influenced interpretations of diverse civilizations. The course highlights transformations from early agro-pastoral Neolithic cultures with an emphasis on examining cultural transitions, the origins of agriculture, and the spread of domesticated plants and animals. We discuss the influence of environmental changes on the rise, spread, and decline of civilizations. We highlight issues related to the diverse manifestations of settlements, urban architecture and spatial organisation, governance, socio-economic structures, intellectual and religious lives, technologies, architecture, literature, art/craft, and more. The course discusses ancient population migrations as inferred from archaeological, linguistic, and genetic studies. It concludes by situating ancient worlds within modern contexts as related to changing perceptions and constructions of the past.

title: Revolutions
description: How do you stage a revolution? Why do revolutions happen at some places and times but not others? What will the revolutions of the future look like? These are some the questions that this course will try to answer. Starting with the cognitive revolution thousands of years ago and ending with the ongoing revolution in artificial intelligence, this course will tell the story of world history through social as well as political revolutions. We will look not only at the four great political revolutions in America, Russia, France and China but also at many smaller ones that shape our world in subtle ways from Haiti to Vietnam. We will also study several social revolutions that have been no less instrumental in shaping humanity from the industrial revolution to the sexual revolution. We will explore the causes, ideologies and methods that animated revolutionaries as well as the impact of many of these revolutions on life in the present. In doing so we will also learn about key themes in historiography such as change, contingency, agency and progress.

title: Ramayana
description: This course will deliberate on the historical, political, ethical and literary concerns that frame the epic tale of Ramayana. We will explore the rich and diverse Ramayana tradition, delving into various retellings ranging from textual, to audio-visual to performance arts. Through the course, we will see how the Ramayana narratives have traveled, the story, story-tellers and the audiences, and how, if at all, do we read these various literary and cultural texts as historical sources.

title: The Rise of Civilizations in India
description: This course on early India explores the political, social, economic and religious developments from 2000 BCE up to 800 CE. We will move chronologically through the trimester to understand the changes and continuities that defined ancient India. At the same time, each block will be explored thematically, ranging from differing ideas of sovereignty and governance, the emergence of heterodox sects and Puranic traditions, and their inter-linkages with modes of production and social organisation, changes in material culture, craft technologies, commerce and urbanisation. Together these themes will provide an overview not only of what happened in early India, but why do we study early India? We will use a combination of primary sources and scholarship, and survey the relevant historiographical debates.

title: Food and Power
description:
To eat, like breathing, is a biological instinct of our bodies, necessary for daily functioning. Unlike breathing however, the ways in which we eat, the food items we choose or reject, are linked to societal norms and economic capacities, beyond individual agency. This course will read foodways as systems of communications that encode identities in terms of state and household institutions, geographical markers, religious affiliations, labour and class positions, and caste and gender norms. 
This course will move chronologically through the turn to agriculture, ancient states and empires, religious sacrifices and asceticism, medieval mercantilism, industrialisation and circulation of food and labour, and end in the present day post-globalisation world. We will learn to read primary sources ranging from the pots and pans of the ancient world, medicinal texts, religious canonical literature, oral and written recipe collections, and modern day popular culture. Together, we will use these contexts and sources to understand how food functions as a marker of identity.

title: Biography – a Historical and Literary Exploration
description:
This advanced seminar course (300, 400 and 600) intends to engage with the form of the biography, both as a narrative artefact and as a genre of historical scholarship.
By exploring biographies of ordinary and significant individuals, it will facilitate the discussion of the following questions. What is the relationship between individual lives and their experiences to those of the collectives of which they are a part? How do their lives tell us about the age and the larger events which they might have witnessed, participated or influenced? What light can be thrown on the classic social theory debate on structure and agency through a theoretical study of biography?
A second major concern of the course is the craft of writing biographies. How is the choice of biographical subject made? Is it limited to great man theory or is it possible and desirable to pluralize the subject of biographical writing? How do we write the biographies of different kinds of subjects - pre-modern subjects, modern subjects and living subjects all of which pose different kinds of challenges to a biographer? Should different approaches be adopted by biographers for different subjects?
The course will be reading intensive and will include biographies of a variety of subjects as well as scholarly reflections on the craft of Biography writing. In its first iteration, the course will be team taught with one course coordinator anchoring the course but future iterations of this course may also have a single instructor. The course readings will cover ancient, medieval and modern Indian as well as world history, the themes of race and gender, the fields of science, literature, and social activism, studies of a single person plus of two or more biographical subjects together.

title: Modernism: The Art and Architecture of Anxiety
description:
Modernism: The Art and Architecture of Anxiety, begins by exploring the pivotal artistic and architectural movements of the early 20th century, as attempts to find order and control in an increasingly chaotic world. A growing feeling of alienation and uncertainty about the future owing to the social upheaval of industrialization and the trauma of World War I
 prompted a widespread rejection of traditional artistic, social, and political norms in Euro- America. Modernism, in this “western” sense, was principally an exploration of new forms
 and techniques that shattered existing aesthetic modes, and established a new kind of truth or order that was centered around fragmentation.
 In the initial leg of the course students will therefore explore how the crisis of certainty in turn of twentieth century Europe, eventually led to an artistic embrace of abstraction. A sense of an intellectual and existential vacuum prompted artists to abandon representational art, as they felt that objective reality could no longer be accurately depicted. Instead, they embraced non-figurative art to express inner, subjective “truths” and new, non-Euclidean approaches towards comprehending space and time.
 
 In the second portion of this course we will examine how the anxiety undergirding the advent of Indian modernism was distinct from its Western counterpart. While European modernists grappled with the alienation of the industrial age and the fragmentation of reality, Indian artists faced a different, more complex set of concerns: the trauma of colonialism, the struggle for national identity, and the challenge of synthesizing tradition with modernity. In her influential book, "When Was Modernism," the art critic Geeta Kapur, for instance, highlights how Indian modernists were not simply rebelling against a bourgeois establishment, but were instead engaged in a "double discourse." The anxiety in this context was not about societal fragmentation but rather the existential struggle to forge a new national identity amidst the pressures of colonial rule. Indian modernists grappled with the tension between preserving cultural heritage and embracing the future, a creative anxiety that defined their artistic and architectural expressions. Drawing from Kapur’s writing, and from the art of Nasreen Mohamedi, and the architecture of Charles Correa and BV Doshi, the final leg of the course will therefore examine the extent to which abstraction in the context of Indian Modernism may be viewed as a profound effort to impose order on a world that appeared increasingly divided up between the national and the global, between the inner and the outer, and between the mind and the body.

title: Moving Home: Migrations in Deep Time
description:
For millions of years, people, plants and animals have moved across continents, adapting to
 dynamic past climatic changes and responding to evolving ecological niches in multiple
 ways. This course explores the when, where, how and why of ancient population migrations
 across South Asia. Here, pre- and protohistoric populations inhabited diverse environments,
 leaving behind a wealth of evidence from which archaeologists address questions of
 interest. Who were these populations, and where did they come from? How did their use of
 space across ancient landscapes change through time? Here, we trace the story of migrations
 and mobility of prehistoric populations in South Asia. We begin our story around 3 million
 years ago in Africa and move across the world in the footsteps of hunter-gatherers, farmers
 and urban communities, culminating in the Indus Valley Civilisation. We look at evidence
 drawn from archaeology, past environmental changes, fossils and genetics. We explore
 debates in models that reconstruct the timing and nature of past migrations, on species
 involved and complexities arising from extreme events and environments. We culminate by
 discussing how archaeologists interpret migrations and the implications this has had on the
 evolution of conceptual approaches in archaeology and other disciplines.

title: Gendering South Asian History: 1200-1800 CE
description: The present course uses gender as a lens for looking into the history of medieval and early-modern South Asia. It especially looks at the categories of ‘masculinity’ and ‘ femininity’, how these were constructed and mapped during the period, in relation to one another. In doing so, it considers how evolving ideals of manliness came to inform kingship and domesticity in the Sultanate and the Mughal period. To what extent was the courtly and domestic spaces segregated? What were the ways in which the royal women responded and negotiated with the prescribed norms and participate in politics and court society ? How had art and architectural productions served as sites of gendered patronage, aesthetics, labour and performance ? These are some of the questions that we will address in this course. The course will also explore the non-royal social and political groups, the concubines, dancing girls, women slaves and labourers as well as the gender-liminal figure of the eunuch. The processes of gender marginalisation and defiance of gender normativity will also be taken up, particularly through a study of some of the women saints who challenged societal hierarchies in their pursuit of spirituality. The course will culminate with a discussion on how the notions of gender normativity were reoriented and subverted at the wake of colonialism in the eighteenth century.

title: Diversity and Unity in Medieval Europe 500-1500 CE
description: Too often, especially in Europe itself, the European trajectory of history is taken to be not just a typical template, but one which somehow explains how this relatively small portion of the globe found a path to world domination. We miss too easily that that domination was really achieved by only three or four of Europe’s very numerous polities, not even all the largest ones, and that the continent remained and remains broken up and contentious in identity, even though it is often treated and even acts like a single politico-religious entity. This course looks at Europe’s first and formative millennium, and tries to distinguish what worked against its unity and maintained its distinct identities and practices, as well as the more usual opposite. Looking especially at religion and government, as well as the basic resources of life, it sets out to make clearer how Europe’s foundations mean it has never quite been one thing together, despite how much its components share.

title: West Asia and the Mediterranean 200-700 CE: Empires, Religions and Replacement
description: The early centuries of the Common Era in West Asia are dominated in historiography by two opposed empires, that of the Romans and that of the Persians. Arguably the whole of European history, which has subsequently been exported to much of the globe, is the process of dealing with and occasionally trying to reverse the end of the Roman culture; Persia, though less well-recorded, is no less significant for its inheritors, Islamic and otherwise. This course charts the entwined fates of the two empires in their long final phase, which ended with their replacement, in whole or in part, by a new competitor in the form of the first Islamic caliphate. Religion, ethnic identity and ideas about power come to the fore in this course, which will leave you understanding better both the shape of the world which West Asia has affected today and the enduring cultural significance of Rome, and Persia, as archetypes and aspirations.

title: Indian Historiography
description: This course introduces students to modes of history writing in India with a specific focus on modern and contemporary periods. We will begin with a brief survey of how the past was remembered and documented in ancient and mediaeval India. Then our goal will be to study different schools of modern historiography such as Colonial, Nationalist, Cambridge, Marxist, Subaltern and Hindutva. Students will learn to recognize the underlying conceptions of past and history present in different schools and also the narrative strategies deployed.

title: Indian Historiography
description: This course introduces students to modes of history writing in India with a specific focus on modern and contemporary periods. We will begin with a brief survey of how the past was remembered and documented in ancient and mediaeval India. Then our goal will be to study different schools of modern historiography such as Colonial, Nationalist, Cambridge, Marxist, Subaltern and Hindutva. Students will learn to recognize the underlying conceptions of past and history present in different schools and also the narrative strategies deployed.

title: Exploring the Social and the Historical
Introduction to Literary Studies
description: This course is designed to introduce Literature majors to some of the fundamental concepts and practices of literary criticism. We shall begin with a preliminary survey of the history of literary study as a way to propose working definitions of a few key terms: What do we mean by literature? What is a text? Who is an author? And what constitutes literary criticism? This last question will bring us to questions that pertain directly to method: In what ways can a text be read? Does it make sense to speak of a literary method in the same way as we speak, say, of the scientific method? Or, to put it another way, is there anything that all works of literary criticism share in common, or is it futile to look for such a common ground?

title: Android Dreams: Technological Imaginaries in Literature and Film
description: We often hear that technology will solve our biggest problems—inequality, governance, even loneliness. But why has technology become the main way we imagine the future at all? And what kinds of futures does it make possible—or impossible? This course approaches these questions through literature and film. We will read short stories, speculative fiction, and literary texts alongside cinema, treating them not as entertainment or illustration, but as forms of thinking—ways in which societies imagine, desire, or resist technological change. Focusing on South Asia, we will explore technological imaginaries: how narratives give shape to ideas of progress, control, care, and the human. We will practice close reading and interpretation, paying attention to voice, form, metaphor, and narrative structure, and ask how stories make technological futures imaginable.

title: Creative Writing
description:
The Introduction to Creative Writing is an intensive writing workshop designed to give students the opportunity to develop their craft via in-class workshops, readings, discussions, and one-on-one tutorials. The discussions will also focus on publishing and the publishing industry. The course will include Zoom sessions with authors and literary agents. 

The class will mimic the frenzied pace of real-life publishing. There will be deadlines, drafts, and redrafts. We will learn to read like writers and write like writers under pressure. 

Students will turn in one fully realized piece of fiction (a short story or the first chapter of a novel in progress) and a book review for the course. For the book review, students will choose a work of fiction by an author who comes from a background different from theirs (we will discuss in class what this means) on which to write a paper and give a presentation. The paper will be divided into two sections – the first will be a 1,000-word review of the book, and the second will be an analysis of the reviews the book has garnered in the media. The analysis should include students’ thoughts on the audience the book was written for, the type of marketing that might have gone into the book, the cover, the hooks used to gain publicity, author interviews, etc. You will need to search The New York Times, New Yorker, Guardian, Washington Post, Hindustan Times, Hindu, Financial Times, and other publications for reviews and features on the book. You will give a 10-minute presentation on your review.

title: Genre (Shakespeare on Screen)
description: This course will look at how the poetry of modernity - as a ground-breaking, insurgent â€˜genreâ€™, as a congress of ideas, and as a symptom and experience of modernity - thrived between the mid-19th and mid-20th centuries. Through a series of readings of primary and associative texts, the fundamental task of the course will be to think through the idea of the â€˜poetry of modernityâ€™. The poetry of modernity thrived in the metropolises of modernity but also away from it; found form in both heavily modernising imperial cities as well as in the cities forged by coloniality; was debated in the artistsâ€™ salons as much as in islands of individual genius; it talked back to the technologies of modernity as much as it turned away from them. Broadly it was a poetry of animation, alienation and contemplative ennui. The poetry of modernity was also transmedial (it found kinship with photography and art, cinema and new fiction), transnational (it flourished in several centres of contact between nationalities) and transitional, responding to an ephemeral, delirious, radically remade world. It is this network of opposites - the need to respond and revolt, to accommodate and alienate, to comply and dissent, to find fellowship but through extreme individuation- is what triggered the difficult and productive search for a new idiom and a new language of poetry. From the fundamental question of a broad definition, the course shall hence proceed to the more difficult question: is the poetry of modernity primarily a genre of poetry; or is it thus only when it is part of the experience and consciousness of modernity?

title: Literary Movements
description: This course will aim to introduce concepts such as literary â€œperiods,â€ â€œmovements,â€ or â€œinfluencesâ€ as a fundamental instrument of criticism. They enable scholars to understand, by way of comparison or contrast, innovations in form and genre that go beyond the particular practices and choices of individual writers. Focusing on a specific literary movementâ€”English Romanticism of the nineteenth centuryâ€”we will examine what a periodising approach to literary studies looks like. When and how is a literary or artistic movement born, named, periodised, and canonised?
