And what does organising texts and writers into particular movements or periods do to the way in which we read them? The course will then make a distinction between historical periods and literary or artistic movements, the latter being defined, not merely chronologically, but in terms of specific literary and artistic goals shared across time, place, mediums, and genres. We will regard the movement in question as defined by critics retrospectively, as well as by the members themselves. And finally we will read Romanticism in relation to movements that preceded and succeeded it, as a way to gain insight into how movements fit into a historical continuum, how some movements are distinct and well defined while others are more nebulous and fluid, and why the notion of movements have at times been a point of contention among scholars.

title: Brief Encounters: The Short Story through Histories and Cultures
description: If brevity is indeed the soul of wit, then the short story is the fictional equivalent of modernity: it captures an instant, a hovering mood, a passing shadow. In fact, in some ways the short story is the arch-genre of modernity. In the early to mid-19th century, the modern metropolis was being forged by capital, migration and anonymity; here rapid industrialisation made demands on uninterrupted time; the telegraph and the railways atomised distance; photography made visualising of a moment possible. It is in that kind of a city where print modernity took sharp turns and the short story became one of the founding genres to mirror the harried, hurried, fleeting life in the new metropolis. It came to belong to a space in between a sketch and a tale, a fable and a saga, an anecdote and a long narrative. This course would look at the cultural and social origin of the short story; enquire into the ways in which it has transformed over the last century and a half; look at some of the critical approaches to it; and study its astonishing fecundity and flourish, including in the Indian subcontinent. In short, this course will be a survey of the genre as well as one which would look closely at some of its most representative specimens, and in several languages.

title: An Introduction to Poetry
description: This course is a deep dive into the reading and practice of poetry. What is a poem? How is it fashioned? What makes it such a powerful form of literary enchantment? This course explores the building blocks of poetry, interspersed with readings of poems from around the world – canonical and less familiar. As it delves into questions around the role of sound and metaphor, free verse and fixed form, inspiration and craft, it will examine how we might become better practitioners, as well as better listeners. The course will combine immersive practice sessions with readings, group discussions with one-on-one interactions. In addition to multiple writing and reading exercises, students will turn in a final assignment that includes six rigorously-workshopped poem drafts and one poem review.

title: Twentieth Century Women's Literatures
description: In recognition of the difference in experiences and history of those identifying with the category of “woman” (as opposed to their “male” counterparts), it was felt by many literary feminist critics in the twentieth century that literatures produced by these women would inevitably bear the marks of this history of difference that must be attended to. Following this tradition of feminist literary criticism, this course will involve studying selected writings of women in the twentieth century. As one would expect, any imagination of such a course would present several challenges. First, the category of “women” is a contested one and one must account for the diversity of experiences—along the lines of class, caste, race, ethnicity, sexuality—that resist such a universal categorization. Given this, one must contend with the following question: Do women across these boundaries have any unifying experiences or is the point of such a course to excavate difference even as it seeks to bring together disparate groups of persons under the category of “woman”? Second, one must inevitably be cautious while trying to use traditional (masculinist) theories of literary criticism in order to read women’s literatures even as one must resist a hasty assimilation of all women’s literatures into existing categories of feminist literatures (and leave it at that). How has feminist literary criticism negotiated these challenges and sought to construct an analytical lens that is drawn from the works of these women writers? This course will provide students with an opportunity to think through some of these challenges and questions with the help of literary works written—poetry, short stories, and essays—by women in the twentieth century. The course’s focus is primarily on Western literary traditions and thus, most writers included are from the West. Through close reading of these texts and attention to historical traditions and contexts within which these writers wrote, this course will unpack the shape of literary imaginations and landscapes that are specific to women writers of this century. In doing so, students will be encouraged to think about the role that women’s literatures and feminist literary criticisms might play in shaping mainstream literary studies.

title: Voice and World: The Literary Essay
description: Voice and World: The Literary Essay is a twelve-week course designed to give students the opportunity to read a number of important literary essays and learn how to write their own. It is a vital addition to the writing program of Krea University. Students will get the chance to engage with this thriving literary form, reading such writers as Nora Ephron, Julian Barnes, DR Nagaraj, William Hazlitt and Umberto Eco, among others. A good essay relies on a personalistic style but brings forth crucial understandings about the world we live in. Students will learn how to research an idea they are interested in, develop their thoughts along suitable lines, and forward an argument in elegant, concise language. Students will work on multiple short essays over the course of the term and one final longer essay. This is a reading and writing-heavy course, in which we will encourage exploring ideas from other academic disciplines.

title: Out on a Quest: Writing a Research Essay
description: Researchers are questers asking research questions to better understand the worldly wilderness we inhabit. They track and read sources, reflect on ideas, form alliances, combat misreading - wielding reading skills and writing implements. They return transformed by the quest, to tell their tale with a well written research essay that adds to how we know the world. This upper-level writing course for literature students will advance the skills learned in WOC and LAA. The drafting process will include basic archival research to find sources for a topic of one’s choice; distinguishing between different kinds of sources; asking research questions; making claims supported by evidence; sustaining an argument; getting and giving revision feedback; and, learning citation systems in addition to MLA. Motivated by the guiding principles of asking questions that perhaps stay unanswered in the process of knowledge creation, this writing intensive course aims to introduce students to the work of research as it gets bigger in scale and complexity. To meet the final goal of writing a proofed and polished 2,500 words research essay by the end of the term, students will complete shorter, targeted tasks for the new skills they are learning. For instance, if they have been introduced to an online archive, or have found one on their own, they may submit a description of it. Other exercises may include annotating a text, creating a glossary of conceptual terms, close-reading, writing summaries of sources they will work with, giving peer feedback, interspersed with revising and submitting drafts at incremental word limits.

title: Writing in Genre: Speculative Fiction
description: This course will engage significantly with a specific form of creative fiction writing: speculative fiction. It will be one of a rotating series of Genre courses that we hope to offer as part of the Creative Writing minor. Speculative fiction is an extremely popular genre among writers and students. At the outset of this course, we will engage with a fundamental question: What makes a piece of writing speculative? As the term progresses, we will look deeply at the most popular forms of speculative fiction: dystopic literature, fantasy writing and alternate history fiction. Students will work on short pieces during the first weeks, and then are expected to develop and complete a longer story by the end of term.

title: Make or Break?: The Literary Canon
description: This course explores how literary canons are formed by a multitude of different forces such as nation, culture, language, and economics. Beginning with a case study on the “western” or “English” canon in the form of one of the most canonical female writers of all time, this course teaches students how, why, and when certain “great” works gain their importance or place in the canon. In doing so, students will learn how certain forces of inclusion and exclusion create so-called literary canons. This course also asks students to consider what it would mean to imagine canons (or their absence) differently: for example, what would a “global” literary canon look like? How would you structure a canon of women’s literature? Do we need canons at all? To begin to answer these questions, our reading will explore the idea of the canon and its relationship to adaptations, translations, intertextuality, and literary prizes through key writers and texts and a trio of literary events in 2025: the global celebrations of the 250th anniversary of Jane Austen; the Nobel in Africa symposium in Stellenbosch, South Africa (November 2025), featuring literary prize-winners J.M. Coetzee and Abdulrazak Gurnah; and, closer to home in south India, the 2025 International Booker Prize for Heart Lamp to Banu Mushtaq and Deepa Bhasthi

title: Translation
description: This course aims to introduce students to Translation Studies (TS), by engaging with specific questions central to the domain. These questions revolve around the concept of equivalence, including issues of equivalence at various levels of language and text; they relate to challenges specific to non-literary and literary translations. At the same time, this course exposes students to various theoretical perspectives on translation in its interactions with culture. Beginning with a broad outline of the scope, history and central issues of TS, this course goes on to discuss various levels of equivalence. It begins with a focus on non-literary translation, and, thereafter, opens up to challenges specific to literary translation. Beginning with a close-up view in order to engage with these ‘building blocks’ of translation, it then goes on to view the process of translation from its place within culture and addresses issues that flow from it. Finally, it brings up some philosophical perspectives on translation. Thus, the course aims to give a comprehensive view of the act of translation and of issues concerning the domain of TS.

title: Advanced Creative Writing
description: Advanced Creative Writing is a twelve-week course in which students expand on the skills they acquired in Introduction to Creative Writing. You will master the elements of fiction via workshops, one-on-one tutorials and multiple rewrites. You will wax eloquent about plot and dialogue (did someone groan at “action beats”?). You will talk craft and lyricism and resolution. You will finesse your voice and form. You will birth compelling characters in well-thought-out settings. You will continue learning the rules of writing and break them with aplomb. This is a painfully intensive course. Be prepared for double the reading and writing you did in Introduction to Creative Writing. At the end of the term you will produce two fully realized short stories, which, the professor realizes, is difficult to accomplish in three months. You, the student, need to realize this, too, and embrace the chaos of real-life publishing. There will be innumerable drafts, redrafts and deadlines. Each draft you produce will be up for your peers’ consumption. You will all work as editors to help make a story the best it can be. Zoom meetings with practitioners of fiction, editors and agents will further your understanding of the publishing world.

title: Adaptation as Translation
description:
This course aims to expand the study of translation to examine adaptation as integral to it. Some theorists (notably Vinay and Darbelnet: 1958) see adaptation as one translation procedure amongst many others; it is seen as a means of attaining ‘situational equivalence’ to deal with issues of cultural transfer that might affect the receiver’s reception or understanding of the text of departure. Whereas, for others (e.g., Gambier: 1992), all translations inevitably involve adaptation, not least because all acts of translation are, simultaneously, acts of rewriting (Lefevere: 1992). In any case, both poles of opinion, in their own ways, underline the importance of adaptation to translation.
Adaptations of literary works to cinema [sometimes described as translation from literary language to cinematic language (e.g., by Cahir: 2006)], offer a fascinating opportunity to study this enmeshed nature of translation and adaptation, and to enrich our understanding of both these crucial procedures of cultural transfer. 
This course will first employ theoretical perspectives to understand processes of translation and adaptation, and to situate them vis-à-vis each-other. As a practical development of this theoretical work, it will then examine the adaptation/translation of works from three literary genres (viz. novel, play and short story) to cinema; by picking up the nuances of cinematic language (montage, mis en scène, camera-pen, auteur-cinema, among others), it will study the translation of the works from words to moving images and sounds.

title: Humour in the Twentieth Century
description:
The course revisits the idea of humour as an artistic, cultural and humane practice and powerful, potential and often radical form of critique across nations, genres, tongues and political climate. The course intentionally mixes up canonical and comparatively unknown texts so that students are able to respond to them both in terms of their own power, as well as their location in cultures from which they emerged

Learning Outcomes:
1. Understanding with various forms of humour.
2. Understanding humour as a historical praxis.
3. Deep engagement with humour as critique of politics, modernity and society .
4. Interrogating the 20th century from the vantage of laughter, satire and insurgent
critique.
5. A wide engagement with works of culture from a variety of contexts.
6. Engaging with a key question of our time: is humour possible in an age of political
correctness.

title: Women's Authorship in Narrative Cinema
description: The epithet “auteur” in cinema studies is applied to influential filmmakers who incorporate a distinctive aesthetic in their films and stamp their creative work with their unique personality. However, using the concept of the “auteur”, canons of cinema (and culture) often tend towards highlighting the works of “great” male directors, at the cost of ignoring the participation of women in cinema since the inception of film as a cultural form. In this course, we focus on women directors and their contributions to cinematic production in the area of narrative film. We study theoretical perspectives from feminist and queer film theory to engage with how creative work is undertaken by women in patriarchal, capitalist media production industries. We ground selected film texts in their socio-political contexts, situating women’s directorial voices work within feminist, queer, race, and caste movements that advocate for the greater visibility and representation of women’s voices in filmmaking.

title: Editing and Publishing
description: This is a 12-week course in which students learn the nuances of editing and develop a thorough understanding of the publishing industry. By the end of the term, you will have mastered the intricacies of wielding the red pen by picking out holes in stories, learning to make every word count, and knowing your semi-colons from your commas. You will learn to differentiate between editing a short story and a news story. As expert editors, you will realize that editing is as much a science of exactitude as it’s an art. To write, you will discover, is to edit. The class will be heavy on workshops. You will learn not just to edit but to edit under pressure. You will also learn what it means to be an editor in the age of AI. Editing is a small component of the publishing journey, which is often a long, drawn-out affair. We will become familiar with this somewhat opaque process and understand the complexities of modern-day publishing. We will learn what happens to a book once it is written, the various roles professionals play to get it published, and why a writer needs an agent. We will cover editorial pitches, book design, and marketing and publicity. How does one find work in publishing? What are some new-age responsibilities of writers in an era of literature festivals and shameless self-promotion? How do some books become bestsellers while others fade into irrelevance? We will address all these questions via in-class lectures, seminars and meetings with professionals.

title: Shakespeare on Screen
description: Much of the appeal of William Shakespeare’s seemingly inexhaustible power as a playwright lies in some of the most astonishing adaptations of his plays. This course will discuss how his plays have travelled across culture and medium, regions and most importantly, languages; and how the inherent potency of a Shakespearean play is unlocked in tongues far removed from the original. By bringing together some of his most well- known plays to stand in comparison with some of the most interesting and landmark cinematic adaptations, the course hopes to highlight both older and newer issues that have surfaced in Shakespearean studies over the years: from honour, state, authority, ambition, filial love, jealousy and madness to the more recent explorations of race, culture, sexuality, identity, gender and authorship itself. Also, the course would want to understand the politics and poetics of adaptation, elemental film theory and f ilm form, the language of cinema and how iconic texts perform as visual imagery. The primary focus of the course are four of Shakespeare’s most canonical works: Macbeth, Hamlet, King Lear and Julius Caesar. Having said that, the course will immediately get into challenging the very idea of their canonicity by entering them into a productive encounter with their cinematic adaptations. These adaptations, some of which will be studied closely, not only reinterpret these much revered literary classics, but also tend to push them away from having an ontological centre. To that end, the course is equally a study of how literary texts are both iconised and destabilized by the image.

title: The Body in Medieval and Early Modern Europe
description: Visceral, often uncontrolled and in states of excess or restraint, the body confounds the imagination, transforming and transmuting as it moves through the world. It consumes and is consumed, and is an infinitely malleable entity. The Medieval and Early Modern periods reimagined the relationship between bodies— political, philosophical, spiritual, social and aesthetic— articulating new possibilities for the ways in which bodies manifested themselves and their own positioning within a larger world; one opened up by trade, travel and encounter. In this course, we will explore different understandings and expressions of the body, embodiment, and corporeal subjectivity in European literature from the 6th through 18th centuries. Designed to be interdisciplinary, the course examines discourses of the body and its relationship to questions of biological, chronological, ontological, and epistemic subjectivity. Scholars including Peter Stallybrass and Stephen Greenblatt, have placed the genesis of modern ideas of embodied subjectivity in the early modern period, while Geraldine Heng, JRR Tolkien, Harold Bloom, and others, have theorized the importance of examining medieval discourses of embodiment as precursors to contemporary understandings of race, gender, disability, monstrosity and more. This course draws together scholarship from across disciplines– history, art history, literary studies, performance studies, disability studies, and critical period studies, to complicate, enrich, and diversify how the body becomes and is a site of interrogation and inquiry in the humanities and humanistic social sciences. The course structure is driven by its primary texts, which will change in every iteration. The current iteration of the course focuses on performance and expressive culture, primarily drawn from the Western European canon. Primary readings include Beowulf, the lais of Marie de France, and theatrical texts by Shakespeare, Corneille, and Moliere.

title: Cinema and the Idea of the Political
description: This course looks at the critical moments of encounter between two defining intimations of public space — cinema and mass politics — without collapsing the autonomy of cinema as an art, and politics as an hermeneutic of collective self-determination. Cinema’s birth at the summit of industrial modernity is no news, and neither is its capacity for both mass enrichment and manipulation. But there is relentless and often renewed debate about ‘political cinema’ and its ‘uses’, which lead us to the very genesis of the idea of mass culture in the early years of modernity. It must be stated at the very onset that the course looks at ‘narrative cinema’ rather than on documentary, cinéma vérité, or at the visual cultures of Lettrists, Situationists, avant-gardists, surrealists etc., all of whom have done pioneering work in the domain. How did cinema capture the political zeitgeist of the 1920s, 1940s and 1960s? Or even after? On the other hand, how does politics - as a thought and practice - allow for cinematic/spectacular enunciation? Habermas scholar Robert Porter pointedly asks, “Does cinema express or engender political thought? Can we think of cinema, or certain specific cinematic texts, as bodies of political theory?” His is an assertive nod. As an undergraduate course, this one would not set the high ambitions of teaching political theory through cinema. Therefore, the course does not name itself ‘political cinema’. There are, if one could say so, as many political films as there are kinds of politics, but more importantly, unlike other ‘studio-defined’ and ‘market-refined’ genres like ‘horror’, ‘crime’, ‘musical’, and ‘social’, political cinema has remained notoriously undefined (and undefinable). The way Soviet Cinema was ‘political’ is not the way James Bond Cold War spoofs were, nor were the French or Czech New Wave; or say, Satyajit Ray’s political fables made for children. But they are all political in the wide sense of the term. Hence, this course would not like to begin with an apriori idea of ‘political cinema’ but rather inquire if such a conceptual framework emerges through and with the course. To that end, the course would follow in the steps of Walter Benjamin, the Frankfurt School, Third Cinema and its legacies, and postcolonial uses of cinema. Claire Molloy and Yannis Tzioumakis, in The Routledge Companion To Cinema And Politics says that cinema “remains central to the formation and transformation of geopolitical discourses, imagining new geographies and connecting (or separating), in complex ways, the concepts of boundaries and territories with ideas about nation and identity.” At the same time, cinema has often found expressing working class and feminist solidarity as much as it has bored into the pervasive and pernicious nature of political memory, politics as stimulus, and the abiding lust for tyranny in political regimes. These will be some of the lines of argument/reflection in this course.

title: The Lives and Afterlives of Great Books
description: New course description: "This course offers a foundation in literary studies, through the medium of great books, and their reception across time. Engaging questions of what constitutes a great book, canonization, intertextuality, and methods for reading, we will study some of the greatest and most influential works of literature in translation, adaptation, and discursive dialogue. This class is reading-intensive, and of particular importance to students in the humanistic disciplines. Each iteration of the course will focus on a single intellectual, literary or performance genealogy, be it through the centering of specific texts, or through specific concepts, genres, or media. In Trimester 1 of the 2026-27 academic year, students will close-read and interrogate the Greco-Roman Homeric intertextual canon, with the Iliad as our core text. All students must purchase physical copies of the required texts for the course, without exception, due to the annotative nature of assignments.

title: Fictions of History
description: This course looks at representations of history in fiction, film and auto/biography. Focussing on texts in English geographically ranging from England to South Africa, India and Australia, and temporally from the eighteenth century to the present day, we will examine the intersections of history and fiction in selected works from around the globe. What are the implications of reading a novel for its historical content or accuracy? How does the memoir or biography negotiate intergenerational histories and ideas of veracity? How do different writers reflect on questions of authorship and audience? How might archival research and films – documentaries, biopics, and adaptations – expand our readings of novels and histories? This is an interdisciplinary seminar which is designed to emphasise a high level of critical thinking and creativity. Students will be encouraged through their worksheets and their ongoing notebook assignment to be fully prepared and to contribute to each session productively, as well as to reflect on connections between each week’s topic. The final assessment is a visual archive essay which will require independent and original research, and which will be workshopped and presented to the seminar group at the end of term.

title: Southern Spaces
description: This interdisciplinary research-led module explores the cartographical South – from e.g., the port cities of Cape Town, Durban, Chennai, Adelaide and Sydney to the islands of Sri Lanka, Zanzibar and Mauritius. These transoceanic southern spaces are also transhemispheric, so what might be the continuities and connections geographically between southern sites on different latitudinal lines? Sri Lankan historian Sujit Sivasundaram’s marvellous monographs, Islanded and Waves Across the South, suggest more navigational and narrative strategies for conceptualising and rethinking what we count as archives, and what we call the ‘South’. Our goal in this module is indeed visual, archival and cartographical, as we travel across novels, maps, photographs and other materials to register coordinates on coastlines and seascapes. The texts also take us into the heart of the country, e.g., to the interior landscapes of Namaqualand, the Karoo, Flinders Ranges, Pulicat Lake, Yala National Park, and the botanical gardens of Kandy, Kirstenbosch and Kew. Examining the legacies of the ‘networks of empire’ that bring many of these sites and texts together historically and geographically, the module is excellent preparation for further interdisciplinary research on South-South mobilities, and asks questions about colonial legacies, ideas of ownership, belonging, cultural identity, and migration. The current variation of this module, first launched at SOAS in 2014, is inspired by a series of events: the travelling exhibition, Scenes from the South that I curated in collaboration with universities and museums (2020; 2022; 2024); the public programme, ‘Speaking from the South’ at the University of Adelaide in 2024 that was inspired by this work; the Cátedra Coetzee Literatures of the South programme from 2015-2018 at UNSAM in Argentina, led by Nobel Prizewinner J. M. Coetzee; and the crucial forerunner of my more recent research, a 1992 University of London conference, ‘Southern Spaces’, from which the module takes its name.

title: Tools for Mathematics and the Sciences: Algebra
description:
This course will expose students to certain basic tools and calculations in algebra. Some of the material may be familiar to those who studied mathematics in high school. Familiarity with the material discussed in this course may be assumed in subsequent courses across various disciplines including mathematics and physics. 
In an article titled ‘The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences’, physicist Eugene Wigner wrote “… the enormous usefulness of mathematics in the natural sciences is something bordering on the mysterious and that there is no rational explanation for it”. Mathematics has emerged as the natural language using which the laws governing the working of the universe can be described; it is also a discipline with a rich internal structure explored through powerful frameworks for description and justification. Whether one is studying black holes or neural networks, molecular bonds or climate models, tiling patterns or cryptography, the use of mathematics is unavoidable. A solid foundation of mathematics is therefore an essential part of the skill set required of every student of the natural sciences; a good grasp of basic tools, examples, and calculations is also essential for those planning to study mathematics in greater depth and rigour.
Note: This course does not count as a required or elective course contributing to the graduation requirements in either Mathematics or Physics.

title: Tools for Mathematics and the Sciences: Calculus
description:
This course will expose students to certain basic tools and calculations in calculus. Some of the material may be familiar to those who studied mathematics in high school. Familiarity with the material discussed in this course may be assumed in subsequent courses across various disciplines including mathematics and physics.

title: Proofs and Ideas: An Introduction to Mathematical Thinking
description: In this course, we will start to think carefully and rigorously about mathematics, mathematical objects, and the idea of proof. We begin with a discussion of the basic mathematical notions of sets, functions, and relations, and proceed to discuss some fundamental properties of the natural numbers and integers. After this foundational background, we will further develop our ability to read, understand, and write proofs through a short study of select mathematical topics.  After taking this course, students will have been exposed to the idea of mathematical proof and equipped with the basic tools they will need to study further in the discipline.

title: Analysis I
description: The course begins with a rigorous discussion of the real numbers and an investigation of their basic properties. Certain special subsets of real numbers (open, closed, bounded) are introduced and studied. The course culminates in a formal study of the idea of a limit in the context of sequences and infinite series.

title: Analysis 2: Single variable calculus
description:
In this course, students will develop an understanding of the foundations of calculus. The course will provide a rigorous introduction to limits, continuity, differentiability, and integration, in the context of real-valued functions of a single real variable. Students will also be exposed to some of the applications of this material in the form of a short introduction to the Gamma function, a function with numerous applications in many branches of mathematics including mathematical physics, number theory, and probability. 
 After completing this course, students will have the ability to prove many of the fundamental theorems of calculus, thus providing a rigorous justification for results they may have seen previously in other circumstances. The material studied here is a fundamental part of any mathematician’s training: it will be used repeatedly throughout the rest of the mathematics major in a variety of courses.

title: Multivariable Calculus
description: This course is designed to be a concrete introduction to the ideas and methods underlying (differential and integral) calculus of several variables. The emphasis is on examples and computations. The basic techniques from this course are useful in a wide variety of subjects: analysis, probability, (differential) geometry, applied mathematics. This course is designed to be useful for students in both mathematics and areas such as computer science, economics, physics, and data science.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations
description:
This course is  an introduction to differential equations from a modern perspective, with a view towards dynamical systems. The course begins with an introduction to the art of modelling real life situations with differential equations: this will help develop an intuition for the subject, and introduce students to the basic ideas behind mathematical modelling. 
The course will then examine the techniques used to solve differential equations, including qualitative, analytical, and computational techniques. In particular, students will be asked to understand the algorithms that lead to numerical solutions, to interpret the resulting pictures produced by the computer, and to relate these images back to the original application.

title: Linear Algebra
description: Linear algebra provides a systematic unified framework to consider the theory of vectors, matrices, determinants, and systems of linear equations. This course will provide a concrete introduction to these ideas.

title: Algebra 1
description: Groups are the mathematical formalisation of symmetry: in this course, students will study their definition and basic properties. In particular, the important notion of a group action will be introduced. Group theory provides an organizing framework for describing the internal symmetries of mathematical objects across many branches of mathematics, while also serving as a useful language for describing many mathematical invariants.

title: Writing in Mathematics and Quantitative Sciences
description:
Writing and communicating mathematical ideas are becoming more and more important to practitioners of Mathematics and mathematically oriented sciences. While Mathematics is concerned with theorems and proofs, disciplines such as Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Computer Science, Economics, and Data Science additionally employ mathematical formalism for modeling and mathematical statistics for data analysis. Writing and communication in these disciplines take the form of research publications as well as writing in public forums in accessible language. This course explores writing and communicating mathematical knowledge in two distinct but related registers: technical and non-technical (specifically, journalistic) writing. The first register discusses how to convey mathematical ideas in the form of proofs, model derivations, and statistical analysis to a technically trained audience, while the second register explores how science journalists disseminate these ideas to a wider readership. In this course, the students will read exemplary pieces of academic and journalistic mathematical writing to derive principles of effective communication and implement the same in their
 own writing.

title: Analysis 3
description: This course builds upon Analysis 1 and Analysis 2 by helping us generalise our understanding of notions like limits and continuity from sequences of real numbers and functions of a single real variable to more sophisticated contexts. The course begins by developing the theory of sequences of functions, and introduces the important notion of uniform convergence: continuity, differentiability, and integrability are studied in this context. This material is then used to better understand the role that polynomials play in spaces of functions and introduce the important idea of a power series.

title: Complex Analysis
Probability
description: Probability is the branch of mathematics that deals with the study of randomness. The study of probability provides a foundation to systematically explore processes in the natural and social worlds around us. In this course students will be introduced to the basics of probability theory including the underlying axioms, conditional probability and independence, random variables, and distributions. The course will also cover proofs of some of the classic results in probability theory, the Weak Law of Large Numbers, and the Markov and Chebyshev inequalities. At the end of this course, students will have an appreciation for using mathematical formalism in exploring randomness, and develop a basic set of tools to rigorously model phenomena with underlying uncertainty.

title: Numerical Methods
description:
This is a course in numerical analysis for mathematics students which means that the algorithms are motivated from mathematical theorems and the convergence analysis of these algorithms converts those theorems into quantitative estimates. For example, Taylor’s theorem serves as motivation for many algorithms for solving algebraic as well as differential equations. Broadly, this course will cover floating point arithmetic and errors they produce, numerical linear algebra, root-finding, polynomial interpolation, numerical integration and differentiation, numerical solutions of ordinary differential equations, and optimization. This course will have a computational component which will involve learning a programming language (Julia) to implement the algorithms of this course.
 
 After this course, you will know a variety of standard numerical algorithms in linear algebra, root-finding, interpolation, integration, ODEs, optimization that are relevant in applications. You will also have learnt how to implement these algorithms on a computer and be wary of errors and artifacts.

title: Algebra 2
description: In this course, students will be introduced to the theory of rings and fields. The language of ring theory and field theory helps describe fundamental relationships between algebra, number theory and geometry and geometry, and provides a unifying framework for describing certain types of number systems and operator spaces.The course will begin with a study of important families of rings such as Euclidean domains, Principal Ideal Domains, and Unique Factorisation Domains. After a brief discussion of polynomial rings over Unique Factorisation Domains, the course will then develop the theory of fields. We will describe how to adjoin roots of polynomials to fields, and introduce the idea of an algebraic field extension. The course will conclude with a discussion on splitting fields.

title: Algebra 3
description: After a recap of material from Linear Algebra (generalised to arbitrary fields), we will introduce quotients of vector spaces and study their properties. The course then covers a spectrum of foundational material: spaces of linear transformations; duality; determinants; minimal and characteristic polynomials; diagonalisability and triangularisability; inner product spaces; spectral theorems; singular value decompositions; bilinear and sesquilinear forms; Jordan normal forms.

title: Topology 1
description:
Topology is the study of spaces and sets and can be thought of as an extension of geometry. It involves the examination of the local as well as the global structure of a space or set. The foundation of General Topology (or Point-Set Topology) is set theory. There are other areas of topology including Geometric Topology, Algebraic Topology, Differential Topology, Low-Dimensional Topology, and various others. 
 
 This course provides a bridge between the basic knowledge of metric spaces and the more abstract knowledge of algebraic topology. In this course, we see how metric spaces can be generalized to objects called ‘topological spaces’ and the properties of metric spaces can be formulated in a more general way for these spaces. We will cover topological spaces, open and closed sets, interiors and boundaries of sets, continuous functions, homeomorphisms, connectedness, and compactness.
 After the completion of this course, a student should be able to:
 Define and illustrate the concept of topological spaces and continuous functions,
 Define and illustrate the concept of product topology and quotient topology,
 Prove a selection of theorems concerning topological spaces, continuous functions, product topologies, and quotient topologies,
 Define and illustrate the concepts of the separation axioms and countability axioms,
 Define connectedness and compactness, and prove a selection of related theorems.

title: Graph Theory
description:
Graph Theory is a central area of discrete mathematics concerned with the study of
 graphs—mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects. This
 course provides a rigorous introduction to the fundamental concepts, results, and methods of
 graph theory, together with selected topics from algebraic graph theory and network
 optimization.
 The course begins with the basic definitions and properties of graphs, including paths, cycles,
 trees, connectivity, and degree sequences. It then develops algorithmic techniques for
 spanning trees, shortest paths, and related optimization problems. The second part introduces
 algebraic tools for studying graphs, including adjacency and Laplacian matrices, eigenvalues,
 eigenvectors, and their interpretations in terms of structure and centrality.
 Building on this foundation, the course explores network flows, duality, and the Max-
 Flow/Min-Cut theorem, along with applications to combinatorial optimization. The final
 module addresses advanced topics such as graph coloring, random graphs, and some more
 algebraic graph theory.
 
 By the end of the course, students will have a clear understanding of the theoretical principles
 underlying modern graph theory and will be able to apply mathematical reasoning to analyze
 and solve problems involving discrete structures and networks.

title: Mathematics for Machine Learning
description:
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the mathematical principles that underpin modern machine learning and data science. It is designed to equip students with the essential tools from linear algebra, calculus, probability, and optimization that are fundamental to understanding and developing machine learning algorithms.
  
 The course begins with vector spaces, matrix algebra, and linear transformations, emphasizing their role in representing and manipulating data. Key concepts such as eigenvalues, eigenvectors, orthogonality, and matrix decompositions—including spectral decomposition and singular value decomposition (SVD)—are explored with applications to dimensionality reduction and data approximation.
 
 Building on this foundation, the course introduces core machine learning techniques such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), regression models, and classification methods. Students will also study least squares approximation, model evaluation metrics, and the mathematical structure behind widely used algorithms.
 The course further develops essential tools from calculus, including gradients, Jacobians, and the chain rule, which are crucial for optimization in machine learning. Concepts from convex analysis and numerical optimization, including gradient descent and its variants, are introduced and implemented computationally. A review of probability theory is provided, leading to their applications in statistical learning and classification models such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs). Advanced topics such as duality, Lagrangian methods, and kernel-based classification are also discussed.

title: Geometry of Curves and Surfaces
description: Surfaces are all around us, walls and ceilings of our rooms are planes, bottles are cylinders, the football in the playground is a sphere and the rugby ball is an ellipsoid, the vada we eat is a torus and the ice cream cone is, well, a cone. The shape of these objects will be studied using calculus. The course will begin with the study of curves in plane and in three-dimensional space. The concepts of length, orientation, speed, curvature, and torsion will be introduced and studied. Motivated by the study of curves, several notions of curvatures of a surface, like principal curvatures and Gaussian curvature, will be examined. Intuitively, the way a surface is curved seems to be a property of how it is embedded in space. But Gaussian curvature turns out to be intrinsic, that is, an ant confined to moving on the surface will be able to measure this quantity. This hints at the possibility of the study of shapes of higher dimensional analogues of surfaces.

title: Introductory Fourier analysis
description:
This course is an introduction to the basic notions of Fourier analysis. Three classical topics will be explored: Fourier series, Fourier transforms and the discrete Fourier transform. The basic notions, tools and techniques of Fourier analysis are very important in both pure and applied mathematics (in areas such as signal, image and data processing, etc;) and in physics and computer science. This course is designed to be a gentle, concrete introduction to the subject, with a focus on basic examples and with an eye towards applications. 
 Prerequisites include the basic notions of linear algebra (matrices, vector spaces and linear independence, linear transformations, eigenvalues and vectors and inner product spaces) and single and multivariable calculus.
 It is hoped that this course will be accessible to 3rd year and 4th year students in mathematics, physics, computer science, and data science.

title: Number Theory
description:
The course covers the following topics: Notion of Divisibility, Congruences, Chinese 
Remainder Theorem, Quadratic Reciprocity, Quadratic Forms, Arithmetic Functions, 
Mobius Inversion Formula, Solving certain Diophantine Equations, Farey Fractions, 
Rational Approximations and Irrational Numbers, The Geometry of Numbers, 
Continued Fractions and Pell’s Equation, Algebraic Integers in Quadratic Number Fields, 
Partitions and Euler’s Pentagonal Number Theorem. We will also cover Gauss and Jacobi
sums, Cubic and Biquadratic Reciprocity, Zeta function, some topics in elliptic curves.

title: Problem Solving Strategies/Seminar
description: Problem solving activity is an important activity which gives deeper understanding of the theory. Learning theory and solving problems go hand in hand. It gradually enhances the ability of a student to gain deeper understanding of mathematical concepts in different areas and leads the student to the frontiers of research fields. It also helps them to develop skills to write in a logical and comprehensive manner. In the course, problems not only from different international mathematical competitions such as Putnam competition, International Mathematical Competition, International Mathematical Olympiads but also from problem journals such as American Mathematical Monthly and others are used. These are undergraduate competitions as well as plus-two level competitions.

title: Measure theory and integration
description: The theory of measure and integration is an essential prerequisite for further study in areas such as functional analysis, PDE, numerical analysis, ergodic theory, dynamical systems and probability theory. This course shall explore the basic notions of measure theory (using the Lebesgue measure as a basic example) and Lebesgue integration in Euclidean spaces. An outline of the topics are as follows.

title: Statistics
description: This introductory course is aimed at providing a theoretical foundation in Statistics intending to build a strong quantitative orientation. The course assumes some basic knowledge of calculus and builds on the probability theory course offered in the earlier term. The course is designed to be mathematical (theoretical) in nature and many results and theorems will be derived and proved. The students are expected to learn and implement them primarily using R. Some of these will be covered through assignments.

title: Partial Differential Equations
description:
This is a first course in Partial Differential Equations for Mathematics students interested in Analysis as well as Applied Mathematics as a discipline. After developing some taxonomy of partial differential equations and mathematical prerequisites, the course will be broadly divided into hyperbolic equations on the one hand and elliptic and parabolic equations on the other. While a broad theory will be developed for first order equations; for second order equations, we will focus on the three prototypes, viz., wave, Laplace and heat equations. An attempt will be made to highlight counterexamples since they drive the theory. Those interested in analysis should get a glimpse of how analysis is the bedrock of all PDEs while those interested in applied math should see how Mathematics can be used to explain physical phenomena.
 
 After completing this course, the students should be equipped with the theoretical tools to analyze first order and second order partial differential equations. They should have a good understanding of first order PDEs and the physical models they represent. They should understand well the three prototype equations – wave, Laplace and heat – that underpin and motivate much of the modern theory of PDEs.

title: Topics in Analysis 2
description:
Complex analysis sits at the crossroads between algebra, analysis and topology / geometry and is fundamental and indispensable to much of modern mathematics. This course is envisaged as a first level graduate course for graduate students in Complex Analysis. After the completion of this course, a student should be able to understand:

The classical theory of  holomorphic functions such as complex exponential, complex logarithm and complex trigonometric functions; and branches, branch points, Evaluate complex differentiation, analytic functions, power series representation and the Cauchy-Riemann equations. 
Cauchy’s theorem and Cauchy's integral formula, compute contour integration, winding number, use Cauchy's theorem for simple paths and simply connected regions, homotopic version of Cauchy’s theorem and Simple Connectivity, Goursat's theorem, Classification of Singularities, Residue theorem, Argument Principle.
The Maximum Principle, Schwarz Lemma, Phragmen-Lindelof Theorem, Meromorphic Functions, Riemann Mapping Theorem, Weierstrass Factorization Theorem, Runge’s theorem, Mittag-Leffler’s theorem, Picard’s theorem
Harmonic functions, Subharmonic functions, Superharmonic functions, Dirichlet Problem, Green’s functions.
Functions of Several Variables and any material of interest based on the instructor.

Course instructors have a choice to modify the contents of the course depending on the requirement.

title: Topics in Analysis 3
description: This course covers properties of infinite dimensional normed linear spaces and their essential properties such as existence of norm-preserving extensions to maps on linear subspaces, consequences of completeness, weak topologies and compactness theorems. The latter part of the course will focus on concrete function spaces such as L^p spaces and their properties as well as talk about Hilbert spaces and Spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators. A suggestion is to run a parallel/subsequent course on Sobolev spaces and modern theory of Partial Differential Equations for interested students to which this course would form a complement.
