title: Foundations of Indian Epistemology
description:
This course aims to introduce students to the foundational principles of acquiring knowledge in Indian philosophy. Indian epistemology covers the nature of knowledge (jñāna), the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the criteria of valid knowledge (pramā). This course deals with two major schools – the Nyāya philosophy and the Buddhist philosophy – which have built the foundation of what is known as Indian epistemology. While briefly introducing major Indian philosophical schools, it will focus on these two and learn about their major texts and thinkers. We will briefly touch upon the points of debate between both the schools.

We will be reading an excerpt (i.e., from statement 34 to 54) of the Tarkasaṅgraha for understanding epistemology of Nyāya. Written by Annambhaṭṭa, this is a concise text which presents the ontology and the epistemology of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika systems. For understanding Buddhist epistemology, we will be reading the first chapter (direct perception) of the Nyāyabindu. This is a short treatise by Dharmakīrti, one of the most influential philosophers of Buddhist epistemology. Since this is an introductory course, we will only be reading the texts in translation and not their extensive commentaries. This course will familiarize students with the primary texts of Indian epistemology and will give them a glimpse of the significance it holds in the larger philosophical domain. This course also paves the way for studying ontology and metaphysics in Indian philosophy.

title: Self, State and Society: Philosophical Perspectives
description:
There is an intricate dialectical relation between the concepts of self, state and society, and these relations are negotiated in every age, differently. It is important to understand these relations, as they provide us with the rationale for our understanding of ourselves, and our place in the social and political domains. These relations also determine the possibilities and limits of our own agency and actions vis-à-vis others. This course will introduce some of the fundamental philosophical presuppositions that allow this negotiation to take place in the modern age. The course is divided into three modules that discuss the constitution of the self, the state, and the social, in the contemporary modern western age. The objective of this discussion is to not only present a philosophical analysis of these concepts but to also open them up for critique and alternative readings, either from the classical tradition or in some cases contemporary
perspectives. The course is not intended to be comprehensive in its approach to the readings presented, but rather the focus is to have an in-depth engagement with the philosophical
presuppositions of the perspectives presented. Some of the fundamental issues taken up would be: How is the notion of the self, constituted and what relation does it bear to the understanding of the modern age, and the state? What are the fundamental presuppositions that characterise the foundations of the modern state? What are some of the theoretical alternatives to this understanding of the state? What is the role of the social, as presented through the institution of the family, in this matrix? What is the relation that the family bears to the state, and the self?

title: Concepts in Aesthetics I
description: Aesthetics is an integral philosophical enquiry which is deeply concerned with our experience of the world and our perception of it. This course will introduce the students to basic concepts in aesthetics and with a focus on the various kinds of aesthetic practices and their entanglement with socio-political, geographical, historical contexts as well as the larger philosophical debates around aesthetics. Concepts of sense perception, beauty, taste, judgment and poetics will be discussed based on core readings including Aristotle, Abhinavagupta, Kant, Bourdieu, Kumaraswamy, and others. A foundational understanding of aesthetics gives students a philosophical grounding in approaching any form of literature and art with the relevant vocabulary and conceptual frame of reference. This will enable students to pursue their interests in engaging with the arts in any way forward - through theory or practice.

title: Vedānta
description: This course provides an introduction to Vedānta, one of the major schools of Indian philosophy. It explores the key concepts of Vedānta as discussed in the three sources (prasthānatrayī) i.e., Upanishads, Bhagavadgītā and Brahmasūtra. It begins with exploring the fundamental concepts of Brahman, ātman, māyā, jagat and jīvanmukti in these three source texts. Vedānta philosophy employs a number of approaches to unfold the identity between the individual and consciousness (the self). We will discuss some of the important approaches, such as, the cause-effect, the three states, the five sheaths and the seer-seen approach in detail. Through these, we gain a deeper understanding of Vedāntic thought. Moving forward, the course discusses the sub-schools of Vedānta. While the non-dual (advaita) Vedanta of Śankarācārya has become synonymous with the whole Vedānta philosophy, we study it in contrast with two other schools, dual (dvaita) Vedanta of Madhvācārya and qualified non-dual (viśiṣṭādvaita) Vedānta of Rāmānujācārya. The idea is to understand that while relying on the same source text, the variety of interpretation and analysis gives rise to a new philosophy within a system. The course gives an insight into the significance of Vedānta within the larger framework of Indian philosophical thought.

title: Reason and Experience and the Foundations of Modern Western Epistemology
description: This course will take up a discussion on the epistemological views of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, David Hume, and Immanuel Kant. These are three canonical thinkers in the Modern Western tradition, whose writings discuss the relations between reason and experience, which is fundamental to understanding modern western epistemological thought. The objective of the course is to take the students through a discussion of the primary texts (i) in order to locate the dominant trends in modern western thought through their writings, and (ii) to do a close reading of the texts, and see how, they as independent thinkers, challenge or conform to the dominant trends. The course restricts itself to reading Leibniz, Hume and Kant as these thinkers are typically characterised as a rationalist thinker, an empiricist thinker, and as someone who brings together rationalism and empiricism, respectively.

title: Logic in Philosophy
description:
How do we reason about reason? Are there underlying principles that can connect reasoning about philosophical abstractions, legal and politics argument, analysis of texts, scientific and social scientific theorisations, solving puzzles and writing mathematical proofs? Can we make precise what we mean by reason or codify what we mean by a reasonable argument? How have philosophers lent meaning to make sense of the human quest to discover the laws of reason?

This course attempts to trace the long standing intellectual project of identifying the laws of deductive reasoning. We begin with historical attempts and philosophical underpinnings underlying these attempts, before diving deep into contemporary formal frameworks that fall under the aegis of logic.

In the process, we use precise formulations of deductive reasoning using symbolic abstractions which enables us to answer the following questions:

How do we ensure that a set of sentences are mutually consistent?
How do we make sense of paradoxes?
How do we ensure that deductive arguments are logically sound?
What can and cannot be deduced from a given collection of statements?
How do we reason precisely when confronted with ambiguities such as knowledge or lack of it, and belief and contingency?

We further extend our set of questions to attempt to answer the following questions about the method of reasoning itself:

What kind of statements are amenable to formal deductive reasoning?
What is the nature of the relationship between reasoning and language?
How do we reason within a given formal reasoning system as well as about a given formal reasoning system?

The course intends to provide access to ideas and contemporary vocabulary which will enable to deploy logic as a means to reason within philosophy, as well as enable pursuit logic and philosophy of logic as philosophical disciplines. Further it will bring alive challenges which makes the process of sound reasoning difficult even for sophisticated Artificial Intelligence tools today.

title: Justice as a Virtue in Classical Philosophy
description: The virtue of justice has not been given a ‘just’ treatment in contemporary virtue ethics. Due to vagueness in its scope, justice as a personal virtue has often been sidelined since the aretaic turn in the 20th century. Restricting its scope to socio-political dimensions, contemporary discourses on the virtue of justice often miss the origin, nature and function of justice in individual persons. Elizabeth Anscombe rightly says: “One of the most important insights of modern times…[is] that injustice may be nobody’s fault, and that what is required is good [socio-political] arrangement” (“Does Oxford Moral Philosophy Corrupt Youth?”, 1957). This course aims at bridging this existing gap between the socio-political and the personal dimensions of the virtue of justice. What better way to do this than by looking at the holistic approaches to justice in classical philosophy? The course will explore the notion of justice both as a moral virtue and as a political virtue through the selected works of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. It will begin by examining Socrates’ call for justice in Apology and then his refusal to ‘unjustly’ break his agreement with the city laws in Crito. The course will then shift its focus to Plato’s treatment of the ethical and political dimensions of justice in his Republic. This will involve discussions on Plato’s account of a just city (kallipolis), its analogy with human soul, justice & happiness, family, political regimes, role of women, philosophers & artists in society, and education. After an extensive discussion on Plato, the course will move on to discuss Aristotle’s account of justice using his Nicomachean Ethics and Politics. It will first explore his idea of justice as a virtue of character through themes like general & particular justice, justice & virtue, justice in friendships, equity, and voluntariness in just actions. Students will then be introduced to Aristotle’s account of political justice through his notions of political animal, city-state, its structure & goals, good citizens & their virtues, and ideal constitutions. The course will conclude by highlighting the relevance of the classical treatment of justice as a moral-political virtue in contemporary times.

title: Morality and Its Rationality: Aristotle & Kant
description: An age-old moral fable places Hercules at the challenging crossroads of choices: the easy life of pleasure and the hard life of virtue. Aristotle and Kant, two distinguished philosophers from distinct time-periods, unanimously claim that the hard life of virtue alone is a worthy life. Both justify virtuous living by tracing its necessary roots back to the central core of human nature – our rationality. Yet, as has been long supposed, the disagreements between their ethical positions are conspicuously loud: Aristotle favors happiness as the highest end of virtue, while Kant considers virtue to involve duty unadulterated by happiness; Kant favors a life of action towards a human world under moral laws, while Aristotle glorifies the life of contemplation as an ideal life of an individual. Whose position is valid and tenable? How do we account for the differences in their rationalist accounts of goodness? This course aims at a critical and comparative exploration of the moral theories proposed by Aristotle and Kant. It will begin with an introduction to the broader themes and trends in the history of moral philosophy to locate Aristotle and Kant in their respective contexts. It will discuss the metaethical underpinnings of their respective moral theories: Aristotle founds his eudaimonian virtue ethics on his commitments to a purpose-driven natural world (in Physics) and to the psychology of human soul (in De Anima). Kant on the other hand derives his deontological ethics from a critique of the faculty of reason, and by grounding our morality in the idea of freedom (in the first Critique and Groundwork III). The central focus of the course will be to address the dialectic of Aristotelian ‘happiness’ and Kantian ‘duty’ through an exploration of their respective ethical theories. Students will be introduced to the central themes of Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics and Eudemian Ethics including the notions of virtue (aretē), happiness (eudaimonia) and practical wisdom (phronēsis). They will also be introduced to Kant’s formulations of the moral law and the taxonomy of moral duties through selections from his Groundwork and Metaphysics of Morals. The course will also highlight the significance of Aristotle’s and Kant’s moral theories to enable students to reflect on the relevance of their ideas in today’s world.

title: Freedom
description:
What does freedom mean? How does it go beyond the lay definition that it lies in the ability to act and speak without constraint? What are the implications of parsing this concept at the individual level or examining it in a relational or collective way? Philosophically, the concept of freedom plays out in the domain of metaphysics and ethics, with theories ranging from the libertarian, the compatibilist, and the deterministic. These transcendental ideas have had a subtle but definite impact on our constitutional guarantees for free speech on the one hand, and the restrictions placed on them on others. What implications does the information we have about inner processes have for the issue of agency? What are
the grounds, if any, for coercing opinion and behaviour through pressure? What is the space for freedom of religion in a secular state? What is the distinction between positive and negative liberty and how are these related to notions of libertarianism, collectivism, autonomy and free will? Finally, where is freedom situated in discussions on fairness and justice and what are alternative notions of freedom, for example, as a form of self-realisation or as a model for non-domination. This inter-disciplinary course touches on philosophy, constitutional law, political theory, ethics, jurisprudence and media law.

title: Practical Reason and Moral Emotion: Early Modern Moral Philosophy
description:
The views of Hume and Kant on morality are arguably the two most significant approaches to
moral philosophy during the early modern period. As Thomas Nagel rightly puts it, contemporary moral philosophy “continues to be dominated by the disagreement[s] between [the ethical views of] these two giants” (Nagel, “The Taste of Being Moral”, 2012). It is a well- known fact that Kant initially subscribed to the moral sentimentalist tradition that Hume belonged to, before breaking away as a hardcore moral rationalist. The nature of this decisive break is the starting point between many contrasting perspectives within contemporary meta-ethics and moral psychology –  emotivism/cognitivism, moral sense/intuitionism, Humean motivation/Kantian motivation etc. There is therefore a need to backtrack and read Hume’s and Kant’s original contributions to moral philosophy. Through selected primary source readings, the course aims to provide an overview of the central tenets of Hume’s and Kant’s moral philosophy. The course will begin with a useful background on the broader themes in early modern moral philosophy. Students will be then be introduced to Hume’s psychology of action via readings from the first two books of his Treatise. Then, the focus will shift to the core of Hume’s moral philosophy – his anti-rationalism and sentimentalism – that he develops in the third book of the Treatise and in some sections of his second Enquiry. After discussions on Hume’s moral theory, the course will shift its direction towards the rationalist account of morality that Kant propounded as a reaction to the moral sentimentalist tradition. Students will closely engage with Kant’s Groundwork for a deep understanding of the central themes of Kant’s moral theory - practical reason, categorical imperative, autonomy, duty, good will and dignity. Elements of Kant’s moral psychology such as moral motivation, moral incentive, choice and responsibility will also be explored through readings from his second Critique. The course will conclude by highlighting the significance of Hume’s and Kant’s moral theories to
contemporary moral philosophy.

title: Close Encounters!: Philosophical Approaches to Science Fiction and Fantasy
description:
 Can science fiction and fantasy suggest questions of a philosophical kind? Do they provoke
philosophical thinking?
 Can they help us imagine our own lived experiences and realities differently?
 Is science fiction and fantasy of any use at all in helping us understand otherwise difficult
philosophical concepts, problems, and theses?
In this course, we will examine an interesting array of philosophical topics seen through equally interesting science fiction and fantasy (SFF) in their different transmedial avatars. Beginning with fiction that challenges our everyday understanding of language and communication, we will
proceed to discuss texts that touch upon our ethical responsibility toward others, on the philosophy of race and gender, as well as on post- and transhumanism. We will learn about the concepts of possible and impossible worlds and see for ourselves whether they apply to imaginary, fictional worlds. We will also experience how SFF narratives confound us with their treatments of time travel. Confronting the (in)famous paradox of fiction, we will conclude this course by reflecting upon our own experiences of believing what we know about SFF.

title: Introduction to Philosophy of Technology
description: Human evolution is tied to the question of technological evolution, or perhaps vice versa. In either scenario questions of – what is technology? How does technological design structure the world around us? What are the requirements of adapting to the demands of technological change? What are the larger socio-political and ethical implications of technological change? All these questions need to be situated as part of a discussion on the philosophy of technology. The course seeks to introduce the students to some of the seminal thinkers and their positions in this respect and engage them in fundamental ontological queries regarding technology.

title: Concepts in Aesthetics II
description: In this course, modern and contemporary aesthetic theories will be discussed in the context of the development of artistic discourse. Contemporary philosophers like Jacques Ranciere, Jean Luc Nancy, Geeta Kapur, Griselda Pollock, Boris Groys, Asta and others offer varied pushes and pulls to the landscape of aesthetic discourses in the arts be it through philosophical, feminist and socio-political perspectives as well as through the critique of the very field of aesthetics from the informed by various social categories. These perspectives will be engaged with alongside select works from contemporary practitioners of art. These aesthetic cultures will be discussed both from their theoretical groundwork and practical groundwork within the context of artistic practice.

title: Pre-Socratics and the Socratics - History of Philosophy
description:
This course will introduce students to thinkers who collectively formed the philosophical tradition of the ancient Greece. It will first familiarize students to the philosophical thoughts of
the pre-Socratic thinkers like Thales, Pythagoras, Parmenides, Heraclitus and Democritus. Then, the focus of the course will shift to Socrates, and the two major Socratic philosophers – Plato and Aristotle. Students will be introduced to the ethical and metaphysical concerns of these three thinkers through the selected works of Plato and Aristotle. Philosophical themes including moral virtues (like justice, wisdom, piety etc.), good, beauty, happiness, death, God and soul will be explored in these classes. Taking a historical approach, the course will enable students to systematically and critically reflect on specific philosophical issues that were relevant to the ancient Greeks.

title: Philosophy of the Image
description: The ‘Image’ is a powerful concept that fuels foundational discourses in philosophy of art. The phenomenologists were captivated by the image and what it could tell us. From the practices of creating death masks, to painting, to capturing, to making images move, to projecting images still and moving, the fascination with alterity underlines much of the aesthetics of modernity. In this course, we shall particularly focus on three European philosophers who have extensively theorized on the image – Jacques Ranciere, Gilles Deleuze and Villem Flusser with minor detours into the phenomenological ruminations by Sartre and Husserl. The course will be reading intensive and will engage with works of art in conversation with the readings prescribed.

title: Curatorial Frameworks: Theory and Praxis
description: In this course, we shall study the emerging interdisciplinary field of the Curatorial as an expanded theoretical discipline that is pertinent to not just the Arts, but also Humanities and Social Sciences. Developed into a full-fledged discipline in the past two decades globally, the ambiguity around the term often evades its complete understanding. Understanding curation outside of its museological origins theoretically opens up radical philosophical windows into understanding constructs of knowledge and experience. In this course, students will study the various frameworks offered by the curatorial mode, explore the ways in which the practice impacts its fields and its objects. They will grasp some basic tools that will help them in their practices in the future which may be as diverse as that of managers, mediators, interlocutors, dj’s, walkers, care-givers or just simply - becoming allies. Founded in the concepts of care - ‘curare’ – the frameworks provided by contemporary curatorial methods enable curious epistemological and metaphysical transformations and are critical to understand the creative acts.

title: Physics Exploration – An experimental approach
description: Physics is fundamental to our comprehension of nature in all its dimensions.  But that does not make the discipline scary and dry.  In fact, it is fun to discern some of its principles from simple experiments.  This course attempts to provide demonstration-based reasoning to learn physics.  In particular, we will demonstrate experimentally, discuss and understand concepts such as inertia and mass, friction,  energy and its conservation, momentum and its conservation,  electric charge and field, conduction of electricity, magnetism, waves and related phenomena.  Each class will be devoted to performing an experiment,  observation and synthesis of the apt law of nature and a quantitative discussion.  This is a 2-credit course and there will be at least ten demonstrations.

title: Mathematical Methods I
description: This course will equip students with the essential mathematical tools and techniques required for advanced studies and research in chemistry and physics. Students will learn topics like linear algebra, differential equations, calculus, and complex numbers

title: Mathematical Methods II
description: Mathematics has been the language to express the laws of physics. Students doing physics must be trained in mathematics. Almost every branch of mathematics has been found useful to physicists. This course builds on the foundations laid in Mathematical Methods I. In these courses, ideas from linear algebra, multivariable calculus, complex numbers, ordinary differential equations, partial differential equations and probability are discussed. It is not the purpose of this course to take the theorem-proof route which is of importance to mathematicians. Rather, it aims to cultivate a sense of thinking that has precision and rigour which are essential to physics, and a bent of mind to understand mathematical texts. Completing the two courses on mathematical methods will further equip students to access mathematical biology, econometrics, econophysics, data science and mathematical modelling.

title: Electronics I
description: One cannot imagine the modern world without the impact of electrical and electronic devices. This course will start with a discussion of the basics of electrical circuits, both static and transient. The main course content is centered around the theory of electronic devices based on semiconductors, such as P-N junction diodes and transistors. A study of these basic devices and their applications gives us the necessary background to design advanced circuits. Finally, the course will introduce the basics of digital electronics, covering Boolean algebra and logic gates.

title: Qubit Mechanics
description:
Quantum theory is changing information processing in fundamental ways. At the root of this revolutionary change are superstition, entanglement and exponentially large size of the state space of multipartite quantum systems. These features are nonexistent in classical systems, and therefore, (classical) mechanical models of computation such Turing or Post machines have limitations. Quantum Information Processing (QIP) offers computational advantages and exponential speed up. The most fundamental element needed to harness these advantages is a
quantum bit (qubit, in short) array. In this course, we introduce quantum theoretic notions using
qubit as a protype quantum system. This allows us to quickly acquire enough skills to explore the
theory and its ramifications that form the basis of QIP

title: Computational Methods
description: Analytical methods are often inadequate to deal with real systems, whether in physics or economics or any data-driven field. The alternate route is to carry out numerical computations. In recent times, this has become an important tool to be learned by any budding physicist. Learning this early enables one to go beyond idealised problems. It gives them the freedom to take up more challenging problems. Needless to say, numerical solutions will motivate us to seek analytical solutions, at least in an approximate sense. The course will focus on numerical techniques to handle linear systems, ordinary differential equations, etc.

title: Classical Physics: Energy and Force I
description: Dynamics is the study of the response of objects to applied forces. Motion has been a subject of philosophical investigations since the time of Aristotle. It took a very long time before its foundations were laid during the 18th century. In the process, the subject of calculus was formulated as the then existing mathematical framework was inadequate to succinctly express the empirical observations. Newton, who finally formalized the required notions to describe dynamics, encoded the known observations in three laws that bear his name. Two major themes that underlie the conceptual framework of dynamics are force and energy. Later developments proved Newton’s laws to be inaccurate at high speeds and small distances. How approximate are they? Landing on Mars at any specified location still relies on the predictions made using these laws. For many of our endeavours in science and engineering, these laws are fantastically accurate. An understanding of dynamics is essential to pursue any of the specialized topics in physics. Classical dynamics is possibly the beginning of both physics and mathematical analysis. Nevertheless, it continues to inspire new ideas in both subjects.

title: Classical Physics: Energy and Force II
description: We explore the applications of the laws of classical mechanics to a variety of dynamical systems, such as the motion of fluids (which allows for the flight of airplanes), the orbits of planets and other celestial bodies under the influence of gravity, and the movement of bodies in non-inertial frames (such as winds and ocean currents on the rotating earth). These form the basis for more advanced fields such as astronomy and climate science. Deeper questions about motion in inertial and non-inertial frames lead naturally to Einstein’s general theory of relativity.We explore the applications of the laws of classical mechanics to a variety of dynamical systems, such as the motion of fluids (which allows for the flight of airplanes), the orbits of planets and other celestial bodies under the influence of gravity, and the movement of bodies in non-inertial frames (such as winds and ocean currents on the rotating earth). These form the basis for more advanced fields such as astronomy and climate science. Deeper questions about motion in inertial and non-inertial frames lead naturally to Einstein’s general theory of relativity.

title: Classical Physics: Spacetime
description: Newton’s formulation of dynamics assumes the existence of a frame of reference and time that are absolute. This assumption summarizes our sensory perception of the world. Also, physicists believed that a suitable medium is essential for waves to travel. To accommodate the electromagnetic waves in this scheme, a medium called ether was proposed. Its sole purpose was to support the electromagnetic waves. To prove its existence, Michelson and Morley carried out an ingenious experiment to measure any change in the speed of light if the earth dragged the ether along. The experiment did not confirm any change in speed. Attempts to reconcile this result with the then-existing physics framework were unsatisfactory. Einstein, from a theoretical perspective, announced his reformulation of the basic structure of physics in the year 1905. This course is about telling this story in detail.

title: Classical Physics: Fields I
description: In the 18th and 19th centuries, the work of Faraday, Oersted and others showed that the forces of electricity and magnetism can be explained by postulating the existence of a ‘field’ that pervades through space. This field concept allows us to formulate a combined theory of electricity and magnetism called electromagnetism. We will discuss the laws of Coulomb and Gauss in electrostatics and Biot-Savart’s law of magnetism. The properties of these fields in a medium allow us to understand polarization and magnetization of materials. On the theoretical side, these concepts lay the foundation for the first major ‘unification’ of forces in the history of physics – modern theory of electromagnetism.

title: Classical Physics: Fields II
description: The properties of electric and magnetic fields in material media allow us to understand polarization and magnetization of materials. These have tremendous applications in the form of microwaves and electromagnets, and are useful in explaining various chemical phenomena. On the theoretical side, the work of Faraday, Maxwell and others laid the foundation for the first major ‘unification’ of forces in the history of physics – the modern theory of electromagnetism. The behaviour of electromagnetic radiation (light) emerges naturally from this theory, giving us the laws of classical optics. The fundamental incompatibility of electromagnetic theory with Newton’s mechanics was what led Einstein to his special theory of relativity.

title: Oscillations and Waves
description:
Physics describes nature using particles and waves as basic entities. Newton's laws
 of motion govern the dynamics of particles. Sound, ripples on water, etc. are
 undulations of the medium in which they propagate. These waves arise due to
 interactions among the particles of the medium. Equations governing them are
 derivable from the laws of dynamics of particles. But electromagnetic waves do not
 require a medium for their propagation. Despite such fundamental differences,
 these waves are describable by the same mathematical structure. Physics students
 need a good grasp of these ideas since the concept of waves appears in many
 contexts such as the wavefunctions in quantum theory, the phonon modes in
 condensed matter, etc. This course presents the relevant physics and the
 mathematical details required to understand the subject.

title: Optics I
description: Light, being the medium of most observations and measurements, is our window to the physical universe. In this course, we study geometrical optics, where light is described by rays. This deals with basic components like lenses, mirrors and prisms, from which instruments like telescopes and microscopes are built. In addition, we study the wave properties of light at an introductory level. It includes phenomena such as light interference that accounts for the colours on soap bubbles and has applications ranging from quantum studies to gravitational wave detection. We will also study polarization, which is of importance in photography. In addition, we will discuss diffraction, which is used extensively to study the crystal structure of solids.

title: Mechanical Properties of Matter
description: This course discusses some inherent properties of matter such as surface tension, viscosity, fluid dynamics, elasticity, and various elastic constants. It also discusses the variation of these properties with temperature, pressure, and shape.  The basic understanding of these topics is helpful for our day-to-day life as well. The knowledge about the above-mentioned topics can bring openings for research in nonlinear dynamics, soil research, and many interdisciplinary engineering domains, especially if somebody wishes to move into the career path of engineering physics such as civil engineering, fluid engineering, etc. Apart from this, a general knowledge about fluids, beams is helpful in many day to day events of life as well, such as why milk spills easily in a carrying container but not oil. In a nutshell, the students studying this elective course can benefit from having more career paths in the future.

title: Quantum Physics 1
description: Physics is an empirical science. Its conceptual framework is revised to accommodate new empirical evidence from experiments. One of the earliest indications for the need to relook at classical physics was the blackbody emission spectrum. The experimental results were at variance with the prediction of classical physics. Max Planck proposed quantized exchanges of energy between the walls of the blackbody and the radiation within. This resolved the discrepancy between the theoretical predictions and the experimental observations. Einstein proposed quantized energy for the radiation field to explain the photoelectric effect. Bohr proposed non-radiating orbits for electrons to account for the stability of atoms and quantized angular momentum to explain their emissions spectra. All these ad hoc procedures found natural explanations in the quantum theory formulated by Heisenberg and Schrodinger. Their ideas were refined and put on firm scientific footing by Dirac, Pauli, Born, von Neumann, Jordan and others.

title: Energy and Entropy
description: Einstein said, “Thermodynamics is the only physical theory of universal content concerning which I am convinced that, within the framework of the applicability of its basic concepts, it will never be overthrown.” That argument is enough to motivate learning thermodynamics. Empirical information gathered over centuries has been consolidated in a few statements called the laws of thermodynamics. In that sense, this subject is also one of the earliest theoretical formulations. Thermodynamics, in particular its nonequilibrium extension, is very important in biological sciences, environmental sciences, climatology and energy studies, to name a few. Entropy, one of the enigmatic notions in physics, was originally formulated by Clausius in the context of heat engines, the objects of study in this subject. A microscopic understanding of thermodynamics is sought in statistical physics. The contributions of greats like Boltzmann and Gibbs still form the foundation of the subject while Jayne’s approach based on information theory is equally important. A brief introduction to these aspects is provided towards the end of the course. Why should one learn this subject? Extension to nonequilibrium systems is still an incomplete program. Of course, significant contributions in recent times include Jarzynsky-Crooks work fluctuation theorems, non-extensive thermodynamics and quantum thermodynamics. The subject is well and alive with unanswered questions.

title: Physics of Computation
description:
Computation is processing of information. We strive for faster and energy efficient
 computation. Are there limits? Processing is carried out by physical objects obeying laws of
 physics. This informs us about possible fundamental limitations to computing. Creation of
 information costs energy. What is surprising is it cost as much energy to delete information. 
 One approach to minimize this energy cost is to do reversible computations. The conceptual
 framework to understand this is thermodynamics. Quantum theory adds further possibilities. 
 In this course, these ideas will be presented at a level accessible to undergraduates. This course
 relies more on research articles than books as the subject is still developing. An exposure to
 these ideas may help students contribute to the subject.

title: Nuclear Energy
description:
Basics Nuclear Physics, Structure of Nucleus, Radioactivity, Induced Radioactivity, Chain
 reaction, Reactors, Types, Nuclear Energy program, Nuclear Bomb,

title: Introduction to Astronomy & Astrophysics
description:
Plato said, “Are you unaware that the true astronomer must be a person of great wisdom?”
 Twenty-four centuries later, our understanding of the universe is vastly better but still
 incomplete. This course on introductory astronomy and astrophysics will introduce
 students to the basic ideas and vocabulary of modern astronomy. The course will discuss
 observational methods of astronomy while giving students a chance to engage in taking
 quantitative data in practical sessions. This course acts as a gateway to the other two
 courses in the Astronomy track which will cover astronomical bodies, phenomena, and
 the overall structure of the universe.

title: Statistical mechanics
description:
Newtonian mechanics is deterministic and applies to a system
 with many degrees of freedom. However, propagating a typical initial condition of the
 many-body system as per the Newtonian dynamical laws is fraught with difficulties,
 both conceptual and analytical. Luckily, if we are interested in a class of macroscopic
 properties which correspond to a myriad of microscopic states of the system, one can
 profitably employ the language of probabilities. Statistical physics of systems
 thermodynamic equilibrium is such a description. A major success of statistical physics
 is it provides a dynamical origin to the laws of thermodynamics, though for a restricted
 class of systems called ergodic systems. The theory, nevertheless, is applicable to all
 systems, microscopic and macroscopic systems included. This course is an introduction
 to some of the research questions in statistical physics. Specifically, the course deals
 with order theorems, critical phenomena and scaling theory.

title: Mathematical methods III
description: Mathematics has been the language to express the laws of physics. Students doing physics must be trained in mathematics. Almost every branch of mathematics has been found useful to physicists. This course builds on the foundations laid in Mathematical Methods I and II. In these courses, ideas like tensors, complex analysis, integral transforms, and some special functions are discussed. It is not the purpose of this course to take the theorem-proof route which is of importance to mathematicians. Rather, it aims to cultivate a sense of thinking that has precision and rigour which are essential to physics, and a bent of mind to understand mathematical texts. Completing this will equip students to solve advanced problems in physics and other quantitative fields.

title: Electronics II
description: Following from the Electronics course, this elective will discuss the applications of diodes, transistors and integrated circuits like op amps in designing advanced circuits. These have applications not only in the electronics industry but also in measurement and control systems across all fields. Signal amplifiers, analog-to-digital converters, buffer stages, waveform generators and oscillator circuits are some of the circuits that can be constructed. Finally, the course will discuss some digital integrated circuits and their applications which are at the heart of the computer revolution

title: Optics II
description: In this course, we study the wave properties of light such as interference, polarization, and diffraction in more depth. It includes the study of interferometry methods, working principles of diffraction gratings, lasers and holography. Much of it finds applications in photonics, a technology based on the utilization of light radiation. Through the lab, one will find the correlation between theory and practice and learn how to derive theories from experimental approaches within a laboratory environment.

description: Physics is an empirical science. Its conceptual framework is revised to accommodate new empirical evidence from experiments. One of the earliest indications for the need to relook at classical physics was the blackbody emission spectrum. The experimental results were at variance with the prediction of classical physics. This resolved the discrepancy between the theoretical predictions and the experimental observations. Einstein proposed quantized energy for the radiation field to explain the photoelectric effect. Their ideas were refined and put on firm scientific footing by Dirac, Pauli, Born, von Neumann, Jordan and others.

title: States of Matter
description: Matter is in the realm of our direct experience. Matter exists in different forms. Most common forms are solid, liquid and gas. Other forms of matter could be defined as well. But even among the solids, we encounter variety. Some solids are fragile while others are strong. Many solids expand on heating while some shrink, some liquids flow easily while others are sticky, and so on. Also, matter changes from one state to another on altering external parameters such as the temperature, pressure, electric field, etc. There is an obvious need to go beyond cataloguing these properties. Seeking to understand the basis for this vast variety of properties should be interesting, and could lead to innovations. For instance, the origins for revolution in information technology can be traced back to the availability of semiconductor transistors. This course introduces matter and its forms using the conceptual framework of physics.

title: Subatomic Physics
description: The discovery of radioactivity opened up a whole new realm of physics beyond the classical gravitational and electromagnetic interactions. The properties and structure of the nucleus within an atom, and the forces that bind their constituent protons and neutrons together will be discussed in this course. Using the basic tools of quantum mechanics and special relativity, one can understand the phenomena of alpha, beta and gamma decay, and radioactive transmutations. Even more fundamental than protons and neutrons are the elementary particles -- quarks, leptons and the bosons that mediate interactions between them. Their description as given by the Standard Model of particle physics will be introduced. Finally, the course will discuss detectors and experimental techniques relevant for nuclear and particle physics.

title: Introduction to General Relativity
description: Gravity was the first of the fundamental forces of nature to be modelled mathematically. Newton’s law of gravitation was our best theory of gravity for over two centuries, and is used even today for launching space probes. Einstein, expanding on his Special Theory of Relativity, proposed the General Theory of Relativity which described gravity not as a conventional force, but as an effect of the curvature of space-time. This could explain the slight shift of planetary orbits from their Newtonian expectations, and the bending of light in the vicinity of a massive object. This theory – our most successful theory of gravity to date – is used to explain phenomena related to black holes, the recently discovered gravitational waves, and has important applications such as GPS technology. Perhaps one of the most interesting uses of General Relativity has been to model the evolution of the Universe as a whole – its expansion since the Big Bang and its possible future fate. This course covers the mathematical prelude to the study of general relativity, the formulation of Einstein’s field equations, and finally some of the applications of this theory.

title: Quantum Information
description: There is plenty of room at the bottom” is a succinct expression by Feynman about the richness of the quantum world. How do we harness this abundance? In this course, we attempt to answer this question. Peter Shor designing a quantum search algorithm that is much faster than any known classical algorithm marked the beginning of a new paradigm. The most relevant aspect is the way we process information. Doing it the quantum way speeds up the process, makes it more efficient and surpasses, in many cases, the limits known from a classical perspective. This course begins with a discussion on information theory and introduces ideas about quantum information processing (QIP). Other topics to be covered include quantum algorithms and their experimental implementations. Students will learn to program the IBM quantum computer as well. Major corporates in IT and many leading institutes have strong research programs in QIP. That vouches for the importance of this science.

title: Quantum optics
description: Quantum optics is the study of physical processes involving the electromagnetic field which require considering quantum effects of the later.  While the need for quantum formulation may not arise in the description of all the optical phenomena, it is essential in many processes involving the electromagnetic field.   The quantum nature of the electromagnetic field was introduced as an adhoc requirement by Einstein to explain the photoelectric effect.   Of course, it is not Adhoc anymore.  Quantum field theory has formalized these notions.   Availability of laser has made it possible to perform experiments explicitly requiring quantum description.  These experiments range from testing the foundational aspects of quantum theory to manipulating quantum bits to perform computations.  This course provides an introduction to the subject, paying attention to both the theoretical and experimental aspects. Ideas on quantum metrology and  quantum control will be discussed.  This course is accessible to anyone who has had an introduction to quantum physics.  Also,  those interested in quantum information processing stand to gain by taking this course.     In his letter (y1951) to Michale Besso, Einstein wrote, 'All these fifty years of brooding have brought me nowhere nearer to the question "What are light quanta". Nowadays, every Tom, Dick and Harry thinks he knows it, but he is mistaken."  Hopefully,   students taking the course  will be able to explain what photons are.

title: Fundamentals of Classical Field Theory
description: Every student of physics, irrespective of whether they wish to pursue theoretical physics or experimental physics, needs a thorough training in the core principles and conceptual structure of physics. The exposure should bring out the coherence and structure in the theories that shape our understanding of nature at all length and time scales. This course is an advanced overview of the discipline that teaches the language of physics as it is practised at advanced levels. This course will enrich and enable students so that they see experiments not as data generating endeavour but as the only way to uncover the deeper principles that seem to be at work in nature.

title: Introduction to Particle physics
description: The Standard Model of Particle Physics is the most successful model of physics that describes the Universe at the most fundamental scales. In this model, the electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions between matter particles are described by their mediation through vector bosons. The predictions of this model have been experimentally verified to high precision. While the Standard Model unifies electromagnetism and the weak force into a single electroweak interaction, research aims to achieve ‘grand unification’ including the strong interaction too. This course introduces the Standard Model through gauge theory and particle phenomenology, and involves calculation of various observed processes using Feynman diagrams.

title: Molecular spectroscopy
description:
This course provides the basic knowledge of interaction of light with matter in terms of the relationship with the molecular structure. An overview of the various types of molecular motion and how they can be recorded using optical spectroscopic techniques will be discussed in some detail. In addition, students will be performing experiments using spectroscopy apparatus available on campus.

Course Objectives / Learning Outcomes
On successful completion of this course students will
Basics of molecular motion and light matter interactions
Overview on various molecular spectroscopy techniques
Hands-on experience with the spectroscopy techniques

title: Advanced Computational Techniques
description: Analytical methods are often inadequate to deal with real systems, whether in physics or economics or any data-driven field. The alternate route is to carry out numerical computations. In recent times, this has become an important tool to be learned by any budding physicist. Learning this early enables one to go beyond idealised problems. It gives them the freedom to take up more challenging problems. Needless to say, numerical solutions will motivate us to seek analytical solutions, at least in an approximate sense. The course will focus on numerical techniques to handle linear systems, ordinary differential equations, etc.

title: Advanced Condensed Matter Physics
description:
Over the past century, condensed matter physics has evolved from a nascent discipline into
 one of the most influential pillars of modern science and technology. Today, it is integral to
 countless aspects of contemporary life—shaping innovations in memory devices, electric
 vehicles, advanced battery materials, medical imaging technologies, alternative energy
 solutions, and experimental tools for both astronomers and particle physicists. This
 remarkable growth has been driven by the study of how materials respond to diverse
 external stimuli such as temperature, pressure, and electric or magnetic fields. This course
 offers a strong foundation in the theoretical framework of condensed matter physics,
 complemented by an introduction to key experimental techniques. By integrating these
 perspectives, it equips young researchers with both a broad overview of the field and the
 insight needed to choose impactful research directions aimed at sustainable solutions to
 global challenges.

title: Understanding Indian Politics
description:
This course offers a critical introduction to the evolution and practice of democratic politics in India, with a focus on the postcolonial state and its institutions. Through a thematic exploration of the Indian state, constitutional vision, institutional frameworks, and contemporary political challenges, students will gain a grounded understanding of how democracy was imagined, built, and contested in India.
Beginning with philosophical and historical reflections on the idea of the state, the course situates the Indian experience within broader traditions of political thought. It then traces how India's Constitution emerged as a blueprint for reconciling diversity with unity, exploring foundational principles such as federalism, secularism, and social justice. The course examines how these ideals were institutionalized through the Parliament, Judiciary, and Election Commission—and how they have evolved in response to changing political contexts, including the rise of majoritarianism, debates on federalism under the Modi government, and policies like "One Nation, One Election."
Emphasizing both historical depth and contemporary relevance, the course interrogates how India’s democratic project has negotiated its plural society marked by caste, religion, language, and regional identities. Through key political episodes—such as the Emergency, Mandal vs. Kamandal, and hijab and language debates—students will explore tensions between liberty and order, rights and identity, and state power and popular resistance. Engaging with primary texts, constitutional debates, and critical scholarship, the course encourages students to think analytically about the Indian state and its evolving role in shaping democratic citizenship.

title: Politics in Multiple Frames: Approaches, concepts and theoretical perspectives
description: This course seeks to outline various perspectives of understanding politics at multiple levels from the local to the national to the global. Is politics essentially about power, government and elections, or is it about friends and foes? Could it be about a deep yet contested conversation about public goods or an art of bringing political differences into an integral but tension-ridden whole? Students will develop a foundational understanding of historical, empirical and normative dimensions of politics at each of these scales. What are the pressing questions that we encounter at different levels of politics, and how did the systems that organise them come to be, and what are the epistemologies and power dynamics that underpin them? How does the academic discipline of politics constitute its objects of study and protocols of enquiry? Can the focus of politics be exclusively on human action, and such a focus be sustained in times of deep ecological crises?

title: Comparative Politics I
description:
This course is designed as an introduction to Comparative Politics, a sub-discipline in the study
 of politics. Comparative Politics is traditionally defined in two ways. First, in contrast to
 International Relations, it used to refer to the domestic politics of countries, usually other than
 one’s own, which Political Science students would devote an entire course to. Second, it is
 defined by the use of the Comparative method, the underlying assumption of which is that all
 knowledge is relative. We learn new things with reference to what we already know, and our
 assessments are usually implicitly or explicitly relative. Comparative Politics as a field trains
 us to do this systematically with regard to matters political.
 In this course, we will step aside from both these traditional definitions. Familiarity with
 everyday ideas, such as the ‘state’ or ‘nation,’ and with the most common arrangements of
 government, will be this course’s priority. Thus, as an introduction, this course will cover
 foundational concepts, the organization of government, political systems and central political
 questions. The idea is that students who are interested in politics and who are interested in
 informed citizenship, will leave the course with clarity about the words, ideas, arrangements
 and processes that make up everyday politics—such as different kinds of legislatures or
 different levels of government or different election procedures. This clarity is the foundation
 of advanced, complex political analysis.

title: Global Politics I
description: This course offers a general introduction to global politics by combining historical insights, conceptual tools and empirical accounts connected to international issues. The course begins with a brief historical review of political formations and conceptual overview of international relations. Contemporary issues of identity, inclusion, justice and welfare are examined in subsequent weeks, complicating traditional academic perspectives by considering real world debates and cases. Writing exercises, individual and group research projects and informed, structured discussions will be supplemented by lectures as needed.

title: Social and Political Thought: Intimations of Modernity
description: This course deals with ideas articulated by individual thinkers such as Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Mill, Weber and Marx on society, politics, and power. In addition, it covers different ways of thinking of ‘past’, their attendant imaginaries, and the politics of identity and recognition in the modern world.  Both these parts are connected by and anchored in the stories of ‘modernity’. ‘Modernity’ is a large  and complex theme that encompasses transformations in the sphere of economy, politics, society and  morals. It does not offer a unitary story. We also know that it has become a global currency for  justifying as well as critiquing power. Separated by a long stretch of time, how do we make sense of  these ideas? How these thinkers, spanning a period of four centuries, were not only shaped by  significant sociopolitical changes but also created new ways of comprehending them? The course  brings interpretive and methodological resources from sociological theories, political philosophy, and historical imagination to examine ideas and experiences that define ‘modern’ life and their embattled presence in our time

title: Comparative Politics II
description: In broad continuity with the course Introduction to Comparative Politics, this course involves a deeper engagement with the key themes and methodological approaches that constitute the dynamic field of Comparative Politics. This course offers an advanced exploration of conceptual variables such as state formation and state capacity, social movements, and civil society as well as ideologically conditioned political processes such as democratisation, and development across supra-national, national, and local levels. The thematic composition of this course is informed by gender and intersectional lenses. Beginning with the evolution of the field beyond its Euro-American moorings, the course will delve into the diverse methods that characterise comparative research. This is followed by a historically contextualised study of dominant political ideologies. Other key themes covered in the course include political parties, representative democracy, and contemporary phenomena such as populism.

title: Global Politics II
description:
How do we make sense of global politics in an era where the state appears at once both durable and highly permeable and interconnected, when the increasing power of corporations and media transcend national borders, and when the structures that determine our collective political life appear to be both institutionally obdurate and physically unsustainable?
This course builds on POLT 205 Global Politics I (formerly titled Global Politics in the 21st Century: An Introduction), focusing on contemporary challenges and systemic perspectives that have been developed to help us grasp the structures, agents, and mechanisms of global political order. We begin with an engagement with genealogies of how “the global” emerges as a domain and frame of systemic analysis, as distinct from the idea of the “international”. We move to three major conceptual domains in which global politics is theorised: structures and institutions of global democracy, governance, representation, and participation; changes in the temporalities and frameworks of conflict and its resolution – from new modes of warfare to new regimes of global justice; and the ways in which movements and flows – of people, commodities, capital, knowledge, ideas, identities, and solidarities – shape and restructure global politics.
Throughout this course, we will grapple with the question of how to identify and theorise changes, as well as to see the durable dynamics underlying changing systems, on a global scale.

title: Indian Politics II
description: The process of establishing an identity as a modern democratic sovereign state was not easy for India. Especially because this required the diversity and plurality of identities to be anchored to a common universally accepted idea or imagination of the nation. The history of india is replete with civilisational encounters and invasions. However, India distinctively transformed invasions into accommodation, rupture into continuity and division into diversity as argued by Sunil Khilnani. Thus, the success or failure of the state is deeply contingent on understanding its constraints and compulsions. It is deeply connected to the success of democracy in accommodating and nurturing the diversity of identities. Diverse identities often come in conflict with each other unsettling the democratic fabric of the state which significantly relies on the principles of liberty and equality to defend itself. Thus, the course will engage with the idea and imagination of India though contemporary debates and challenges around the working of Indian politics. Some of the debates that the course identifies are: the paradox between democracy and development, frequently raising the question of equality; caste and the question of social justice that brings under review state performance and affirmative action; religious freedom and the communalisation of politics that demands secularism be understood through democracy, equality and liberty; regionalism and secessionism that challenges territorial state sovereignty while accommodating ethnic diversity; and the universal and uniform language of representation that addresses the women’s question, nonetheless failing to accommodate the inter-sectionalities and diverse lived experiences. The course is divided into five broad units: Imagining India: Democracy and Development; Caste, Social Justice and Reservation; Religion and Communalism; Regionalism and Secessionism; and India and the Women’s Question.

title: Political Imaginings from the Global South
description: This course will introduce a complex world of ideas connected to society and politics created by thinkers and political actors of the Global South. Although a majority of thinkers discussed in this course will be from postcolonial societies of Africa, Latin America, and Asia, the term ‘Global South’, here, is not used as a spatial category but rather as a transnational subjectivity, a structure of sensibility shaped by the historical forces of colonialism, capitalism and nationalism. Ideas of society, politics, justice, and freedom as articulated in speech and text, and practiced in political organising, social mobilisation, resistance and rebellion, and education, by Frantz Fanon, B.R. Ambedkar, Babytai Kamble, Paolo Freire, Stephen Biko, Ho Chi Minh, Angela Davis, Stokely Carmichael, Jose Carlos Mariategui, Edward Said, and others will be discussed in this course, as well as more contemporary thinkers and practices building on these genealogies, including Linda Tuhiwai-Smith, Achille Mbembe, Chinnaiah Jangam, and EZLN. The course will encourage the students to interpret their work not only by placing them in their historical contexts but also by seeing their significance for contemporary times.

title: Introduction to Political Theory: Concepts and Conundrums
description:
This course is based on the conviction that theoretical concepts are indispensable to fully
 comprehend political realities and the ways in which they change. How do concepts emerge and
 develop, and what are the elements constitutive of their connection to empirical realities?
 Although abstract, political concepts are often deployed for the purpose of supporting as well as
 contesting concrete social arrangements, ideological positions, and institutions. They also act as
 necessary scaffold for alternative imaginings of political futures. This course is reading-intensive,
 and will pay close attention to the architecture of concepts as well as to their complex, and
 often conflicting, social mobilization. It is a course that highlights the connection between
 theory and practice, and explores new ways of doing political theory in our troubled and
 agonistic times.

title: Indian Foreign Policy
description: This course is designed as an analytical, contextualised introduction to Indian foreign policy and strategic thinking. The course is designed to enable students to follow contemporary debates in an informed and critical way, and from multiple points of view. Traditionally, this topic is taught through a historical approach and an overview of bilateral relationships. This course will merge that with elements from foreign policy analysis courses, that is, by including themes such as the influence of domestic politics and non-political issues. It will begin with a contextualising historical overview and then briefly examine contributing factors that shape thinking and policy on India’s external relations before looking specifically at key relationships and important policy areas.

title: Political Theory II
description: The study of politics is much more than the study of the state. It involves the examination and engagement with the social and political structures, concepts, ideas and values. Thus, concepts like equality, liberty, rights, justice, sovereignty, power, democracy, modernity, nationalism, identity, state, legitimacy and dissent become central to the discipline of politics. Political Theory I exposes the students to some of these concepts. However, the course on Political Theory II will engage with the remaining concepts through the ongoing debates around some of the concepts like sovereignty, power, nationalism, democracy, identity and modernity. The engagement with these debates bring to the surface how certain concepts complicate or simplify the understanding and applicability of other concepts in a polity. The engagement with these concepts manifests in political action. Political action aims at either preservation or change guided by the thought of better or worse. This is deeply embedded in finding the good or the right driven by what starts as a question and ends with knowledge. Thus, political theory is driven towards the pursuit of knowledge for the good of society, polity, people and collectives exhibited in the establishment of order and resolution of contestation or conflict. The engagements with ongoing debates enhances this pursuit of knowledge which is deeply embedded in explanatory wisdom for the truth. Thus, the course will engage with such a quest for knowledge while resolving ongoing contestations, conflicts and debates that aim at generating consent and acceptance for an ordered polity. The course will be anchored to the challenges to state and sovereignty, contestations over power and legitimacy, debate around dissent safeguarding democracy or democracy being dissent, paradox of modernity and identity and the elusiveness of nationalism. It is through a critical engagement and coherent analysis of the concepts and the ongoing debates and challenges around them that the course will enrich political theory and the discipline of politics as it will create the knowledge of the whole by putting the parts together.

title: Politics and Theories of Urbanisation
description: The course aims to provide a foundational understanding of what constitutes the urban and urbanisation by combining critical theories and concepts crucial to understand urban spaces and urbanisation processes with contemporary empirical literature, primarily focusing on urban and peri-urban India. The course offers a broad understanding of the social and political dimensions of the urbanisation processes that helps students identify structural realities and agentic transformations in different urban contexts across time and space.

title: Debating India: Key Deliberations in the Constituent Assembly of India
description: The Constitution of India with 395 Articles that are organized into 25 Parts and 12 Schedules was the handiwork of the Constituent Assembly that comprised 389-members, who came from diverse social, economic and political backgrounds.  It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950. During its more than seven decades of existence the Constitution of India has so far been amended 105 times. Despite such a large number of amendments the Constitution’s Basic Structure and other essential features, such as Fundamental Rights, remained more or less the same. In a country of vast diversity, divisions around caste, religious and racial identities, and glaring economic inequities, such an endurance of the Constitution is an astounding achievement both of the members, who drafted the Constitution, and the vast Indian populace that took the vision of the former into their stride. But what is overwhelming is the way in which the Constitution came to be formulated in the Constituent Assembly, the arguments and counter-arguments put forward and the justifications made in the making of every Article of the Constitution. This is because prior to 1950 India never had any written Constitution. Of course, during the later phase of its rule in India the British regime had introduced a few administrative related Acts in the written-form. But then these Acts became concerns of the British rulers and the educated elite of the Indian. A vast majority of the Indian population, who were largely illiterates, remained unconcerned with those Acts of the colonial rulers. Besides this, the socio-cultural diversity; divisions around caste, religion, region and language questions, economic inequities and other divergences and differences that we experience in our times were also very much alive and present at the time of the making of the Constitution for the nascent independent India.  Therefore, two most pertinent questions to be asked are: despite all those divergences how did the members in the Constituent Assembly come to agree upon a constitutional framework for the future India; and what were the arguments and justifications made in the Constituent Assembly in the making of certain essential features of the Constitution? A critical exploration of these questions would help the students not only to understand the key debates in the Constituent Assembly, essentially it facilitates a critical thinking, a constitutional perspective and a democratic way of finding solutions to numerous problems that plague our current public life.

title: Politics of the Body
description: The socio-cultural construction of the body is intrinsic to the constitution of the self. The body does not just define the ‘self’ but also the ‘other’ or ‘non-self’. The body is a source of knowledge while understanding social positioning and is understood through everyday living. Beauty is closely connected to the body. It is defined in terms of the perfect body and bodily appearances. In fact societies have been obsessed with a beautiful body for long. The body is a strong communicator and has a specific political anatomy of its own. It can see and is also constantly seen by the others. The course will look at the body from a political perspective and navigate through questions like what constitutes the body and how we see them. It will help in understanding the process of othering that constantly takes place in the socio-economic-political-cultural milieu we inhabit. By taking the body as the source of intervention, the course will engage with questions of self, identity, subjectivity and objectification. Thus, engaging with the sociological construction of the body, politics of visibility or that of seeing and be seen, heightened presence of technology, bodies as embodiment of caste, religion, space and disability becomes unavoidable and pivotal. It opens up the domain of alternative narratives that make us look at the body as made up of a plurality and multiplicity of bodies. The course will draw from articulations and conversations that have already been initiated by scholars like Judith Butler, Michel Foucault, Erving Goffman, Bryan Turner etc to enrich the discourse on body politics.

title: Coping with Diversity and Conflict: A Global Survey of Strategies
description:
The human kind is not homogenous. Various forms and
 degrees of ethnic and cultural diversity permeate most societies across our
 world—and often lead to conflict. The regulation of diversity and conflict is therefore
 a foremost task and challenge of governments and governance, and have been so
 throughout the era of late modernity that we live in. It is as salient as ever as the 21 st
 century completes its first quarter and enters the second.
 Coping with Diversity and Conflict: A Global Survey of Strategies is an in-depth
 analytical scrutiny of the repertoire of strategies sovereign states—and sometimes
 other actors—have used and continue to use to eliminate or regulate diversity and
 conflict in their territories and societies. The five strategies we study are: genocide,
 mass expulsion, partition, secession, and
 devolution/autonomy/federalism/consociation. Students are introduced to the terms
 and to the concepts that underlie the terms, which are then fleshed out with
 discussion of recent and current examples (case studies) drawn from across the
 world. The course will be offered in the second trimester of AY 2025-26.

title: Global Conflicts: Causes, Consequences, Solutions
description:
This course is about the most intractable genre of political
 conflict. This type of conflict arises when two or more contending entities—which
 may be nation-states, and/or communities that self-define as ‘nations’—assert
 ownership (sovereignty) over the same territory. The competing claims to ownership
 of/sovereignty over the same land have often given rise to bitter, protracted conflicts,
 viewed through a zero-sum lens by the antagonists. What is common to the
 polarized antagonists is that all invoke the right to national self-determination (NSD)
 in support of their claim. The conflicts produced by these clashing aspirations to NSD
 are highly resistant to accommodation and compromise. The violent enmities they
 often generate further entrenches polarization and condemn entire world regions to
 prolonged instability. NSD conflicts are a global phenomenon—examples are found all over the world in
 recent and current times. Structured in a comparative case-study format, this course
 looks in depth at five such conflicts in the contemporary Middle East (the case of
 Israel and the Palestinians), South Asia or the Indian subcontinent (the cases of
 Kashmir and Sri Lanka), the Balkans region or southeastern Europe (the post-
 Yugoslav case of Bosnia-Hercegovina), and western Europe (the case of Northern
 Ireland). Students are exposed to the specific histories and contexts of these cases
 but are also encouraged to think and analyze comparatively across countries and
 world regions. The course is particularly focused on the great challenges of buildingpeace processes and crafting peace settlements in NSD conflicts. The course will be
 offered in the second trimester of the 2025-26 academic year.

title: Caste in Critical Perspective: From Scriptural Order to Everyday Politics
description:
This course offers a critical and interdisciplinary introduction to caste as a structure of power, a mode of social organization, and a lived experience in South Asia. Moving from scriptural origins to colonial codification, from ideological debates to embodied practices, the course unpacks how it continues to organise everyday life, maintain hierarchies, and shape access to dignity, justice and knowledge. Rather than treating caste as a static tradition, the course approaches it as a dynamic system sustained through everyday interaction and institutional design, yet constantly challenged by movements of resistance and assertion. Through a progression of thematic modules, students explore how caste is normalized and contested across time via scriptural codes and colonial enumeration as well as in ideological debates and sensory experiences.
The course begins by interrogating the religious and philosophical foundations of caste before examining how colonial governance transformed caste into a system of classification and political identity. It engages with the ideas of Ambedkar and Gandhi to highlight competing visions of reform and annihilation of caste. Moreover, students explore how caste operates through the body, gender, sexuality, memory and humiliation, and how it becomes tangible in practices of food, touch, smell and labour. The final module emphasizes academic responsibility by training students to write about caste critically with attention to standpoint and representation.
Drawing from sociology, politics, anthropology, Dalit studies, feminist theory, and cultural studies, the course uses a range of sources—including testimonies, autobiographies, ethnographies, films, and public texts. Emphasizing reflexive learning, it encourages students to connect theoretical debates to lived realities while developing intellectual rigor and sensitivity. The course fosters critical inquiry and social awareness, enabling students to question hierarchies and engage meaningfully with ongoing struggles for equality and dignity in anti-caste movements.

title: Democracy and Autocracy in the Contemporary World
description:
This course critically interrogates the notions of ‘democracy’ and ‘autocracy’ with empirical reference to the contemporary world of the early twenty-first century. So often juxtaposed as binary opposites along with related terms—freedom versus tyranny, liberty versus dictatorship—the line between democracy and authoritarianism has become empirically blurred a mere three decades after an American author proclaimed ‘the end of history’ with the ideological triumph of liberal democracy and its likely universalization. In the 1990s, the comparative study of ‘democratization’ was a booming sub-field of political science. In the 2020s, the scales have flipped and the comparative study of ‘autocratization’—also referred to as ‘democratic backsliding’—is a prime preoccupation of political scientists.
The abrupt swing of the pendulum shows that the binary distinction between ‘democracy’ and ‘authoritarianism’ in the 1990s and 2000s was an ideal-typical—and ideological—construct. The 2010s and 2020s represent a wake-up call to a far more complicated empirical reality, in which the politics of the leader of the Western/Euro- Atlantic ‘free world’ of democratic nations have taken an unexpected turn, along with that of the ‘world’s largest democracy’ in the non-Western world. The course is particularly focused on what the political scientists Stephan Haggard and Robert Kaufman call ‘the incremental erosion of institutions, rules, and norms that result from the actions of duly elected governments’ (and their leaders).
