This is a comparative politics course that draws on cases from around the world.
The Routledge Handbook of Autocratization (Aurel Croissant and Luca Tomini, eds), published in 2024, is a key course text. It consists of forty chapters organized in five parts. All the main readings for specific weeks are given below. The course will be offered in the third trimester of AY 2025-26.

title: Nationalism and National Identity in the Contemporary World
description:
Belying predictions and expectations around the beginning of the third millennium CE of the inexorable forward march of ‘globalization’ and the advent of a post-national age, passionate expressions of nationalist identity and pride animate and indeed dominate the politics of countries around the world. This is especially true of what Charles Tilly called ‘state-led nationalism’ and Benedict Anderson termed ‘official nationalism.’ Contemporary examples include the White, Christian brand of American nationalism championed by Donald Trump in the United States, the massive growth of English nationalism in Britain, the ascendancy of Hindu nationalism in India, and the rise to prominence and power of messianic forms of Zionism in Israel.
This course focuses on and explains the transition of these forms of nationalism from a deceptive marginality to the political centre-stage, and the transformation in their status from oppositional to mainstream and in some cases official ideologies of nation-statehood. The first part of the course covers the major theoretical perspectives on, approaches to the study of, and debates about nationalism and national identity. The second part is devoted to making sense of, and comparing, a selection of contemporary cases from different world regions. Nations and Nationalism: A Reader (Philip Spencer and Howard Wollman, eds, Edinburgh University Press, 2005) will be a key course text. The other major readings for each week are specified below. The course will be offered in the third trimester of AY 2025-26.

title: Faith, Freedom, and the Constitution: Religion and Law in India
description:
Faith, Freedom, and the Constitution: Religion and Law examines the relationship between religion and law in contemporary India through the constitutional governance of religious diversity. It explores how courts, legislatures, and administrative institutions define religion, protect religious freedom, regulate religious practices, and adjudicate conflicts involving equality, citizenship, caste, and religious identity. While centred on India, the course adopts a comparative perspective by engaging debates from the United States and Europe concerning secularism, religious liberty, legal pluralism, and minority rights.
Organised around four foundational questions that have shaped some of the most significant constitutional controversies in modern India, the course first asks, under the theme of secularism: How should a constitutional state govern religion? It then examines, through the lens of religious freedom: What protections should individuals and communities enjoy? Turning to personal law and legal pluralism, it considers: Can religious diversity coexist with equal citizenship? Finally, through the study of caste and conversion, it investigates: How does law regulate religious identity and social hierarchy?
Drawing on constitutional texts, judicial decisions, and interdisciplinary scholarship from law, political theory, history, sociology, and religious studies, the course encourages critical reflection on the challenges of governing religious diversity in democratic societies. Particular attention is paid to the ways in which constitutional commitments to liberty, equality, secularism, and minority protection intersect—and at times come into tension—in contemporary legal and political debates.

title: South Asian Politics and International Relations
description: The people of South Asia are bound by history and a common destiny, as they inhabit what Barry Buzan termed as a ‘security complex.’ That is, millennia of intersecting stories and a more recent shared colonial experience have brought them to their separate post-colonial journeys as modern states and societies. The course will review structures and issues of politics in each South Asian state (Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka), as well as conflict and cooperation between the states.

title: Texts on Interrogating the Political and Social Imaginaries
description: This seminar-based course explores critical political and social ideas regarding their constitution and deployment. Through the strategies of close and comparative readings, the course will highlight the entangled character of political visions and the struggles through which they occupy troubled residences in our part of the world.

title: The Strongmanand the Fakir: Understanding the Populist Phenomenon
description: How do we understand contemporary events such as Brexit, the surge in radical right political parties, left-wing anti-austerity movements, and the rise of ‘strongman’ leaders such as Donald Trump, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Narendra Modi? Connecting these phenomena is the concept of Populism that has emerged as a buzzword in contemporary times and holds a relevance that cuts across geographical boundaries. This course discusses the different theoretical approaches to populism such as the ideational approach, the discursive approach, and the performative approach. The course also offers an empirical and contextualised focus on the varying incarnations of populism and populist leaders in global politics. It pays particular attention to the gendered content of populism as a phenomenon and the field of populism studies. The course also explores different approaches to understanding populism’s relationship with democracy, and traces possible responses to the ‘populist challenge’.

title: Infrastructure Technologies and Planetary Politics
description:
This course focuses on infrastructural technologies as a mode of political power that operates on a planetary scale. Infrastructures are integral to the organisation of our collective life: the kinds of energy and material we use; the systems we build to extract and move material and energy around the planet; the ways in which we create and circulate value and waste; and the logics of property and space that shape and limit human (and nonhuman) mobility and accelerate the movement of capital. To understand these workings of power, we draw on recent theorisations of “planetary politics” that challenge us to go beyond our usual conceptions of political time and the placement of human agency at the centre of political life. 
 In our everyday lives, often seemingly mundane technical infrastructures shape our relationships to the nonhuman and to each other, inculcating norms of habit and sensing, and everyday rules and logistics, that come to have authority. At national and global scales, changes to our political economies of extractivism, production, information, and waste have restructured “politics as usual”, with consequences ranging from corporate capture in democratic politics to the shaping of new modes of authoritarianism. Our infrastructures entangle us in common logics that complicate many of our common distinctions of governance, public vs. private, centralisation and decentralisation, and political ideology. Drawing on multidisciplinary work in Science and Technology Studies, technopolitics, critical theory, and design, we will engage with a range of debates about how to grasp, theorise, and respond politically and collectively to forms of power enacted through our built structures and systems, their modes and logics of production, and the multiscalar, networked, and often diffused ways in which they work.

title: Media and the Public
description: Why does media ownership matter? Is media freedom genuinely safeguarded in democracies, or is that merely a myth? How does social media contribute to community polarization in India? What constitutes the public sphere, and to what extent is it shaped by gender? How do diasporic communities negotiate cultural identity through food and engage in political discourse via social media? In what ways do diasporic communities engage with social media for political participation, debate and mobilization, and how does this impact political dynamics in both their host and home countries ? This course seeks to critically examine these pressing questions by engaging with key theoretical and empirical scholarship at the intersection of media, politics, society, and diaspora. It will provide participants with conceptual tools to analyze how media practices are shaped by power relations, and how they, in turn, influence public life, and shape up identity. The course concludes with a project, allowing participants to apply core concepts and analytical frameworks to contemporary empirical media related issues or case studies. Emphasis is placed on critical thinking, interdisciplinary engagement, and reflexive analysis.

title: Politics and Theories of Urbanisation
description: The course aims to provide a foundational understanding of what constitutes the urban and urbanisation by combining critical theories and concepts crucial to understand urban spaces and urbanisation processes with contemporary empirical literature, primarily focusing on urban and peri-urban India.

title: Research Methods in Politics I
description: The purpose of this course is to introduce students to qualitative and quantitative modes of inquiry while understanding social and political phenomena. Through course material, students will become familiar with the philosophical foundations and perspectives of interpretive qualitative research and basic quantitative data. The course will highlight essential concepts and techniques, as well as explore key interpretive research questions such as the following: What kind of knowledge claims can be made and what counts as evidence to support those claims? How does a researcher’s positionality shape the direction, context, and the structures of power involved in the inquiry? What considerations regarding the representation of the ‘Other’ should a researcher address? What are the ethical issues that arise for interpretive researchers? In addition to such reflections during in-class discussions, students will also have an opportunity to develop their own qualitative and quantitative research proposal and conduct preliminary data collection. Through this preliminary process they will gain direct experience with the practice of research including developing an interpretive qualitative and quantitative research questions, crafting a research design, establishing a conceptual framework, engaging in data collection and analysis techniques, and learning some of the conventions of writing up research. By the end of the course, students will not only understand how qualitative and quantitative researchers produce knowledge but will also appreciate the possibilities of qualitative inquiry within quantitative research and vice versa.

title: Introduction to Psychology
description: The Introduction of Psychology course (PSYC201) introduces students to conceptual building blocks of Psychology, including topics on perception, learning, memory, intelligence, motivation, emotion, and personality. In this way, it levels the field for students from varied educational settings in school who may have a differentiated exposure to psychology as an academic discipline, and prepares them for an undergraduate training in the field. The course seeks to facilitate students in their engagement with the lasting questions around which the discipline has evolved. PSYC201 is also designed to introduce students to some of the classic psychological studies and thereby demonstrate the principles of some of the key areas of modern psychology as a diverse and interdisciplinary science. Students will be expected to read and evaluate classic psychological research studies and critically reflect on the real-life implications of psychological insights.

title: Brain and Behaviour
description: This course examines the biological basis of behaviour and develops an understanding of the complexities of the brain and the mechanisms underlying various behavioural phenomena. How is our brain organised? How do neurons function? What is the brain's basis of psychological phenomena? How do our genes and hormones influence behaviour? We will be exploring answers to these questions through interactive lectures. This course introduces brain disorders as a clinical method to better comprehend the complexity of the mind-brain connection. In addition, we will discuss various techniques such as brain imaging and recording and how they unravel the mysteries of the brain. By integrating knowledge from biology and psychology, students gain a holistic understanding of how biological processes shape human behaviour and cognition. This course is designed to provide an introduction to the major concepts, theories, and methods in the field of behavioural neuroscience.

title: Cognitive Psychology
description: This course delves into the transformative period known as the cognitive revolution,offering students an in-depth exploration of its profound impact on the field ofpsychology. The cognitive revolution marked a paradigm shift, moving away frombehaviorist approaches and emphasizing the importance of internal mental processes.Students will investigate the theoretical frameworks and methodological advancementsthat define cognitive psychology, focusing on understanding the formal nature ofcognition. Throughout the course, we will trace the historical development of cognitivepsychology, highlighting key figures and landmark studies that catalyzed this scientificshift. Emphasis will be placed on how cognitive psychologists approach the study ofmental processes such as perception, memory, language, problem-solving, anddecision-making. Building on foundational knowledge, this course will explore how thecognitive revolution redefined psychological research, moving it towards a moreinterdisciplinary and scientifically rigorous approach. Students will gain insight into thevarious methodologies employed in cognitive psychology, including experimentaldesigns, computational models, and neuroimaging techniques. By engaging deeply withthese concepts, students will develop a nuanced understanding of how cognitivepsychology addresses complex questions about the mind. They will learn to criticallyevaluate research, appreciate the interplay between theory and empirical findings, andrecognize the ongoing challenges in determining the formal nature of cognition. Throughthis comprehensive exploration, students will be equipped with the skills necessary tocontribute to the dynamic and evolving field of cognitive psychology.

title: Statistics & Research Methods I
description:
“Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known.”
-Dr. Carl Sagan, astronomer, 1934-1996
What factors determine student grades? What is the correlation between student attendance and grades? Does breakfast improve attention? The answer to these questions is not factual but requires evidence, which involves gathering data from a sample and then synthesising the information using a relevant statistic to draw conclusions. We leverage statistical tools and techniques to gather evidence. This course provides an overview of the research process, including the use of scientific methods, research designs, and the role of theory in psychological research. Students will further gain hands-on experience in analysing real data using statistical analysis like measures of central tendency, t-statistics, ANOVAs & correlations.
Students will learn the basics of between-subjects and within-subjects design, as well as descriptive statistics, including measures of central tendency and dispersion. They will also explore surveys, such as probability, scales, and their uses, and learn about ANOVA. The course exercises will rely on hands-on exercises using statistical packages to explore, visualise and analyse these data. Students will delve into hypothesis testing, probability theory, and the concept of statistical significance. Further, they will learn about various sampling methods, considerations of sampling biases, and the complexities of generalising research findings to broader populations. A student emerging from this course will not only be equipped to use these tools and apply them, but also evaluate any ‘scientific evidence’ critically and judiciously. The students will learn to report and present data in a meaningful way and transform it into different visualisation formats, demonstrating an understanding of experimental design. This course provides the foundation for Statistics and Research Methods II (PSYC 209).

title: Introduction to Qualitative Approaches in Psychology
description:
This course aims to familiarise students with qualitative research methods, which are increasingly recognized and utilised within the field. Notably, there has been a notable rise in the prominence of qualitative inquiry, evidenced by its inclusion in bodies such as APA's Division of "Evaluation, Measurement, and Statistics". Moreover, the British Psychological Society recommends incorporating qualitative research into undergraduate courses. Qualitative methods are prized for their ability to capture rich, nuanced data and unveil themes and categories inherent in the data. They enable researchers to derive meaning from lived experiences and narratives, decipher the nuances of language in expressing underlying psychic structures, and gain profound insights into human behaviour and social interactions. 

Throughout this course, students will delve into the philosophical foundations that underpin qualitative approaches in psychology. These approaches encompass a range of methods, including narrative analysis, language analysis, visual methods, and naturalistic observation. This course will be delivered using a workshop model, wherein students will engage in hands-on learning experiences, collaborative activities, and practical exercises to explore qualitative research methods. By the end of the course, students will have gained an understanding of the philosophical underpinnings of qualitative research. Additionally, they will have developed the skills to evaluate the quality of qualitative research, considering factors such as sampling techniques, triangulation, and the potential for generalizability.

title: Statistics and Research Methods II
description: This course builds on SRM I (PSYC207) and offers more advanced methodological and statistical tools to students.  The statistical techniques in the course include non-parametric tests, standardized scores, correlation, and linear regression. Students will learn to critically think about  experimental procedures, sampling, randomization, manipulation, apparatus, validity issues, and ethical concerns in conducting experimental research. This course will equip students with basic skills to plan an experimental design, analyze research studies that illustrate  varied experimental methods across different areas of psychology, and understand the underlying philosophy that guides empirical research. In doing so, this course provides the foundation for guided empirical research and critical analysis required in the final year of the program.

title: Organisational Psychology
description: This course offers an introduction to the field of industrial and organizational (I/O) psychology, which focuses on scientifically studying behavior within organizational contexts, and applying psychological principles to comprehend and shape work behavior. The course should help students appreciate the human aspects of organisations at individual, interpersonal and group levels. Topics in this course encompass exploring the intricacies of employee satisfaction and workplace motivation, analyzing how various leadership styles influence employee performance and organizational outcomes, and locating sites of intervention for changes. The primary objective of the course is to foster a critical examination of the intricate fabric of workplace dynamics. This includes scrutinizing prevalent workplace practices,  exploring decision-making processes, and examining the criteria used to measure both success and failure within organizational contexts. Through this course, students will be exposed to the multifaceted nature of organizational behavior and the complex interplay between individuals, structures, and culture within the workplace.

title: Psychology as Human Science
description:
Psychological sciences probe human behavior and mental processes in a rigorous and
 systematic manner. Through this course, students will explore the implicit philosophical
 underpinnings of psychology as a science, and the kind of psychological phenomena,
 specific aims, methods emphasized, and purposes for which this knowledge is used. In
 doing so, students will reflect and review the empirical, positivistic, quantitative,
 determinable, predictive and scientific nature of psychology, addressing Giorgi’s call for
 psychology as a human science. We will then learn about a plurality of theoretical
 developments that offer new pathways for what psychology can become a discipline and
 what it means to be a human.
 Fundamentally rooted in Giorgi’s existential phenomenological approach, psychology,
 conceived of as a human science, offers an established way of understanding the life world,
 and subjective meanings as it is experienced and lived by human subjects. Drawing from
 existentialist, humanistic, and phenomenology, hermeneutics, psychoanalysis, and cultural,
 liberation and decolonial, and feminist perspectives, students will examine and reflect on the
 role of language, intersubjectivity, and interpretation in knowledge construction. Addressing
 Giorgi’s call for inventing new methods and approaches, students will tackle the problem of
 investigating the complexity of human phenomena scientifically.

title: Psychology of Self & Identity
description:
This course explores foundational and contemporary perspectives on personality, self, and
 identity in psychology. It asks the fundamental question: Who are we, and what makes us who
 we are? What makes us both unique and part of a shared social world? Beginning with classical
 debates on the nature and structure of personality, students are introduced to how psychology
 has historically conceptualized the individual. The course then moves into critical examinations
 of how selfhood is shaped by social, cultural, and digital environments, as well as by
 experiences of displacement and diaspora. Drawing from diverse psychological
 traditions—including trait theory, psychoanalysis, developmental psychology, and critical/cultural
 psychology—the course investigates how identities are formed, narrated, regulated, and
 transformed. Particular emphasis is placed on Indian psychological thought, contextual
 differences, and the lived experience of navigating multiple, intersecting selves.

title: Fundamentals of Psychophysics
description: This interdisciplinary course starts from an introduction to psychophysics with its definitions, historical background and its intersection with neuroscience, psychology, physics and other interwoven disciplines. Examples from every day and real-life instances will make it more interesting. Adopting an interactive approach, this course will provide an overview of human sensory systems like vision, hearing, touch, taste, and smell and their neural basis. The students will learn about difference between the sensation and perception, responses and their qualitative and quantitative responses to various stimuli. As this course includes the experimental and data analysis aspects, students will not only learn about the data organization but also about its visualization and analysis.

title: Programming for Psychologist
description: Programming for Psychologists is an undergraduate course designed to equip psychology students with computational problem-solving skills. Through hands-on exercises in Python and Octave, students will learn to think like programmers, develop scripts to analyse behavioural data, run simulations, and automate research workflows. Emphasis on real-world applications includes data visualisation, statistical modelling, and research practices. The course also introduces LaTeX for creating professional reports and slides for effective presentations. By integrating coding fundamentals with psychological research methods, students will gain practical expertise in computational tools essential for advanced research, enhancing their ability to design experiments, manage datasets, and communicate findings efficiently.

title: The Psychology of Sexuality and Gender
description: This course introduces students to social, economic, and political dimensions of gender and sexuality with the goal of understanding how the diversity of these two aspects of the human experience impacts psychology and its allied disciplines. We will take a multi-disciplinary approach to explore, in particular: (i) differences and interrelationships between sex, gender, and sexuality; (ii) the relevance of cultural contexts to understanding human variation, especially as regards family, subjectivity, the politics of identification, and the impact of the predominance of ‘WEIRD’ research; (iii) theories of the performative aspects of gender and sexuality and the relevance of labour to gender and sexual roles and identifications; (iv) problems of categorisation and classification of normalcy and pathology, contemporary views on variation in biology, and the historical legacies of pathologisation of women and gender and sexual minorities; (v) problems in the public circulation and communication of specialist research (including overgeneralisation and misrepresentation of scientific findings and clinical practice); and (vi) some contemporary approaches in psychology research and practice that build on these social understandings. Students will gain experience in understanding how gender and sexuality are operationalised in psychology and its related fields of psychiatry and social work in both research and practice, as well as the tools to critically evaluate the promises and limitations of individual research studies by considering them in these broader contexts.

title: Developmental Psychology
description: The course examines changes across different time points in development by addressing four central questions of developmental science: continuity, plasticity, sources of development, and individual differences across the lifespan. Empirical data from infants, children, and adolescents will be examined to explain the developmental processes and learn about the emergence of the human mind.

title: Writing like a Psychologist
description: This course is attuned to the art of writing from a psychological perspective. It will commence by establishing the intrinsic connection between reading scientific texts and crafting them, providing students with insights into reading and interpreting various types of text, such as research papers, science journalism, and fiction. Subsequently, it will delve into the intricacies of articulating the challenging and often elusive facets of human experience that defy straightforward expression, and yet are the work of the psychological researcher. Addressing both abstract concepts and technical elements of scientific writing, students will engage in theoretical discussions, practical exercises, and real-world examples of writing on psychological topics. The primary focus will be on enhancing skills for writing research reports and research papers, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of effective writing principles within the discipline.

title: Health and Sports Psychology
description: There has been a radical shift in understanding of health and wellbeing. The traditional biomedical approach is giving way to a multi-faceted biopsychosocial approach. Similarly, the processes underlying stress, motivation, wellbeing and team performance in sports demand a greater understanding of the athletes as social beings. Psychology has an indispensable place in the scientific knowledge of health and sports. However, the narrow and individualistic theorisation of different micro and macro-level factors remains a critical challenge to overcome. This course seeks to enable the students to navigate these challenges by focusing on the vibrant  psychological processes underlying the fields of health and sports. Taking a lens of groups and identities, we will examine the ‘group’ in the individual that makes these phenomena possible and, at the same time, offers tools for effecting a change. In this course, we shall pursue the questions emerging from the field of health and sports, ground them in scientific knowledge and interrogate them through hands-on exercises.

title: Social Psychology
description: This course will build social psychological foundations for the sociality of the self, interpersonal relationships, and group behaviour in Psychology. This will serve three important and interconnected purposes. Firstly, students will learn to think about social psychological research and some of the classic studies in nuanced and complex ways. Secondly, students will learn to critically appraise the work and findings of social psychological concepts reported in public discourse. Finally, students will learn to expand their concepts of the self as social beings with multiple social identities and bring these to bear upon their interpretation of social behaviour. The course will bridge the gap between simplified concepts in standard social psychology textbooks and the rigour, complexity and uncertainty of findings in the primary literature, including, among others, journals and theses.

title: Psychology of Language
description: This course offers an introduction to the fundamental concepts in the psychology oflanguage, exploring the nature of Natural Language and how it is structured andprocessed by the human brain. Students will delve into key topics such as syntax, orsentence structure, and phonology, the sound structure of language. The course alsoexamines the cognitive processes underlying language comprehension and production,and how natural language is represented and processed in the brain. The course willintroduce to formal theories of Language, focusing on Syntax, Phonology andPhonetics, and subsequently guide them through psycholinguistic theories of linguisticprocessing in the brain. Besides being introduced to the theoretical and experimentalconcepts foundational to the field, the students are also exposed to the history of thedevelopment of psycholinguistic thought, and the various frameworks of psychology thatare relevant to understanding Natural Languages. Through a combination of lectures,discussions, and hands-on laboratory activities, students will gain a deeperunderstanding of the complex relationship between language and the mind.

title: Introduction to Clinical Psychology
description: The exploration of madness has served as a captivating frontier for both artistic expression and scientific inquiry throughout history. This course aims to familiarise students with a scientific approach to comprehending clinical conditions in humans. It delves into fundamental inquiries: How do we understand what is normal and what is abnormal? What constitutes mental health and illness? How are these concepts evaluated and quantified, and by whom? This course will provide an introduction to different ways of thinking about distressing states of mind, beginning in antiquity and moving onto the biopsychosocial model of contemporary clinical psychology. Following this history, the course will introduce contemporary psychopathological categories such as developmental, anxiety, mood, psychotic, and personality disorders along with the assessment instruments that are used to diagnose them. Additionally, students will explore how different theoretical frameworks, including cognitive-behavioural, psychodynamic, humanistic, and systemic perspectives, conceptualise these conditions, offering diverse lenses through which to understand and treat mental health issues. We will enhance our research-based understanding of the categories of mental illness via a close reading of first-person narratives of the experience of mental illness. In the final segment of the course, students will examine political movements that have significantly reshaped the discourses surrounding mental illness, reframing it as distress, disability, or divergence. Through this exploration, students will gain insight into the socio-political forces that influence perceptions of mental health and contribute to the evolution of mental health policies and practices.

title: Motherhood Family and Childcare in India
description: The aim of this course is to interrogate the sociocultural constitution of motherhood as a psychological experience. Challenging the Eurocentric depiction of the mother-infant dyad reproduced in psychology literature, this course approaches a sensemaking process through the intersectionality of cultural psychology, feminist intersectionality, and critical developmental psychology perspectives. Through the course, students will examine motherhood as a social institution and study the nurturing bonds women have with children and others. In so doing, students will focus on analyzing the stereotypical representations of the mothers as “monstrous” and “consecrated”. Subsequently, students will have the opportunity to examine the developmental experiences of women such as pregnancy, childbirth, and caregiving rooted in the family and communal life in India. Students will have the opportunity to understand how family life, cultural practices, technologies, and structural inequities structure multiple trajectories for motherhood and their childcare decisions.  Lastly, taking Burman’s “Child as Method” as an analytic and pedagogical device, students will unpack various contemporary and historical discourses on childhood and parenting shapes and regulates motherhood as a site for “oppression” and “resistance”. We will explore how everyday acts of mothering are performed as resistance to prevailing sociocultural norms.

title: Testing & Measurement in Psychology
description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the theory of psychological measurement and contemporary measurement procedures utilized in psychology. Throughout the course, students will learn to interpret and use existing psychological tests and measures and develop the knowledge and proficiency to evaluate these instruments critically. This course is particularly relevant for psychology majors as it lays the foundation for a deep understanding of the reliability and validity of psychological assessments, which are essential for evidence-based practice and research in various psychology domains.

title: Theories of human development
description: The course delves into the dynamic processes and mechanisms influencing developmental change, emphasizing the interplay of biological, psychological and environmental factors shaping development from infancy to late  adulthood. Additionally, the course provides foundational concepts such as nature vs nurture; continuity vs discontinuity; stability vs instability and the role of critical and sensitive periods in development.

title: Culture, Cognition, and Subjectivity:  Psychological Worlds Across Contexts
description:
Comprehension of cultural factors is a key to critical inquiry onto all major branches of
 psychology such as cognitive, developmental, social, and clinical. Moving across
 mainstream, critical, and non-Western approaches — with a focus on South Asian
 contexts,this course explores how human subjectivity and cognition are embedded in
 and are shaped by culture, history, and social worlds. We will examine how
 psychological processes are mediated through language, embodiment, ritual, narrative,
 and social structures like caste, gender, and coloniality.

title: A General Introduction to Psychoanalysis
description: This course will introduce psychoanalysis, focusing on the groundbreaking work of Sigmund Freud that transformed our understanding of mental life in the late 19th century. Although psychoanalysis is often associated with sex, it actually encompasses a broader exploration of societal pressures and the ideologies surrounding sex and sexuality. Freud challenged prevailing psychiatric and psychological models by introducing the concept of the unconscious. Psychoanalysis provides a unique framework to delve into the internal divisions of human subjectivity, particularly through the study of the unconscious in clinical settings. Moreover, it offers valuable insights into the influence of culture and social forces on the construction of individual difference. The course will examine the dynamic interplay between individuals and society, the intersection of clinical practice and cultural context, and the complexities of sexuality and sexual differences. Students will have the opportunity to analyze and critique Freud's theories and methods, encouraging a critical examination of his work while also exploring how contemporary psychoanalysts continue to build upon and refine his ideas.

title: Psychology of Disaster Response & Humanitarianism
description: Psychology of Disaster Response and Humanitarianism is an interdisciplinary course drawing on thefields of disaster studies, humanitarian aid policy, and psychology. This course will introduce students tothe field of International Disaster Psychology in relation to Humanitarian politics and the intertwinedimpacts that these have on individuals and communities affected by disasters. Through the course, weshall evaluate the defining concepts of disaster, risk, resilience, and humanitarianism, the narratives thatsustain these concepts and which in turn shape policy decisions. From the panoramic view of thepolitical landscape of international agencies like the UN, we shall learn to think with a socialpsychological lens of community and group responses in emergencies and disaster scenarios, bringingthis together in a focused look at particular psychological interventions through different case-studies

title: Helping Skills
description:
This course is designed to provide an introduction to psychotherapy skills. Students will be able to understand elements of ethical and effective counselling practice. They will be able to identify and use various helping Skills at a beginner level with an appreciation of personal and sociocultural factors. The course also aims to enhance students' understanding of self as a tool and increase self-awareness and self-reflective abilities. Students will practice helping skills with each other every week. Attendance is mandatory and contributes to the course grade. Note that the course will involve discussing and working with emotionally charged content. Students should also be prepared to reflect on and talk about (not mandated) some personal/emotional issues in class. 
Important Note: Completing this course does NOT qualify students to practice as counsellors or therapists.

title: Counselling Skills: putting theories into practice
description: This course is designed to provide an introduction to psychotherapy skills. Students will be able to understand elements of ethical and effective counselling practice. They will be able to identify and use various helping Skills at a beginner level with an appreciation of personal and sociocultural factors. The course also aims to enhance students' understanding of self as a tool and increase self-awareness and self-reflective abilities. Students will practice helping skills with each other every week. Attendance is mandatory and contributes to the course grade. Note that the course will involve discussing and working with emotionally charged content. Students should also be prepared to reflect on and talk about (not mandated) some personal/emotional issues in class.

title: Critical Disability & Inclusion Studies
description:
This advanced undergraduate course offers an interdisciplinary introduction to Critical Disability and Inclusion Studies (CDIS), foregrounding disability as a socially constructed and politically mediated category. Moving beyond individual and medicalized understandings, the course approaches disability through frameworks rooted in social justice, political economy, and intersectionality.
We begin by examining the historical and cultural construction of disability and ableism, alongside the emergence of critical theories of access, normalcy, and inclusion. The course then explores how developmental norms shape understandings of childhood disability, and how inclusive education can be reimagined through both psychological and pedagogical models. In the clinical module, we turn to psychiatric disability, community mental health, and cultural critiques of diagnosis and medicalization.
Intersectional concerns—such as gender, caste, sexuality, age, and race—are woven throughout, enabling students to critically engage with how multiple forms of marginalization structure experiences of disability. We also examine institutional practices, with case studies of inclusion efforts in higher education, such as at Krea University. The course concludes with an analysis of legal frameworks and policy debates in India and globally, grounded in the history of the disability rights movement.

Students will engage critically with theory, policy, and practice to design more inclusive and just systems.

title: Introduction to Counselling Theories
description: Counselling psychology stands out as one of the most popular branches within the field of psychology. This course is designed to introduce students to theories in Counselling. Counselling Psychology offers the ways and means to work with human beings in psychological distress. Thus it is the sub-field that not only offers an application of various understandings of the mind, but also an important purpose to the vast knowledge that the discipline generates. The history of counselling is rich and dynamic. It has been influenced by social, political and intellectual movements at various times. This course aims to familiarise the students with this complex past and present of counselling through some of the major theoretical streams that developed within Psychology.Through thorough exploration and critical analysis of various counselling theories, students will delve into the core principles, concepts, and methodologies integral to the counselling process. Engaging with case studies and role-playing scenarios, students will have the opportunity to contextualise theoretical constructs within real-life counselling contexts. By navigating the complexities of counselling theories, students will gain a deeper understanding of the nuanced approaches employed in the therapeutic encounter.

title: Advanced Qualitative Research: Power, politics, pleasure
Testing & Measurement in Psychology
description: This practicum course introduces students to the theory, principle, and technique involved in psychological testing and measurement. The course discusses the history of psychological testing and processes involved in test construction, reliability and validity establishment, and test standardisation. It examines some widely-used tests for Personality, Intelligence, Aptitude, Projective and Ability tests. This course also gives the basic training needed in conducting a psychological test, including understanding the need for a manual, test administration, scoring, interpreting and reporting. It discusses the applicability of psychological testing in various fields including Clinical, Organisational, School and educational, Developmental settings, Career counselling, Forensic, Sports, Defence and Military Psychology. Finally, this course looks into the ethical and practical issues in testing.

title: Political Psychology
description:
Political psychology has been defined as the 'application of what is known about human psychology to the study of politics' (Sears, Huddy & Jervis, 2003, p. 3) and social psychology has influenced the study of political psychology more than any other subfield of Psychology. The course will introduce students to an overview of political psychology with a focus on questions that are currently central to the field’s concerns. These include construction of group identities, emotions and actions, collective mobilisation with a focus on leadership processes, and citizenship (as an example of group membership in a political community) through the lens of psychological theories. I have designed the course with learning built in three phases:
The first phase: will be bringing our common sensical understanding/ opinions/ knowledge/ to the table. We shall collate and think about what we ‘know’ about prejudice, for instance.
The second phase: we shall then interrogate our findings from phase 1 with research from psychological theories. I will lead this with lectures and working with our interactions in class as data points.
In the third phase, we shall work with the theories that we have learned to look at political material including websites/ speeches/ songs/ videos/ social media posts.
Students will thinking with psychological theories and the clarification of many misunderstood psychological studies (including the famous Obedience studies of Milgram, Conformity studies by Asch, and even the supposed bystander effect of not helping people in crisis.) Students of psychology will find that a healthy interest in the world around them, engaged thinking of stepping outside the realm of only the ‘individual’ will help in constituting the psychological selves in political ways.

title: Experimental Social Psychology
description: This course develops on foundational concepts of social psychology and the research methods courses offered in the Psychology programme at Krea, and introduces students to the exciting world of technological mediations in psychological processes. This is primarily lab-based and will use equipments available in the psychology lab at Krea. We shall introduce students to experimental designs in immersive environments through Virtual Reality MetaQuest3 headsets, the use of EEG and Eye-tracking in studying real-world phenomena from climate change responses to social interactions to mental health interventions. The course aims to be a technologically mediated exploratory journey of social psychological research. It shall be taught by instructors of social psychology and cognitive psychology.

title: Advanced Social Psychology
description:
This course is designed for advanced students of social psychology interested in pursuing questions at the boundaries of social psychological imagination. The course aims to teach the nuts and bolts of social psychological research to students who are already familiar with concepts in social psychology and are interested in honing their potential research ideas into ‘researchable’ questions. This shall be done by developing on concepts taught in social psychology to critically reading current cutting-edge research employing various methods, including experimental designs and qualitative analysis. The modules are designed to critically engage with social identity and self categorisation approaches that inform areas in psychological research.

The success of the course depends on student interest as much as instructor guidance and has been designed to integrate both equally. Students will identify their areas of interest (for example, health psychology, feminist interpretations, moral psychology, femcel mobilisation, cultural folklores, military psychology) early on in the course with the instructor’s guidance, which they will then follow with critical reading of both theoretical and empirical articles in conjunction with the modules of foundational approaches, methods, contemporary sites of behavioural analysis (including social networking sites), emotion and cognition, and social norms designed in the course. There will be a fair amount of work in this course, and it will be difficult at times – that’s the “advanced” part.

title: Introduction to Clinical Psychology
description: This course introduces clinical psychology as a field concerned with understanding psychological distress within its broader social, cultural, and ethical contexts. It examines how concepts such as mental health, illness, and psychopathology are shaped by historical developments, theoretical frameworks, and systems of classification. Moving beyond purely individual explanations, the course foregrounds the role of social structures and lived experience in shaping mental health, with particular attention to the Indian context. It encourages students to critically engage with how distress is defined, interpreted, and addressed across diverse settings. Overall, the course positions clinical psychology as both a scientific and socially embedded practice, emphasising reflexive, context-sensitive, and ethically informed approaches to mental health and care.

title: Human Development & Psychopathology
description: In this course, we will learn about the developmental origins, progression, and social contexts of psychological disorders. Taking an integrative approach, this course draws upon developmental psychopathology, lived experience, and cultural perspectives to analyze what gets classified as psychopathology in childhood and adolescence. Case studies will be used to discuss how early developmental experiences shape mental health outcomes in adulthood and later life, and what risk and protective factors influence the nature of psychological vulnerability and resilience.

title: Becoming Reflective Practitioners
description: This course explores the development of the counselor’s personal and professional identities, focusing on the cultivation of self-reflection as a core clinical competency. Students will investigate the "person of the therapist" and how their own internal landscape — values, biases, family-of-origin patterns, and physiological states — influences the therapeutic encounter. Alongside this self-inquiry, students will practice and refine foundational counseling skills, including active listening, empathic responding and purposeful communication, recognizing that technical competence and self-awareness are mutually reinforcing dimensions of effective clinical practice.

title: Common Factors in Counselling
description: This course investigates the common factors across models of psychotherapy and counselling, prioritizing the shared mechanisms of change over school/model-specific techniques. Students will examine the essential elements of successful counseling relationships while critically evaluating the foundational dichotomies and theoretical debates that define the field. By exploring these core tensions, the course provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the diverse landscape of modern approaches to mental health.

title: Counselling Skills I - Systems Approach
description: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of the Marriage and Family Therapy (MFT) field, tracing its historical evolution from foundational roots to modern-day applications. The curriculum investigates the theoretical architecture of both classical and emerging models, equipping students to critically appraise their utility across diverse family structures. Beyond theory, the course emphasizes essential clinical skills in family therapy as well as the ethical complexities unique to systemic work.

title: Communities, Identities and Cultures in India
description: What is identity? How do community identities define socio-political practices? Does identity and othering go hand in hand? How do languages shape community identifications? How does popular culture inform identity formation in India? What is majoritarianism and where do we locate the minorities in India? How are diasporic identities constructed and sustained? In the course ‘Communities, Identities and Cultures in India’ we would ask several such questions and seek answers. This course intends to explore social identities and social locations in India from the perspectives of practices, diversities, and hierarchies around those practices. Expanding on the discourse of personal is political, this course aims to analyse how our everyday practices and identifications stem from larger community affiliations, which also imply stereotypes and othering. The course is divided into four parts - in the first part we will contextualise the significance of communities and identities at large, and survey how scholars have located and critiqued community as an analytical concept to investigate what collective identity might mean in India with special reference to ethnic identities, religious identities, colonialism, nationalism, and secularism. The immersive engagement in this section will deep dive into village studies, and engage with different scholarly approaches to the study of culture through festivals, ritual and other forms of community cultural expression. In the second section we will look into social construction of identities, and how community identity becomes a category of experience through the prism of social categories, cultural expression, and language. This section will also capture the pulse of linguistic nationalism as the defining point of identity assertion in India on one hand and English language elitism as an expression of colonial lingering on the other. In the third segment we will examine the role of mediation, media, and identity and community formation in the diaspora. In this section, students will also engage with transnational frameworks and diasporic identities. Having located the politics around community affiliations and collective identities in the conceptual and theoretical contexts, in the fourth and the last segment, students will undertake a small research project.

title: Political Economy of Development
description:
In the 20th century, the entire world came to be divided into "underdeveloped", "developing" and "developed" countries. Underlying this division was a hegemonic project of "development", an extended process of structural transformation associated with industrialization and modernization of economies and societies, largely led by and operating within nation-states. Since the heydays of modernization, this consensus has unravelled in four ways. First, there have been many normative critiques of development, as well as many alternative normative agendas for development (e.g. human development, inclusive development, sustainable development). Second, the centrality of the national scale is no longer taken for granted; development processes are understood to operate at multiple scales ranging from the local to the global. Third, both in popular and academic discourse, there has been a reconsideration of the respective roles played by governments, firms, non-governmental actors, social movements, etc. in the development process. Finally, in development scholarship, there has been a proliferation of the methodological and theoretical frameworks used to analyze the development process.

In this course, students will be introduced to different intellectual traditions of development scholarship, and their interactions with the world of policy-making and implementation. Accordingly, the course is divided into three modules. The first module, titled the “History of Development Thought”, helps students understand how ideas about development have evolved since the early 20th century. In the second module, titled “Methodological Innovations”, students are introduced to new approaches to development scholarship and its relationship with evidence drawn from the real world. The final module, titled “Development Dilemmas”, picks up a sample of concrete dilemmas emerging from development debates in recent years.
This course will be reading and writing-intensive; in addition to weekly response essays, students will write a literature review and a position paper on a topic of their choice.

title: Introduction to Feminist Theory
description: This course introduces key directions and themes in feminist thought and practice, both global and local, spanning a time frame starting from the eighteenth century to the contemporary times. Examining how gender and sexuality operates in society, we examine how gender is not an individual attribute or a role, but rather a system of social practices that constructs different categories of people—“men” and “women”—and organizes social interaction and inequality around this difference. The course will take a sociological approach in understanding what is sex and gender , how they operate in the labor market, at home, and at school, and how they structure our everyday lives at the individual, interactional, and institutional level. Throughout the course, we will prioritize reading, evaluating, and questioning feminist theory and sociological research on gender. We will also investigate feminist thought from a variety of disciplinary perspectives and theoretical orientations and focus on key debates such as the sex/gender system, intersectionality, sexual difference, and essentialism, amongst others. This course aims to think through the ways in which gender and sexuality intersect with caste, class, community and the nation. The aim of this course is to unravel the centrality of power in the practice of gender.

title: Economy and Society
description:
The human “propensity to truck, barter, and exchange” (a la Adam Smith) lies at the heart of all
modern economies. And yet, social scientists have adopted widely diverging theoretical
frameworks to understand how market economies function and evolve. At one end, the dominant
strand of economics today takes rational and instrumental action by individuals as its starting
point when modelling market exchange. By contrast, an equally influential stream of social
thought assumes that economic behaviour is conditioned by the same set of social and political
institutions that also govern other types of non-economic behaviour. In this course, students will
be introduced to the latter set of intellectual traditions in political economy and economic
sociology, wherein “institutions” are treated not merely as constraints upon economic behaviour
but also as constitutive of both the preferences and norms that inform such behaviour.
The course is divided into two modules. The first module (four weeks) revisits the work of some
original thinkers to locate the intellectual origins of this field of study. The second module poses
a series of comparative and historical questions that help illustrate the evolution of the capitalist
world economy from the 18th to the 21st century. Some of the possible themes to be covered in

the second module will include: the great divergence, industrialization and financialization,
inequality and social im/mobility, mass education and the establishment of professions, tax
reforms and welfare states, and new social movements.

title: Media and the Public
description: Why does media ownership matter? Is media freedom genuinely safeguarded in democracies, or is that merely a myth? How does social media contribute to community polarization in India? What constitutes the public sphere, and to what extent is it shaped by gender? How do diasporic communities negotiate cultural identity through food and engage in political discourse via social media? In what ways do diasporic communities engage with social media for political participation, debate and mobilization, and how does this impact political dynamics in both their host and home countries ? This course seeks to critically examine these pressing questions by engaging with key theoretical and empirical scholarship at the intersection of media, politics, society, and diaspora. It will provide participants with conceptual tools to analyze how media practices are shaped by power relations, and how they, in turn, influence public life, and shape up identity. The course concludes with a project, allowing participants to apply core concepts and analytical frameworks to contemporary empirical media related issues or case studies. Emphasis is placed on critical thinking, interdisciplinary engagement, and reflexive analysis.

title: Anthropology of Violence: State, Power , and Politics
Beasts, People and Wild Environments
description: This introductory and interdisciplinary course focuses on human/animal stories to explore socio-cultural worldviews especially in relation to identity, social justice and the redistribution of natural resources, particularly in South Asia. Through ethnographies, films, novels and paintings we will explore the lives of those living in communities which depend on or live close to wild animals. The course aims to be an informative, provocative and a fun introduction to an exciting and relatively new field of scholarship.

title: Caste, Community, Coloniality: From Victimhood to Political Responsibility
description: The language used by activist and scholars to capture power, privilege, violence, and injustice has for various reasons remained underdeveloped. This course introduces scholarship that seeks to expand this language so as to enable articulation of nuances that are otherwise lost. Critiquing the dominant colonial and postcolonial frameworks, it takes a fresh look at the imbrication of caste, community and coloniality in South Asia. Pushing beyond the usual impasse on the binaries of perpetration and victimhood, blame and guilt, culpability and innocence to concerns like epistemic injustice, collective responsibility, implicated subject and the pure concept of forgiveness, it explores problems like: how we come to inherit collective responsibility for acts of violence and injustice that may have preceded us or may not have committed directly, and yet on closer examination find ourselves variously implicated in. Apart from introducing new concepts, the course offers a reflection on contexts like Kashmir that make the intricacies, contradictions and overlaps between caste, community and coloniality manifest.

title: Social Movements
description:
What constitutes a social movement? Why and how do social movements emerge? Who joins
social movements and why? What strategies do they use? How do social movements differ?
Which resources are essential for social movements? Why are some successful, and some are
not? These are some of the questions that the course intends to address.
Emphasis will be not only on the processes and career of the movements but also on the
conditions and contexts that give rise to collective mobilization. The students will be encouraged
to ultimately reflect on more general questions about the nature of political power, resources,
conflict, and legitimacy, as well as, the relationship between human agency, social structure, and
historical change.

title: Health, Data, Politics
description:
‘The more data the better’! ‘Data is the new oil’! This course problematizes these maxims by familiarizing students with the politics and paradox of data in healthcare. The course examines how data is produced, enacted, cleaned, refined, represented and utilized to diagnose and prevent disease outbreaks, expand access to healthcare, and determine patterns of funding and resource allocation in global health. In recent years, the term data has been attached to a range of approaches and processes, such as data-driven, data-fied, and data-based systems, to signify the promises that data holds for improving healthcare and advancing development.
Central to these approaches are the infrastructures and technologies (digital and otherwise), such as surveys, statistics, satellites, smartphones, apps, algorithms, big data, platforms, and artificial intelligence, that generate, maintain and circulate data from dispersed sites in the pursuit of more precise, predictive, and pre-emptive health outcomes. We ask how these infrastructures reconfigure everyday health work, doctor-patient relationships, and broader understandings of expertise, innovation, accountability, transparency and trust. And, on a more micro level, how digital and data infrastructures encourage new forms of self-care and self-monitoring practices? 
What modes of health governance do data infrastructures enable and what does that tell us about the role of the state in the delivery of healthcare? What happens when an eclectic mix of new public-private actors (technologists, designers, entrepreneurs, and consultants) enter this ecosystem? And, what does that reveal about underlying power dynamics, inequalities and market interests that animate data-driven healthcare? This course brings together scholarship from science and technology studies, medical and political anthropology, and critical data studies. We will read ethnographic accounts (with a significant focus on India and Africa) as well as policy-oriented documents. This approach situates grounded, empirical insights within broader political and institutional contexts.

title: The Social Construction of Nature
description:
Is nature the external world; or are humans part of nature? Is human subjectivity natural; or is it socially constructed? Are relations between human and non-human animals, or actors, social? Is there a pristine nature out there? Such debates around ‘the social construction of 'nature’ have animated discussions of the relationship between nature and society since at least the late twentieth century, and continue to offer valuable insights. This course introduces students to these debates around the perceptions of nature—human, non-human and more-than-human; the historical and often unsuccessful disciplining of more-than-human natures by dominant social, political and economic interests; and the emancipatory and democratic politics for socioecological justice that counter capitalogenic expropriations of more-than-human natures.
The first module examines the binary distinction between human and non-human nature, including human and non-human animals. In the second module we discuss the disciplining of more-than-human natures (including other species and affordances such as land, rivers or forests) by historically particular dominant interests. A fieldtrip animates the discussions in this module through exposure to lived negotiations of socioecological relations in a particular setting. The third module discusses the historical subjection of more-than-human natures to market imperatives in the pursuit of profits, and how their exploitation, depletion and dispossession have accelerated multiple socioecological crises in what has been termed the capitalocene. We end with a discussion of what democratic and emancipatory politics of more-than-human justice might look like.

title: Qualitative Methods: Researching the Social, Political and the Historical
description: This course introduces the students to the various aspects, approaches and techniques of qualitative research. Qualitative research in social studies is significant for theory building and examining empiricism through exploration of the field. Distinct from quantitative methods, qualitative research methods involve close and long-standing interaction with the participants leading to various ethical and subjective considerations in research. This is also implicated in the researcher’s own location on and off the field. In addition, conducting field work involves multiple stages, sample selections, approaching and entering the field and planned process of observation. In the light of this, the course is divided into four sections. First section “Overview: key concepts and definitions” addresses the fundamental concepts related to qualitative research and the subject of methodological awareness required for conducting qualitative research. In the second module, “Various approaches of qualitative research”, the course offers detailed discussions on ethnography, case studies, life history method content and discourse analyses and the stages of theory building following an inductive approach to research. This module also extensively discusses the structural challenges and possibilities of conducting field work. The third module “Political economy of qualitative research” engages with the broad questions of how to conduct auto-ethnography and use the self as a research method; it deals with concepts like cultural insider, covert research etc. The fourth and the last module “Research Project” includes empirical research projects conducted by the students following various stages of qualitative research.

title: Introduction to Political Anthropology
description: This course offers an accessible introduction to political anthropology by tracing how the field emerged, how it relates to allied disciplines, and what makes anthropological approach to power and politics distinctive. Through close readings of foundational texts, key theoretical debates, and ethnographic case studies from diverse contexts, students will explore how political anthropology has evolved, what questions its practitioners grapple with today, and what the framework contributes—as well as where its limits lie—in understanding political life. Organized into five modules, the course examines the field’s origins and boundaries; anthropological perspectives on politics and the political; debates around the nation, state, public sphere, and civil society; anthropological approaches to protest and revolution; and ethnographies of political violence.

title: Introduction to Sociological and Anthropological Thought
description:
This required course introduces students to key moments in the development of sociological and
anthropological thought. Starting with the origins of the two disciplines; the ways in which both
disciplines are from inception implicated in the social, historical, political and economic context
out of which they emerged; we proceed to examine how ideas have emerged over time, through
relentless critical inquiry and engagement with diverse and changing contexts. Each module will
introduce students to a particular moment in the discourse and involve engagement with a
selection of representative texts drawn from key sociological and anthropological thinkers. This
is not an exhaustive course on the history of sociological/anthropological thought, nevertheless
the representative selection of texts is aimed at elucidating key theoretical insights of important


thinkers. Students are expected to undertake immersive reading and critically reflect on the ideas
thus introduced and their relevance (or not) in the contemporary world.

title: Eco feminism
description:
Ecofeminism is a school of feminism that seeks to understand intersectional nuances between
gender and environment under the patriarchal capitalist framework. The central aim of
ecofeminism is to offer an understanding of anthropocentric and androcentric worldviews on
both nature and women. As a school of feminism, ecofeminism is diverse with contradictory and
complementary perspectives about the relationship between women and nature. The course will
encompass the history, theories, and movements of ecofeminism that took place in the United
States, India, and Africa. Based on ecofeminist theories, students will examine the political,
social, and developmental impacts of ecofeminism on gender and climate change, and find
avenues for scholarly conversation in activism and research. The course will engage the students
with creative aspects of ecofeminist thoughts through literature, arts, and other creative projects.

title: Kinship, Family, and Community
description:
"Why are the young women of some communities of Tamil Nadu, for example, expected to marry their maternal uncle i.e. mama? How and why did the Kulin Brahmins of Bengal justify having numerous wives? Traditionally, amongst the Nair, women were financially independent and inherited their mother’s house. Why did British colonialism change certain laws around marriage and inheritance and how did these transform family structures as well as ideas of gender and community in South Asia? Kinship, or how people are related to each other, has been an important way of learning about them and their culture. The categories some of us might have long considered “natural” such as gendered identities, patriarchal norms, social hierarchies, and even political systems, have revealed, especially when considered in light of other cultural systems, as constructed. So when discussing the Nair kinship system or hijra understandings of identity and community, for example, we will explore the role of religion and colonialism to critique traditionally held Western notions as well as deeply engrained religious beliefs, both centring on the patriarchal family and its associated gender essentialisms. 
A close study of kinship patterns from across the world will throw up historically variable, socially produced, and politically charged issues, which will enable us to critically explore the blinkered beliefs held on race, caste, and gender. After briefly situating the anthropological debates on kinship, gender, relatedness, caste, and community, this course will introduce a range of contemporary ethnographies to discuss recent socio-legal and political developments and how these end up refashioning today’s societal norms."

title: Caste and Indigeneity Studies: Critical Perspectives from South Asia
description: Varna, jati, kula, caste, tribe – this course begins by unpacking the historical categories, processes, institutions and practices through which social formations in the Indian sub-continent have been described, prescribed, and governed by rulers, elites, empires, governments and other formations of power on the one hand, and experienced by subjects on the other. Drawing on original texts, scholarly writings, discursive cultural production and social movements, we attempt to unravel how the study of, and response to, social organization in the Indian context generates often contradictory understandings of caste as social fact, experience of cultural identity, social imaginary, a fluid and potentially mobilizable social category, an instrument of power and domination, and dehumanizing technology of subjugation, humiliation, oppression and violence. The course attempts to trace the trajectory of epistemic understandings of caste from colonial understandings of social stratification to critical caste and technology studies, and their critical potential for interrogating the complex socio-economic, political, cultural and religious institutions and processes through which modern Indian society continues to reinscribe caste as an everyday social experience for over a billion people on the planet. Through the arc of the course, we will engage with the troubled ontological implications of social organization in Indian society, which tethers knowledge of self and other through lived experience while perpetuating forms of epistemic, infrastructural and arbitrary violence on historically oppressed and marginalized sections of society.

title: Place and Space in Culture
description:
This course explores Place, and its co-relate Space, as inspiration for poesis, conceptual category, and line of inquiry in investigating humans and non-human social relations and lived
experience. How have humans construed Place in their relationship with their environments, and with each other? How have they responded to, interacted with and shaped place in action
and imagination? How does the experience of place shape notions of self and other, and produce forms of social and political action? How do the body and the senses become
incorporated in producing particular experiences of Place? How do we perceive and make sense of built environments, and nature as distinctive categories of place-based experience?
We will follow poets, philosophers, historians, and anthropologists as they engage and respond to place worlds, across time and space. We explore three conceptualizations of Place and Space here, from poetics, phenomenology and Marxist social theory as ways to attend to humans in place and on the move.

title: Capitalism: Essential Readings
description: This course familiarizes students with diverse classical and critical perspectives to capitalism. We will explore key thinkers and draw connections with contemporary debates around the various manifestations of capitalist relations.

title: The Urban Process
description:
This course examines ‘the urban’ as a field of inquiry and theorization from a relational perspective.
The course discusses key thinkers and debates in urban studies and analyses from the industrial
period, particularly from the mid-19th century, to the contemporary period. The course will enable

interdisciplinary thinking regarding urban phenomena, including urban form, social relations and
theorization. We will discuss key theoretical insights and shifts in understanding urban relations by
situating social contexts historically. The course materials will further disrupt the binary silos of
urban and rural studies by interrogating the co-constitution of the urban and the rural, albeit with an
emphasis on forms of urban life. A field trip will further provide first hand experience of the rural-
urban continuum, and facilitate the theorization of the distinctions therein.

title: Social Conflict and Religious Division: Exploring Contemporary India
description:
How do food practices and taboos perpetuate caste,
racial, and religious divisions in India? In what ways has forced assimilation impacted the cultural and political autonomy of Indigenous communities? What gendered insights emerge from the lived experiences of half-widows in Kashmir in the context of prolonged conflict? Can religious violence be understood as a catalyst for political mobilization and state consolidation in contemporary India?
How does religious polarization shape diasporic politics? Does popular culture in India sustain majoritarian worldviews and contribute to their normalization? To what extent does digital media amplify political and social divisions? How does Bollywood cinema, as a popular culture, intensify stereotypes and othering? This course critically interrogates key questions at the intersection of politics, history, society, and culture in contemporary India. Structured around three interrelated units, Unframing India, Politics of Popular Culture and India in Cinema, the course traces the historical and political trajectories that have shaped the nation’s cultural and ideological formation.

title: Sociology and STS through Science Fiction
description:
Sociology and STS Through Science Fiction” treats speculative cinema and short fiction as the basis for a comparative ethnography of power. Across eleven weeks, the course follows a curated sequence of science fiction films (Gattaca, Arrival, Akira, Blade Runner, Snowpiercer, Equilibrium, The Matrix, District 9, Sorry to Bother You, Brazil) alongside anti-caste and South Asian speculative writing drawn primarily from The Blaft Book of Anti-Caste SF and The Gollancz Book of South Asian Science Fiction, Volume 2.
