These materials provide grounded, situated imaginaries of genetic citizenship, infrastructural domination, border regimes, racial capitalism, bureaucratic violence, and abolitionist horizons that are often only abstractly theorized in canonical social theory. Students thus learn to read films/speculative narratives as sites where states, markets, and technical systems are made visible: how metrics fabricate “valid” and “invalid” lives; how simulations and media infrastructures encode ideology; how camps, checkpoints, databases, and documents enact caste/race, gender, and class hierarchies; how insurgent publics, underground networks, and counter-futures contest these arrangements. Each weekly module pairs one film with a small cluster of short fiction and an average of 60-70 pages of sociology, anthropology, and STS (e.g. Benjamin, Browne, Hall, Fraser, Ahmed, Bhattacharyya, Robinson, Suchman, Das & Poole, Gupta), training students to mobilize concepts such as biopolitics,
infrastructures, racial capitalism, social reproduction, surveillance, and ontological
politics through close formal analysis rather than decontextualized summary.

title: Humiliation: Power, Subjectivity, and Social Life
description: This course explores humiliation as both an intimate emotion and a powerful social force. Drawing on philosophy, psychoanalysis, ethnography, military and conflict studies, caste/race scholarship, and literature—with South Asia as a comparative anchor—students examine humiliation as a moral violation, psychological injury, tool of governance, structural condition, and literary motif. The course equips students with theoretical insight, ethnographic sensitivity, and ethical reflexivity while engaging with challenging histories and lived experiences.

title: Social Media & Society
description:
Social Media & Society" examines digital platforms as central institutions of contemporary social life. Rather than treating social media as a discrete technological domain, the course conceptualizes platforms as sociotechnical
infrastructures that mediate visibility, labor, identity, governance, and inequality at scale. The course begins by analyzing the infrastructural and classificatory foundations of social networking systems before progressing to the forms of work, algorithmic reasoning, and public-making that they enable. Subsequent modules address the intensification of harm—misogyny, racism, casteism, extremism—as well as the emergence of illicit economies, trauma narratives, and new forms of digital care. The syllabus combines foundational scholarship in Sociology, STS, and Media Studies with recent qualitative and theoretical studies from diverse global contexts.
Across these readings, students engage with influencers, platform workers, nationalist publics, disability activists, sex workers, extremist groups, and content moderators—each case illustrating how platform architectures and governance regimes shape social practices and political possibilities. By the end of this course, students will be able to articulate how social media systems structure contemporary social life and to critically assess the political, ethical, and epistemic implications of their design and governance.

title: Global Mobilities: Borders, Ecology, and Development
description:
This course offers readings to understand the dynamics of human mobility across the globe, with a particular focus on borders, ecological change, and development-induced displacement. Drawing on interdisciplinary studies, the course is a sociological and anthropological exploration of mobility, whether by force, necessity, or aspiration, in a world increasingly shaped by border security, ecological crises, geopolitical conflicts, and economic development initiatives. One major theme will be the changing nature of borders and how state policies, international regimes, and border technologies mediate mobility, often creating new forms of exclusion and precarity. The second major focus of the course will address ecological displacement—mobility triggered by climate change, environmental degradation, and natural disasters. Students will examine how environmental stressors intersect with existing vulnerabilities, including race, class, gender, and indigeneity, creating complex patterns of mobility and immobility. The third focus will be on development-induced displacement: the forced relocation of communities due to infrastructure projects, urban expansion, resource extraction, and conservation initiatives. Students will analyse the underlying logics of such displacement, often justified by narratives of progress or national interest, and the uneven power relations that shape who gets displaced, who benefits, and who is left behind.

The course, though borrowing readings from all disciplines, is grounded in anthropology as it connects the everyday experience of migration from across the world with questions of power. These are just some of the questions we will ask ourselves throughout the course as students will be encouraged to reflect on the assumptions and concepts that underlie our often strongly held beliefs about migration.

title: Gender, Masculinity and the Languages of Grief
description: This course explores grief as a political emotion and examines how gender is constituted in response to loss. Using a range of texts that draw upon literature, psychoanalysis, and anthropology—including traditions of lament and dirges across cultures, as well as ancient and modern literature on grief, and explorations of gendered modes of grief historically available to men and women—it offers insights into how men and women are socially expected to process loss and perform mourning. The course invites reflection on how such performances, both in everyday and eventful contexts, whether aligned with or at variance with social expectations, enable the articulation of divergent political imaginaries and possible futures that could potentially disrupt the dominant order of things.

title: Quantitative Research Methods in Humanities and Social Sciences
description: This course will introduce students to research methods in the humanities and social sciences. This is designed as a foundational course for those interested in research in the humanities and social sciences. It is meant to familiarize students with a broad range of methods and analytical tools commonly employed in research in these fields.

title: Religion and Society in South Asia
description:
This course is about the study of Religion with a particular focus on South Asian religions (Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, Zorastrianism, Christianity, Islam, and Sikhism), as they have been studied anthropologically, historically and politically – as daily beliefs and practices, and in relation to wider South Asian culture, history and politics. This course will provide both a grounded study of religious practices and religions in Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sikkim, Sri Lanka as well as a postcolonial critique of the study of religions and nationalism in the South Asian realm.
The course will explore why the transformation of the public sphere in South Asia shows the increasing importance of religious movements, and of the political use of religious symbolism in new communication technologies. One of the most important trends in the present era is the attempt to create a homogenous religious community, not only within the national territorial space, but also in a transnational space. If such attempts offer a sense of identity for communities, it also offers a brutal confrontation with “the Other,” however defined. The violent conflicts between Hindus and Muslims, between “high” castes and Dalits, between Shi’as and Sunnis, between Buddhists and Hindus, Buddhists and Muslims are sad reminders of a growing confrontation which is not only regional, but increasingly global.
This course will therefore combine historical awareness, conceptual acuity, spatial mobility. This will lead us to an analysis of the effects of imperial interactions, state formation and how these provide a crucial perspective for the unravelling of the multiple transformations of religion, religious nationalisms, the global framework of religious fraternities, and what informs the choice of certain identities over others.

title: The Political Sociology of Globalization
description: This course provides a critical examination of globalization and its multifaceted impacts across nation-states, analysing the expanding networks that continuously reshape the contemporary world, with particular attention to structural asymmetries between the Global North and Global South. It situates globalization within historical, economic, and cultural contexts while engaging with social movements and practices emerging from transnational flows of capital, people, and ideas. The course is structured into three units. Unit 1 introduces foundational debates and conceptual frameworks in the political economy of globalization, tracing its historical evolution through key readings including Saskia Sassen, Amartya Sen, Anthony Giddens, A.G. Frank, Scholte etc. Unit 2 focuses on Indian society, examining the intersections of culture, religion, and class, drawing on the scholarship of Surinder Jodhka, Sanjay Srivastava, and others. Unit 3 explores international migration and digital media as both outcomes and drivers of globalization, engaging with Arjun Appadurai’s concept of “scapes” alongside the work of Koen Leurs, Karim H. Karim etc  to analyse diasporic formations, cultural flows, and the mediascape in shaping transnational identities and publics. The course concludes with a fieldwork-based research project, enabling participants to apply theoretical frameworks to empirical inquiry and gain hands-on experience in analysing the dynamics of globalization in contemporary contexts.
